To understand this, we propose that effective and learnable Long CoT trajectories feature stable molecular-like structures in unified view, which are formed by three interaction types: Deep-Reasoning (covalent-like), Self-Reflection (hydrogen-bond-like), and Self-Exploration (van der Waals-like). Analysis of distilled trajectories reveals these structures emerge from Long CoT fine-tuning, not keyword imitation. We introduce Effective Semantic Isomers and show that only bonds promoting fast entropy convergence support stable Long CoT learning, while structural competition impairs training. Drawing on these findings, we present Mole-Syn, a distribution-transfer-graph method that guides synthesis of effective Long CoT structures, boosting performance and RL stability across benchmarks. 14 15 [{qgchen,car}@ir.hit.edu.cn](https://arxiv.org/html/2601.06002v2/%7Bqgchen,car%7D@ir.hit.edu.cn), [duyantao@bytedance.com](https://arxiv.org/html/2601.06002v2/duyantao@bytedance.com),[lbqin@csu.edu.cn](https://arxiv.org/html/2601.06002v2/lbqin@csu.edu.cn) 16 17 ![Refer to caption](https://arxiv.org/html/2601.06002v2/x1.png) 18 19 Figure 1: The hypothesis that stable molecular structure in Long CoT arises from three key “chemical” bonds. 20 21 ## 1 Introduction 22 23 Recently, large language models (LLMs) have excelled on diverse reasoning tasks via explicit chain-of-thought (CoT) rationales [^1] [^2] [^3] [^4]. Yet, they struggle to cold-start from instruction-tuned or base models into Long CoT models requiring extended multi-step reasoning [^5] [^6]. Notably, [^7] shows that humans generate Long CoT rationales without imitating DeepSeek-R1 [^8]. Our preliminary studies reveal that standard supervised fine-tuning and distillation from human or Instruction LLM rationales (using randomly sampled Long CoT examples) fail to reliably instill these skills in LLMs. Models often lose coherence over long trajectories or fail to transfer patterns to novel tasks. This prompts a key question: 24 25 > How do Large Language Models learn and represent effective Long Chain-of-Thought? 26 27 ![Refer to caption](https://arxiv.org/html/2601.06002v2/x2.png) 28 29 Figure 2: Comparison of prior chain- or tree-like structures and our molecular structure. Reasoning starts from Mole. 0, uses deep reasoning on strongly related structures, then employs self-exploration for new logic in Mole. 1. When meet errors, reasoning utilize self-reflection to guide chain to optimized Mole. 0 +. 30 31 To explain this, we posit that they acquire the organization of reasoning trajectories. As shown in Figure 2, prior studies model these as *logic nodes* in sequences or trees of steps. Yet, our analysis of Long CoT across strong reasoning models reveals a stable distribution of three core behaviors across tasks and architectures: Deep-Reasoning, Self-Reflection, and Self-Exploration [^5], which node-centric views fail to capture. 32 33 This finding triggers a molecular-inspired, distributional view: we model behavior-labeled *logic edges* as interaction bonds and examine how their global molecular-like structure ensures long-horizon reasoning stability. Specifically, Deep-Reasoning forms dense local clusters of coupled deductions, like covalent bonds; Self-Reflection creates long-range corrective links to prior steps, like hydrogen bonds; and Self-Exploration forges weak bridges between distant clusters, like van der Waals forces. Thus, high-quality Long CoT arises from the stable composition and arrangement of these bond types, guiding effective learning 1. 34 35 In this framework, we define semantic isomers as Long CoT trajectories that solve the same tasks and visit similar semantic regions but differ in behavior distributions and transitions. We demonstrate that multiple near-optimal semantic isomers exist per task family, but mixing stable isomers from different strong teachers destabilizes learning, degrading performance and behavior distributions despite matched token statistics. This structurally explains why combining heterogeneous Long CoT traces often fails, beyond token-level distillation. 36 37 Building on this perspective, we propose Mole-Syn, a structure-aware synthesis framework that first estimates a behavior transition graph from strong reasoning models and then transfers only this behavioral structure to cheaper instruction LLMs via controlled trajectory synthesis, instead of directly copying teacher outputs. This decouples structural transfer from model-specific surface form, enables the generation of Long CoT data that match target behavior distributions from scratch, and yields consistent gains in both Long CoT performance and RL stability across six benchmarks. 38 39 After that, we analyze the shaping function of each bond in the Long CoT structure. Deep Reasoning bonds encode core logical flow, Self-Reflection bonds support folding pathways to previous steps, and Self-Exploration bonds reinforce long-range consistency checks, enabling targeted bond distributions. Moreover, we discuss why a deteriorated molecular structure is hard to restore, which helps explain how private LLMs protect Long CoT structures from distillation-based imitation. Methods such as summarization and reasoning compression can disrupt Long CoT structure, limiting unauthorized replication of internal reasoning processes. 40 41 In summary, our contributions are as follows: 42 43 - We model Long CoT as a molecular structure with 3 bonds: deep-reasoning (covalent), self-reflection (hydrogen-bond), and self-exploration (van der Waals), to understand its effective learning. 44 - We identify effective Semantic Isomers for Long CoT learning, where only entropy-convergent bonds enable stable learning, while competing structures destabilize learning. 45 - We introduce Mole-Syn, which uses distribution-transfer graphs to synthesize these structures, improving Long CoT and stabilizing RL across 6 benchmarks. 46 47 ## 2 Preliminary: Cold-start LLMs for Long Chain-of-Thought 48 49 First, we validate whether LLMs exhibit valid Long CoT trajectories suitable for Long CoT learning. We investigate three data sources: distillation from strong reasoning LLMs, distillation from weak instruction LLMs with in-context learning (ICL), and fine-tuning on human reasoning traces. 50 51 ![Refer to caption](https://arxiv.org/html/2601.06002v2/x3.png) 52 53 Figure 3: The failure of distillation from weak instruction LLMs with ICL and Human-annotated reasoning traces to acquire Long CoT structures, compared to successful distillation from strong reasoning LLMs. See Appendix Figure 15 for the full result. 54 55 ![Refer to caption](https://arxiv.org/html/2601.06002v2/x4.png) 56 57 Figure 4: Performance comparison between human-annotated reasoning traces ( + Human Distill Data ) and R1 distilled reasoning traces ( + R1 Distill Data ). 58 59 ##### Only distillation from strong reasoning LLMs works. 60 61 To identify effective data sources, we curated a synthetic set of reasoning traces from three sources. As shown in Figure 3, only distillation from strong reasoning LLMs enables target models to learn and retain Long CoT structure, improving performance on benchmarks requiring extended reasoning. These results indicate that only high-quality traces reliably support both learning and use of Long CoT structures. 62 63 ##### Distillation from randomly selected ICL by weak instruct LLMs does not work. 64 65 Instruction LLMs without explicit reasoning training lag behind reasoning-specialized models. We test whether LLMs can acquire Long CoT structure by distilling from an instruction LLM using randomly selected ICL demonstrations that emulate Long CoT reasoning. As shown in Figure 3, performance drops sharply. Instruction LLMs can only mimic short CoT traces ($\thicksim$ 6–8 steps) and fail to extend exploration while preserving intermediate steps and trace coherence. This degradation indicates a limitation of ICL-based distillation rather than robust long-chain imitation. 66 67 ##### Even human-annotated Long-CoT-like traces fail. 68 69 Inspired by [^7], we test whether human step-by-step solutions can induce long CoT. We collect human solutions for complex reasoning tasks and fine-tune LLMs on them. Figure 4 shows that human-trace training does not reproduce the long-CoT gains from distilling strong reasoning models, suggesting that human solutions aid local problem solving but may not reliably encode abstractions for long-horizon reasoning distributions. 70 71 72 73 ## 3 Hypothesis: Stable “Molecular Structure” in Long CoT 74 75 To understand these phenomena, as shown in Fig. 1 & 2, effective Long CoT connects nodes in logical space through reasoning behaviors, forming a stable macromolecular structure with mutually supportive components from a global perspective. 76 77 We formalize a Long CoT trace as a behavior-directed graph $G=(V,E)$, where each node $v\in V$ represents a reasoning step or edge $s=(u,v)\in E$ is annotated with a behavior type $s\rightarrow b\in\{\mathcal{D},\mathcal{R},\mathcal{E}\}$. For a trace corpus $\mathcal{C}$, we estimate the behavior transition $P_{\mathcal{C}}(b^{\prime}\mid b)$ over consecutive edges and the marginal distribution $\pi_{\mathcal{C}}(b)$. Empirically, strong reasoning teachers produce stable $(P_{\mathcal{C}},\pi_{\mathcal{C}})$ across models and tasks. Specifically, these include the following three major bonds 2: 78 79 ##### Deep Reasoning as Covalent Bonds 80 81 Deep reasoning forms the bone of the thought process, analogous to covalent bonds defining a molecule’s primary chain. It encodes strong logical dependencies (Step A must justify Step B), maintaining direction and continuity; breaking this bone undermines the following steps and destabilizes the answer. By contrast, “Normal Operation” corresponds to stable local bonds within each step, capturing routine computation and direct semantic expression. 82 83 ##### Self-Reflection as Hydrogen Bonds 84 85 Reflection is a key stabilizer. As proteins gain stability when chains fold and form intra-chain hydrogen bonds, reasoning stabilizes when later steps (e.g., Step 100) test, revise, or reinforce earlier premises (e.g., Step 10). These long-range links constrain drift and hallucination, turning a long sequence into a more self-consistent structure. If later checks fail to align with earlier commitments, the reasoning cannot “fold,” indicating a structural logical error. 86 87 ##### Self-Exploration as Van der Waals Forces 88 89 Exploration resembles transient Van der Waals interactions: it supports abductive and inductive moves by enabling low-commitment associations in semantic space, where concepts can drift, combine, and be probed before stronger constraints are enforced. 90 91 ## 4 Verification: Molecular Structure 92 93 ![Refer to caption](https://arxiv.org/html/2601.06002v2/x5.png) 94 95 Figure 5: Transfer graph on three different models. Pearson correlation coefficients across models are all greater than 0.9 (p<0.001), when sampling examples > 2,000, transfer graphs will become stable and get over 0.95 Pearson correlation between different sampling sizes. 96 97 ### 4.1 Stable Bond Distribution in Long CoT 98 99 To address this, we first verify whether effective Long CoT traces show stable, macromolecular-like organization across models and tasks. As shown in Fig. 5, traces from multiple LLMs across diverse tasks yield Pearson correlations exceeding 0.9 (p<0.001) for over 2,000 samples. These transfer graphs stabilize with correlations above 0.95 across sampling sizes. This indicates that effective Long CoT structures rely on robust motifs: different models recover similar reasoning topologies across tasks, whereas simple human simulation or ICL cannot emulate the global bond distribution. 100 101 ### 4.2 SFT actually learns these bond structures rather than keywords. 102 103 For the SFT analysis, we consider Llama-3.1-8B-Base that is pre-trained but not instruction-tuned on Long CoT data; Then, we consider Llama-3.1-8B-Base trained on R1-distilled data as Think-SFT model obtained by supervised fine-tuning enriched with Long CoT traces. 104 105 ![Refer to caption](https://arxiv.org/html/2601.06002v2/x6.png) 106 107 Figure 6: The learned features in Long CoT supervised fine-tuning. 108 109 From a representation-geometry perspective, the sparse auto-encoder analysis shows that Long CoT behavior in the SFT model is concentrated in a small set of discourse-control structures rather than being uniformly distributed across tokens. As shown in Figure 6 (a, b), we train a cross-coder sparse auto-encoder that jointly models hidden states from the base model and the Think-SFT model, and then identify features whose activation on think tokens is at least threefold higher than their average activation rate. Within this highly activated subset, many features are predominantly driven by a few connective keywords, such as “Maybe”, “But / so”, and “Alternatively”, indicating that the SFT process has carved out dedicated latents for managing local hypothesis revision, contrastive moves, and branch selection in long CoT traces. 110 111 Based on previous analyses, we argue that models learn the characteristic reasoning behaviors these keywords represent, not the keywords themselves. Following [^5], we define three categories of Long CoT reasoning behaviors and test this claim using two training datasets derived from QwQ distillation data. In the first, we replace each keyword with one of four alternative variants. In the second, we remove all keywords while preserving the reasoning trajectories. We then fine-tune identical LLMs on each dataset and evaluate their Long CoT reasoning performance. 112 113 As shown in Figure 6 (c), explicit keywords like "wait" accelerate learning but are not essential. Models trained without keywords, or with arbitrary alternatives, achieve comparable reasoning performance given sufficient training, provided the underlying reasoning behaviors remain intact. This reveals a fundamental insight: LLMs internalize reasoning structure of reasoning rather than surface lexical cues. Consequently, training data should prioritize the distribution of reasoning behaviors over specific keyword choices to effectively enhance model reasoning capabilities. 114 115 However, a key open question remains: do these bonds drive Long CoT structure learning, and if so, why do explicit human imitation or random ICL distillation of these markers often fail? 116 117 ![Refer to caption](https://arxiv.org/html/2601.06002v2/x7.png) 118 119 Figure 7: Verification of the “logical folding” structure on embeddings from Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct and t-SNE-based low-dimensional representations from the OpenAI-OSS-120B-generated reasoning process. 120 121 ![Refer to caption](https://arxiv.org/html/2601.06002v2/x8.png) 122 123 Figure 8: Energy levels of different bonds across two distilled data. 124 125 ### 4.3 “Logical Bonding-Folding” Structure 126 127 To test the hypothesis that Long CoT is analogous to macro-molecular folding, as shown in Fig. 7, we analyzed the topology of CoT in a 3D semantic space. Each trajectory edge was classified as reflection, deep reasoning, or exploration, and its geometric properties were quantified. 128 129 ##### Deep-Reasoning stabilizes logical cluster by Covalent Bonding. 130 131 Modeled as covalent bonds, as shown in Fig. 7 (a), deep reasoning bonds mainly increase local connectivity, forming stable subdomains. After deep reasoning, 72.56% of steps remained within a group distance of less than 3 in the semantic space (generally, group-group distance $>$ 5.6). 132 133 ##### Self-Reflection drives strong folding to previous steps by Hydrogen Bonding. 134 135 Analogous to hydrogen bonds, as shown in Fig. 7 (b), self-reflection transitions fold later steps back onto earlier, semantically similar clusters rather than extending the chain linearly. Quantitatively, 81.72% of reflection steps reconnected to a previously formed cluster with high semantic similarity. 136 137 ##### Self-Exploration gently links different long-distance clusters by Van der Waals Forces. 138 139 In contrast to local stabilization (Fig. 7 (c)), exploration transitions act as loose links between otherwise separated clusters. They show much larger step-to-step distances, with an average trajectory length of 5.32 in the 3D t-SNE projection. Together, these results suggest that effective Long CoT reasoning is not a simple linear chain; instead, it forms a folded, domain-structured topology consistent with the “logical folding” hypothesis. 140 141 ### 4.4 Attention ⇔\\Leftrightarrow Energy Level of Bonds 142 143 In physical chemistry, the behavior probability with energy level $E_{i}$ at temperature $T$ follows the Boltzmann distribution: 144 145 $$ 146 P(\text{state}_{i})=\frac{\exp\!\big(-E_{i}/k_{B}T\big)}{\sum_{j}{\exp\!\big(-E_{j}/k_{B}T\big)}}. 147 $$ 148 149 In Transformers, the attention weight $\alpha_{ij}$ of the $i$ -th token to the $j$ -th token is: 150 151 $$ 152 \alpha_{ij}=\frac{\exp\!\big(q_{i}\cdot k_{j}/\sqrt{d_{k}}\big)}{\sum_{l}\exp\!\big(q_{i}\cdot k_{l}/\sqrt{d_{k}}\big)}. 153 $$ 154 155 The correspondence follows by defining attention energy $(E)$ $\leftrightarrow$ $(-q\cdot k)$, implies lower $E_{ij}$ and thus higher behavior probability. 156 157 Formally, our analysis only relies on the observation that attention weights form a Gibbs–Boltzmann distribution over negative logits. We therefore use the term “energy” to denote reparameterized logits and study how their expectations differ across behavior types. 158 159 | Model | GSM8K | MATH-500 | AIME2024 | AIME2025 | AMC2023 | OlympiadBench | AVG | 160 | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | 161 | LLaMA-3.1-8B-Base [^9] | 7.58 | 3.20 | 0.00 | 0.00 | 4.22 | 1.19 | 2.70 | 162 | + 20K R1-Distill-Data | 63.38 | 30.60 | 0.21 | 0.42 | 14.22 | 8.30 | 19.52 | 163 | + 20K OSS-Distill-Data | 75.89 | 54.20 | 4.38 | 6.46 | 37.34 | 23.85 | 33.69 | 164 | + 20K QwQ-Distill-Data | 64.53 | 32.20 | 2.92 | 0.42 | 16.72 | 8.89 | 20.95 | 165 | Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct [^9] | 75.89 | 35.20 | 4.17 | 1.04 | 23.59 | 12.00 | 25.32 | 166 | + 20K R1-Distill-Data | 79.91 | 60.60 | 2.50 | 3.88 | 33.13 | 23.85 | 33.98 | 167 | + 20K OSS-Distill-Data | 79.00 | 60.80 | 10.83 | 7.71 | 47.03 | 30.22 | 39.27 | 168 | + 20K QwQ-Distill-Data | 82.41 | 60.80 | 4.38 | 8.33 | 32.97 | 25.48 | 35.73 | 169 170 Table 1: Results across six benchmarks. Full results are reported in Table 5 in the Appendix. 171 172 We then compare attention energy across Long CoT transition types. Fig. 8 shows distinct distributions for deep reasoning, reflection, and exploration. Deep reasoning exhibits the largest effective chemical-bond energy $D_{d}$. Reflection is intermediate, whereas exploration shows the weakest effective bond energy. This ordering and the relative proportions are consistent across models, supporting the hypothesis that a bond-like mechanism broadly links these reasoning behaviors. 173 174 175 176 ## 5 Feature: Effective Semantic Isomers 177 178 We now shift to examine the failure of surficial distillation: similar conceptual atoms can be linked by different bonds, producing completely different reasoning chains. We call these as Semantic Isomers. Mathematically, a semantic isomer of $\mathcal{D}$ is any $\mathcal{D}^{\prime}$ whose $(P_{\mathcal{D}^{\prime}},\pi_{\mathcal{D}^{\prime}})$ lies near $(P_{\mathcal{D}},\pi_{\mathcal{D}})$ under a suitable divergence $D(\cdot\,\|\,\cdot)$. Then, we will analyze how they form, are learned, and sometimes destabilize in Long CoT. 179 180 ### 5.1 Bond structure of Semantic Isomers is the key to Long-CoT learning 181 182 ##### Well-structured Semantic Isomers can be effective for Long-CoT learning. 183 184 To assess whether well-structured Semantic Isomers can enhance Long-CoT learning, we constructed a Long CoT dataset by distilling from advanced reasoning LLMs. As shown in Table 1, models exhibit consistent performance gains when trained on these variants (distribution correlation $\thicksim$ 0.9). This suggests that, within a certain range, multiple effective “allotropic” variants of reasoning keys can exist. 185 186 ##### The model has multiple effective Semantic Isomers, and slight differences can significantly affect the results. 187 188 As shown in Table 1, the structural correlation between R1- and OSS-derived chains can reach 0.95, yet for some models performance with R1-based chains drops by more than 10%. This gap indicates the presence of multiple near-optimal Semantic Isomers that are nonetheless fragile, where small changes in the distribution can cause large performance losses. 189 190 ![Refer to caption](https://arxiv.org/html/2601.06002v2/x9.png) 191 192 Figure 9: The performance of LLama-3.1-8B-Instruction under three different distillation setups from ICL-augmented Qwen2.5-32B. 193 194 ##### Simulating effective Semantic Isomer structures is the key to ICL distillation. 195 196 We analyze three ICL setups to simulate Long CoT chains by Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct: demonstrations chosen at random; demonstrations with closely aligned reasoning-key distributions (correlation $\thicksim$ 0.9); and demonstrations with clearly mismatched distributions (correlation $<0.8$). As shown in Fig. 9, substantial performance gains emerge only when demonstrations are constructed to match a specific target distribution of reasoning keys, thereby yielding an appropriate “allotrope” of that distribution. 197 198 ![Refer to caption](https://arxiv.org/html/2601.06002v2/x10.png) 199 200 Figure 10: Information flow analysis for humans and reasoning models.

1	# X 上的 Tropical Value：“Why Palantir Makes New Hires Read a Theater Improvisation Book ” / X
2	
3	https://x.com/tropicalvalue/status/2057859376497701334?s=20
4	
5	Keith Johnstone's Impro is on Palantir's onboarding reading list. It has nothing to do with software, national security, or AI. That's the point.
6	
7	The book is about improvisational theater. Its author, Keith Johnstone, spent decades teaching actors how to stop blocking and start creating. The lessons he extracted along the way — about status, spontaneity, and what education does to raw talent — are among the most precise diagnostics of organizational behavior I've read. [$PLTR](https://x.com/search?q=%24PLTR&src=cashtag_click) clearly agrees.
8	
9	Reading it through the lens of company building, the message is uncomfortable: most of what makes a "good candidate" on paper is exactly what makes someone difficult to work with in practice.
10	
11	**The talent problem isn't what you think**
12	
13	Johnstone's most counterintuitive observation is that talent is not normally distributed the way intelligence is. "Intelligence is proportional to population, but talent appears not to be related to population numbers." You can't recruit for it at scale using standard proxies.
14	
15	Worse, formal education actively suppresses it. "The dullness was not an inevitable consequence of age, but of education." The students most damaged by this process, the ones hardest to unlock, are not the failures. They are "the star performers at bad high schools. Instead of learning how to be warm and spontaneous and giving, they've become armoured and superficial, calculating and self-obsessed."
16	
17	This is a direct challenge to every credential-driven recruiting process in Silicon Valley. The polished candidate who knows how to perform competence is often the one least capable of actual creative output. The armor is the problem. "To actually create something means going against one's education."
18	
19	What Palantir actually screens for is whether someone has preserved the imaginative responsiveness that education systematically trains out. "I began to think of children not as immature adults, but of adults as atrophied children."
20	
21	**Yes-sayers vs. blockers**
22	
23	The most operationally useful framework in the book is the binary between acceptors and blockers.
24	
25	"Those who say 'Yes' are rewarded by the adventures they have, and those who say 'No' are rewarded by the safety they attain."
26	
27	In improvisation, blockers kill scenes. In organizations, they kill momentum. Johnstone's observation is that blocking is a skill. "Bad improvisers block action, often with a high degree of skill. Good improvisers develop action." High-status players block because they're afraid of being humiliated. They'd rather kill the idea than be seen to fail with it.
28	
29	This maps cleanly onto organizational dysfunction. The person who says "that won't work" three seconds after you propose something is not being rigorous, they are most likely just protecting their status. The person who says "yes, and—" and develops the action is the one you want in the room.
30	
31	Palantir's deployment model — putting engineers directly inside customer organizations, often in chaotic, ambiguous situations — selects hard for acceptors. You cannot be a blocker in that environment. There's no script for FDEs.
32	
33	**Status is the operating system**
34	
35	The chapter on status dynamics is the sharpest management reading I've encountered outside of explicit leadership literature. The core insight: "Things said are not as important as the status played."
36	
37	Every interaction in an organization is a status transaction. Most people are running these transactions unconsciously and inconsistently. A manager who can read them — and who understands that high-status security manifests as relaxation, not aggression — has a meaningful edge.
38	
39	"When the highest-status person feels most secure he will be the most relaxed person." The corollary is that leaders who micro-manage, dominate airtime, or punish failure publicly are broadcasting insecurity, not authority. The status play undermines itself.
40	
41	The book's "ten golden rules for people who are Number 1" are worth reading twice. Rule six stands out: "You must reward your immediate subordinates by permitting them to enjoy the benefits of their ranks." Retention is a status problem before it's a compensation problem.
42	
43	**What good leadership looks like**
44	
45	Johnstone's model of the teacher (which translates directly to the manager) is radically non-hierarchical in one specific way: he accepts blame for failure as a tool for liberating performance. "I play low status, and I will explain that if the students fail they are to blame me." By removing the threat of personal failure from the learner, you remove the defense mechanism that suppresses their best output.
46	
47	The parallel in team management is creating an environment where people's first instinct is execution rather than self-protection. That requires the leader to absorb downside risk publicly — to be the one who falls on the sword when an experiment doesn't work. Most leaders do the opposite.
48	
49	The goal, as Johnstone frames it, is helping people "abandon control while at the same time they exercise control." That is the highest-leverage thing a manager can do: build enough safety that the team stops blocking themselves.
50	
51	**The real reason it's on the reading list**
52	
53	Palantir is not a normal software company and it has never pretended to be. The things it needs from its people — comfort with ambiguity, the ability to walk into a hostile room and read what's actually happening, the willingness to develop action in real time without a playbook — are not teachable via technical onboarding.
54	
55	Impro is on the list because it names the underlying capabilities more precisely than any management book does, and because it forces a reckoning with a hard truth: the selection and development of genuinely creative, high-agency people requires dismantling the exact habits that made them look attractive on paper in the first place.
56	
57	"The real avant-garde are not imitating what other people are doing, or what they did forty years ago, they're solving the problems that need solving."
58	
59	That's the job description. The book explains why it's hard to hire for it.

61	第一步，很多MCN出身的操盘手会告诉你立人设、找对标。我认为这不对，包装出来的人设是持续输出的阻力。
62	
63	能成为创始人的人天生不缺故事与愿力、你不需要人设，你需要的只是一些方法。
64	
65	## 创始人品牌的三维坐标系
66	
67	对你的内容建立一个坐标系，就像高中学立体几何一样
68	
69	**X轴：你是谁**
70	
71	喜欢上一个人比喜欢上一个品牌容易一千倍。
72	
73	这个坐标轴承载了创始人的故事，经历，生活，价值观。你的用户比起想了解你的产品，更想知道的是：是谁在做，他为什么做，他相信什么。
74	
75	比如华人老板的硅谷生活、比如九死一生的创业经历、比如瞬间的人生感悟。这些内容无法对标，他们是独一无二的。
76	
77	**Y轴：你的产品**
78	
79	这个坐标轴要讲清楚你的交付，你的产品是什么、功能、优势、更新迭代、愿景。创始人品牌是为交付服务的，
80	
81	比如你做的是一款AI应用，你可以介绍产品价值，记录产品更新，用户的实际使用案例。再比如你做的是一项服务，可以记录方法论、客户案例。
82	
83	**Z轴：行业信息差**
84	
85	作为在所在行业深耕过几年的创始人，或多或少都有对行业的独特见解。这就是信息差：你知道，而离行业中心远的人不知道。
86	
87	对趋势的判断、超出平均水平的讲解，以及独特的视角，对行业热点的观点。这些往往是最容易带来好看的数据的。
88	
89	比如 AI 应用开发者可以讨论新技术范式，币圈创始人可以漫谈行业沉浮，创投圈的人可以分析投融资现状。无需担心自己的洞察不够深。在满是 AI 的信息流中，有业内活人背书的信息最值钱。
90	
91	## 内容不能偏离坐标系
92	
93	建立了创始人品牌的三维坐标系后，你的所有内容都可以当做一个向量放在坐标系内。内容与坐标轴越相关，对应的数值越大。
94	
95	如果该向量的模，也就是距离原点的长度很长，那它起码从选题的角度是一条好内容。
96	
97	举个例子：
98	
99	我现在聚焦的业务是 AI 产品增长与创始人 IP，那我这篇内容则与行业信息高度相关，如果我下文再谈及产品交付，那与我的产品也有一定的相关性，但这篇文章我不想聊我的经历，那与我是谁的相关性就是0。
100	
101	因此，我这篇内容的系数可能是（ 0、60、80），长度为 100。那这就是一篇好内容。
102	
103	再比如我的置顶推文，讲了我从大学学计算机到炒币赚钱的故事，以及对行业的判断，那它的系数用 AI 测了一下就是（94、6、72），长度为 118.56。那么这也是一篇好内容。
104	
105	![图像](https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HIWUu0TbwAAEavU?format=jpg&name=large)
106	
107	用顶顶推文的三维坐标
108	
109	如果举个反面例子，我之前经常喜欢喊单、晒炒币收益。这与我是谁、我的产品、行业信息差均不相关。那它对我的账号来说就是噪音。
110	
111	## 用 AI 搭建内容体系
112	
113	AI 从来不是帮你写内容的工具，而是帮你搭建内容体系的工具。
114	
115	**一、帮你搭建创始人品牌的三维坐标**
116	
117	AI 可以帮你将你在互联网上的语料拆分，映射到对应的三个坐标轴上，保存为 .md 文件。
118	
119	这样你的内容会被提炼到三个文件里，分别是：你是谁；你的产品；行业信息差。
120	
121	比如我把我过去的一篇文章《AI 增长的传教理论》喂给 Codex，它可以帮我从三个维度提炼，由我选择是否存入。没错，和前段时间爆火的 Eiys 很像。
122	
123	![图像](https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HIWVCnoawAAi41J?format=jpg&name=large)
124	
125	三个维度提炼内容
126	
127	**二、帮你创建创始人品牌的语料库**
128	
129	让 AI 更懂你、更像你，一直是 AI 生成内容的难题。在我的 Obsidian 里密密麻麻存了上千条我在互联网上留下的痕迹。但我想让 AI 基于我的语料替我写内容时，感觉如下：
130	
131	![图像](https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HIWV1robgAAbGyE?format=jpg&name=large)
132	
133	开塞露
134	
135	AI 经常会莫名其妙地将我过去提到的毫不相关的往事拿出来提一嘴，就像在说：“看我多懂你，连这都知道”
136	
137	而当你用这个三维坐标系去保存记忆，生成的内容就不会那么莫名其妙。让 AI 的记忆完全围绕你的创始人品牌保存。当三个文件都达到百分之百，你的 AI 就真正懂你的品牌了。
138	
139	![图像](https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HIWV8XQaEAAjdfs?format=jpg&name=large)
140	
141	Memory 积累进度
142	
143	**三、检验你的内容相关度**
144	
145	如何避免东一榔头西一棒槌地发内容，最好的办法就是直接将内容放到三维坐标系里检验。
146	
147	就像我这篇《如何讲好一个故事》，放在坐标系里，它会根据文章本身内容以及 Memory 中的数据检验相关性。
148	
149	![图像](https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HIWWF90a0AAWuxn?format=jpg&name=large)
150	
151	检验相关性
152	
153	如果内容检测完发现处在红色区域，也就是说你这篇内容和创始人品牌关系不大，那就要慎重考虑要不要发。
154	
155	**四、AI 替你写内容**
156	
157	我相信不是每一个创始人都对做内容如此热爱，很多人的诉求的一定是解放双手，完全交给 AI。
158	
159	AI 生成的内容永远是中庸且缺少人味的，但你如果给了它足够长的上下文，让它更懂你后，它的产出也勉强可用，起码会比你找一个内容实习生要好。
160	
161	方法是当你交给 AI 一个写作任务时，让 AI 在三维坐标系里自行迭代，比如设定一个标准，让 AI 迭代到分数高于 120 分再输出。
162	
163	另一个指标是 AI 有多了解你的创始人品牌。当它足够懂你，它才能输出像你的内容。变成一个可量化的指标，就是“可信度”，这取决于你在三个文件里累积了多少 memory。
164	
165	![图像](https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HIWWO0raMAASyn3?format=jpg&name=large)
166	
167	AI生成内容
168	
169	比如说我让他写一个“ 就罗永浩加入 Twitter 这个事件写一篇 500 字的文案”
170	
171	AI 生成的内容分数达到 130，但可信度为 4，说明它还是不够懂我。
172	
173	最后为了方便，我把这套流程打包成 Skill 放在 GitHub 上了。我称之为Founder Brand 1.0 版本，后续还会有 2.0、3.0。 GitHub：[https://github.com/MaxJiang103/founder-brand.git](https://github.com/MaxJiang103/founder-brand.git)
174	
175	**最后的最后：创始人品牌不只是一个账号，而是围绕创始人本人的增长内容体系。**
176	
177	**欢迎拥有有趣灵魂的创始人来交流内容，也欢迎拥有产品 sense 的天才来一起让它更好玩。**
178	
179	**让好的产品被看见，让优秀的人被看见，这是有趣的事。**

1	# 给人文工作者的 AI 使用指南
2	
3	https://x.com/HanyangWang/status/2029362155607474359?s=20
4	
5	![图像](https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HCkrCVba4AAQ92r?format=jpg&name=large)
6	
7	人文工作者没有创造世界变化，但他们却在承受世界变化。
8	
9	有的时候我感觉，那些卖人工智能教程的号总是把 AI 当成一种魔法：给你一个神奇的 prompt，你就能做任何事儿。现实当然不是这样。过去的一段时间里，因为创立了 [FUNES](https://funes.world/), 我们必须每天大量的通过 AI 进行生产。加之还有[《蜉蝣天地》](https://www.youtube.com/@FuyoutiandiMeanders)、我自己的写作等内容生产，光靠人力已经不够了。所以我们大量的尝试如何使用 AI 辅助我们的内容市场与人文学科研究工作。
10	
11	后来公司有新同事入职，我就做了个简单的 Keynote。又一次得到的贾行家老师听说后，就邀请我去做个分享。我和合伙人可达给这个分享起名《给人文工作者的 AI 使用指南》。当时是纯私下的分享，主要是一些大方向上的原则。后来又做过几次，逐渐扩充。
12	
13	不过这个分享一直没公开做过，正好今年和重轻启动了[《诗梳风》](https://shishufeng.com/)这档节目，所以第一次完整公开的聊了一遍。以下文字整理自播客《给人文工作者的 AI 使用指南》，AI 辅助整理，有所缩略。如果你想知道完整版，可以[官网直接收听](https://shishufeng.com/episode/owocaoshiaiwomenyoujiule)，或者在宇宙、[苹果播客](https://podcasts.apple.com/us/podcast/%E8%AF%97%E6%A2%B3%E9%A3%8E/id1870811470)搜索《诗梳风》即可收听。
14	
15	![图像](https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HCm9_ggbgAAfvoi?format=jpg&name=large)
16	
17	小宇宙二维码
18	
19	过去一年多里，把这套怎么用 AI 的经验讲给过很多做内容、做研究、做知识产品的朋友。它的目标不是教你背几个神奇提示词，更不是把 AI 当成灵丹妙药；相反，它更像是一套工作方法：让你在不写代码的前提下，把大模型真正接进自己的写作、研究、编辑、选题、资料整理与生产流程里，并且做到**可追溯、可监督、可验证**，最后你依然愿意在作品上署名。
20	
21	这套方法来自我们在真实项目里踩过的坑：当内容进入规模化生产，纯靠人力会崩；而 AI 直接写一篇又会幻觉、会偷懒、会写得像 AI。于是我们不得不把创作变成产线，把产线变成可迭代的系统。
22	
23	当今天我不想直接给你各种提示词，我希望能给你一些关键的指导思想和原则。
24	
25	## 写在原则之前：这份指南的三条底线
26	
27	在具体方法之前，先明确三条底线。它们决定了你“怎么用 AI”，也决定了你“为什么要这样用”。
28	
29	1. **过程必须可追溯、可监督、可验证** 你不能只要一个结果、不要过程。对人文工作而言，黑箱最危险：幻觉、错引、偷换概念，都会在黑箱里悄悄发生。
30	2. **必须可操纵** 你要能控制它怎么做、按什么标准做、在哪些地方慢一点、在哪些地方严一点。你不是在“抽卡”，你是在生产。
31	3. **最后你依然愿意署名** 「我愿不愿意把名字放上去？」是最终质检。如果你不愿意署名，通常不是道德问题，而是过程里你的意志没有贯彻进去——也就意味着质量不可控。
32	
33	## 原则 0：别对 AI 许愿，把它当作工作台
34	
35	很多人用 AI 的方式，本质是在许愿： “给我一个好段子”“帮我写一篇好文章”“解释这篇论文”。
36	
37	问题在于——**“解释”本身就有无数种解释**：给外行、给本科生、给研究生、给同行，完全不是一个任务。AI 不可能默认知道你的背景、目的、口味和标准。你不说清楚，它就只能用“平均人类”的默认方式糊一份最省力的答案给你。
38	
39	把大模型当工作台，意味着：**你不向它索要结果，而是调动它的工具来完成一个过程**。你要做的是把任务说清楚、把标准说清楚、把步骤安排出来。
40	
41	比如让 AI 解释论文
42	
43	你可以像这样把许愿式请求（给我解释这篇论文）改成工作台式任务：
44	
45	- 明确目标受众：聪明、有好奇心，但不是该领域专家的研究生
46	- 明确讲解方式：启发式、循序渐进、有学术严谨性
47	- 明确结构要求：先讲意义，再补背景，再还原研究历程，再讲关键技术点，再提启示
48	- 明确语气：尊重智力、不居高临下、不假装对方已有深厚基础
49	
50	你会发现：你给得越像“作业要求”，AI 就越不像 AI，越像一个真的会干活的助教。
51	
52	## 原则 1：想要 AI 做好，先反思自己——你才是负责人
53	
54	如果你雇了一个秘书，你不会只说： “把汉洋那篇写美国[锈带的文章改好](https://hanyang.wtf/p/c4b)。”
55	
56	你一定会补充： 这篇文章为什么写、写给谁、现在卡在哪、你希望它解决什么问题、哪些地方不能动、你要什么风格、你最在意的指标是什么。
57	
58	AI 也是一样。你要把它当成一个非常勤奋、非常礼貌、但**不懂你脑内隐含前提**的同事。真正的“提示词工程”不是技巧，而是一种责任感：**任何任务仍然是你在做，AI 只是帮你干活。**
59	
60	当你对 AI 的输出不满意，最有效的第一反应不是“AI 不行”，而是：
61	
62	- 我有没有说清楚“对象/受众/目的”？
63	- 我有没有提供足够的背景材料和约束？
64	- 我有没有把“抽象愿望”拆成“可执行动作”？
65	- 我有没有给到可判断对错的标准？
66	
67	## 原则 2：同一个问题至少问 3 个模型——每个 AI 都有“性格”和擅长领域
68	
69	在我们公司，任何初次接触大模型的同事我会希望他在前期使用中，每个问题问三个不同的 AI。AI 像人一样有差异：有的更擅长写作遣词，有的更擅长推理解题，有的更擅长代码或工具调用。更现实的一点是：同一家产品的模型、同一个模型的新版本，也会不断微调“风格”和“边界”。
70	
71	所以一个很朴素但极有效的习惯是：**同一个问题，至少抛给 3 个不同 AI**，你会快速获得“手感”：
72	
73	- 哪个更会写、哪个更会想、哪个更会查、哪个更容易偷懒
74	- 哪些任务适合谁做“第一稿”，哪些适合谁做“审稿人”
75	- 哪个更适合出“选题/结构”，哪个更适合出“段落/句子”
76	
77	这一步的价值不在于“选出最强模型”，而在于：你开始像管理团队一样管理模型，而不是把它当唯一神谕。
78	
79	## 原则 3：AI 不是全知全能——把它当成“好学校本科生”的常识水平
80	
81	一个很实用的预期管理是： **AI 的常识水平≈一个 985 的本科生。**
82	
83	如果某件事你觉得“一个优秀本科生都未必知道”，那你就应该默认 AI 也不知道；至少默认它会在不知道的时候“编得很像知道”。
84	
85	这会带来两个直接动作：
86	
87	1. **任何超过常识的内容，都要你来教它** 比如：你要它写段子、写真正有独特品味的文案、写高度专业的论证——你不能只给一句“写得好点”，你要给范例、给标准、给禁区、给语料。我相信你现在去和朋友解释你心中什么文字是好的，都需要点时间；那怎么能认为 AI 默认知道呢？
88	2. **你要把它当实习生协作，而不是当神** 它能做很多“微观插值”的工作：把你给的脚手架补全，把你给的材料织成可读文本。但“脚手架”和“方向”仍然来自你。
89	
90	## 原则 4：让 AI 一步一步逼近目标——白盒分步骤，比黑箱一次性更可靠
91	
92	AI 的优势不是“直接给你正确答案”，而是它可以在你设计的流程里，**稳定完成很多小步骤**。你越是要求它“一步到位”，它越容易变成“看似完整、实则偷懒”的黑箱。
93	
94	一个特别直观的例子是做 TTS（文本转语音）或朗读稿的处理。与其说“注意多音字、不要读错”，不如把任务拆成一串步骤，例如：
95	
96	- 标出停顿/重音/语速变化的标记
97	- 识别潜在多音字
98	- 依据词典或权威读音做核对（必要时先检索再确定）
99	- 对容易误读但常见的字提前标注
100	- 实在不行就用**同音无歧义字替换**，从根上消灭误读可能
101	
102	这类“显而易见的正确做法”，人类会默认自己会做；但 AI 不会默认。你不把“显而易见”写进流程，它就会在最省力的路径上犯错。
103	
104	## 原则 5：先工业化，再 AI 化——你不能从农业时代一步跳到 AI 时代
105	
106	如果你的写作/研究流程本身是随机的、凭灵感的、资料不管理的，那你确实很难把它交给 AI。因为 AI 只能接住你“可描述、可复现”的那部分。
107	
108	更现实的路径是：
109	
110	1. 先把工作变成“产线”：可拆分、可复用、可质检
111	2. 再把其中的子步骤交给 AI：让它当工位，而不是当上帝
112	
113	我们做过一个很笨但很关键的工作：把我自己怎么写一篇非虚构文章的过程解出来。包括：
114	
115	- 为什么用这个故事开头
116	- 为什么选这句话
117	- 如何给例子打分
118	- 如何起承转合、如何过渡、如何收尾
119	- 如何把小故事连接到更宏大的图景
120	
121	最后拆成了几十个步骤，让不同的 AI 只做其中一个步骤。结果是： **不是模型突然变强了，而是流程把它“每次只能行一点点”的能力串起来了。**
122	
123	当你能清晰描述“我的文章是怎么做出来的”，你就会发现：决定质量上限的从来不是“用哪个大模型”，而是你有没有把工作方法讲清楚。
124	
125	![图像](https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HCkrsW8awAY5y7S?format=jpg&name=large)
126	
127	当时做测试时的一些步骤
128	
129	不过这段强烈建议你听节目，说得更详细。
130	
131	## 原则 6：预判 AI 会偷懒——它会省算力，你要替它扫清“格式障碍”
132	
133	AI 会偷懒，而且是“系统性偷懒”：能不打开网页就不打开，能不读 PDF 就不读，能跳过就跳过。不是它坏，而是它在算力与时间的约束下，天然倾向于走最省力路径。
134	
135	所以你要做的是：**把 AI 的算力用在“理解文本”，而不是浪费在“处理格式”。**
136	
137	非常有效的改法包括：
138	
139	- 尽量把材料转成纯文本/Markdown，再喂给 AI
140	- 把网页内容复制成干净文本（去掉导航、广告、脚注噪音）
141	- 对长材料先做“事实提炼/结构提取”，再让它写作
142	- 把 PDF/EPUB/网页统一入库成可检索的 TXT，再做后续任务
143	
144	你会发现：很多人抵触这种“体力活”，觉得“机器就该替我干脏活”。但在人机协作里恰恰相反——你愿意做一点点机械劳动，AI 的智力部分才会变得更锋利、更可靠。
145	
146	## 原则 7：记住上下文有限——把任务尽量改成“压缩”，不要指望它“凭空扩张”
147	
148	AI 有上下文窗口，有“记忆上限”。你给它两万字，它未必能记住多少；你给它二十万字，它可能只扫标题。一个形象的类比是：把人关进小房间一天，丢给他一本二十万字的书，出来让他背——能背多少，大概就是 AI 能“记住”的量。
149	
150	因此有一个很反直觉但极重要的经验：
151	
152	- **压缩比扩张容易得多** 把 100 万字压到 1 万字，往往比把 1 万字扩到 100 万字可靠。
153	
154	这直接改变你向 AI 提需求的方式：
155	
156	- 不要用 100 字提示词去要一篇论文
157	- 相反，把材料尽可能喂进去（分批、检索、RAG 都行），让它在充分材料基础上压缩出结构、观点和正文
158	
159	你过去写文章、写论文，本来就是“读海量材料→提炼→组织→写作”（至少我是这样）。到了 AI 这里，不要突然双标，要求它凭空生长。
160	
161	## 原则 8：克制“我妙手一改就好了”的冲动——改产线，不改结果
162	
163	很多擅长写作的人，最容易在 AI 面前翻车： AI 出了个 59 分的稿子，你觉得自己改两下就 80 分，于是你开始改；改着改着变成你重写；重写完你说“还是我自己来吧”，然后从此再也不用 AI。
164	
165	解决办法不是更努力“改稿”，而是把关注点挪到更上游：
166	
167	- 不要追求让 AI 直接写出 100 分
168	- 你的目标是让产线稳定产出 75～80 分
169	- 你要做的是迭代流程，让“平均分”提高，而不是让“单篇”完美
170	
171	## 原则 9：把产线当产品迭代——可靠性本身就是价值
172	
173	当你有一个系统能稳定给你 70 分的起点，它的价值不是“它像不像你”，而是：
174	
175	- 你能在接近零成本的情况下拿到一个可用草稿
176	- 你能把精力集中在更高阶的判断：选题、结构、证据、品味与取舍
177	
178	你要的不是一个能代替你的全能神，而是一个可靠的工厂：它不完美，但它稳定。
179	
180	## 原则 10：数量第一要务——让它多产出，再筛选
181	
182	只让 AI 给你一个版本，通常会得到最中庸、最保守、最“平均”的那一个。你要用“数量”对抗“平庸”。
183	
184	更有效的做法是：
185	
186	- 总结：一次要 5 个版本
187	- 开头：一次要 5 个开头，做 AB Test
188	- 选题：一次要 50 个选题，再分组、再挑
189	- 结构：一次要 3 套结构，再组合
190	- 表述：一次要 10 个不同措辞，再择优
191	
192	当你提高平均分、提高产量，分布里自然会出现 85 分、90 分的“惊喜样本”。很多时候，好的不是“那一次神来之笔”，而是你终于开始用统计学的方式工作。
193	
194	## 原则 11：别越俎代庖——像行政总厨一样指挥、品尝、让它回炉
195	
196	如果你是餐厅的行政总厨，你不会亲自去拍黄瓜。你会：
197	
198	- 尝一口
199	- 判断是否合格
200	- 给出明确反馈（哪里不行、要怎么改）
201	- 让厨师回去重做一遍
202	
203	与 AI 协作也一样。你要尊重它“按它的方式生成”的主体性——你要做的是**教它怎么达到你的标准**，而不是自己跳下去把它每次的结果修成成品。
204	
205	否则你会被无止尽的“修修补补”耗死。
206	
207	## 最后一个底层原则：回到真实世界——材料 × 品味，决定作品上限
208	
209	在 AI 时代，一个作品的质量越来越像是： **材料 × 品味。**
210	
211	模型会变，方法会迭代，但这两件事不变：
212	
213	1. **材料来自真实世界** 如果给你两种选择去写一篇文章：
214	- 用最新模型，但只能用网上资料
215	- 用老模型，但你有完整档案、口述史、实地采访 更可能做出好作品的，往往是后者。
216	1. **品味来自长期训练** 当“生成”变得便宜，真正稀缺的是：
217	- 你知道什么值得写
218	- 你知道哪些证据更硬
219	- 你知道哪种叙述更有力量
220	- 你愿意为材料付出体力劳动：上穷碧落下黄泉，动手动脚翻资料
221	
222	AI 改变的，是你和材料交互的效率与方式；但作品的主语仍然是你，宾语仍然是材料。AI 只是“动词”的一部分。
223	
224	![图像](https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HCm1rf7bEAAcAP_?format=jpg&name=large)
225	
226	上穷碧落下黄泉，动手动脚拍摘片
227	
228	## 结语：把焦虑换成手感
229	
230	很多人用 AI 用不起来，不是因为不聪明，而是因为一直停留在“许愿—失望—放弃”的循环里。真正能让你跨过去的，是把它当作工作台，把任务工程化，把流程白盒化，然后在不断摩擦里长出手感。
231	
232	当你能做到这件事，你就不容易草率地下结论“AI 不行”；你会更像一个能管理新工具的新工种：既不俯视它，也不仰视它，把它放在流程里，放在现实里，放在你愿意署名的作品里。
233	
234	我是汉洋，如果你对我写的文字感兴趣。可以在 [X 关注我](https://x.com/HanyangWang)或者[在个人博客查看更多内容](https://hanyang.wtf/)。
235

We hypothesize that functional viability depends on specific bond distributions: despite sharing identical conceptual nodes, incompatible configurations disrupt information exchange. For instance, excessive exploration bonds cause fragmented reasoning, whereas overemphasized deep reasoning bonds create rigid chains unable to adapt to new inputs.Details are provided in Appendix 14.3. 209 210 ##### Effective reasoning bond distribution influences the information divergence speed in reasoning dynamics. 211 212 To assess this, we compared the reasoning dynamics of R1 models with human cognition in an information phase space [^10]. Mechanistically, LLMs update by maximizing rewards and reducing entropy, whereas human reasoning is additionally constrained by semantic coherence and social feedback. Consequently, machine reasoning converges through accumulated gradient updates, whereas human reasoning stabilizes through iterative self-monitoring and social calibration. As shown in Figure 10, we tracked reasoning unfolding over extended chains in logical deduction tasks. Humans typically exhibit nearly uniform forward information gains (81.3% of cases show changes $<0.1$), corresponding to a near-zero slope in phase space. In contrast, R1 models display accelerating informativeness (76.1% of cases show absolute changes $>0.1$), progressing from low entropy to rapid convergence. These patterns indicate a fundamental difference in how R1 models and humans integrate information over time. 213 214 ##### Effective reasoning bonds cause metacognitive oscillation and alignment. 215 216 We identify the core rationale for this difference as a "metacognitive oscillation" in LLMs. Their responses alternate between high-entropy divergent exploration (slope $>0.6$, $\Delta$ entropy $>0.05$) and stable convergent validation, a dynamic less pronounced in the uniform entropy profiles of humans. Case studies (Figure 10) confirm that R1 models utilize self-reflective revision to adjust reasoning paths against uncertainty. We hypothesize that aligning training objectives with these behavioral structure distributions can narrow the gap between machine and human reasoning dynamics. 217 218 ### 5.2 Conflict between Two Stable Structures 219 220 Understanding how distinct reasoning structures interact reveals fundamental limits of complex cognitive systems. As shown in Fig. 11 (a–c), forcibly fusing stable molecular isomers disrupts their backbone; analogously, combining incompatible reasoning frameworks breaks global logical coherence. 221 222 ##### Learning two heterogeneous stable structures at the same time will lead to structural chaos in the model. 223 224 As shown in Fig. 11 (d), we test this by jointly activating two highly correlated ($r\approx 0.9$) reasoning chains from DeepSeek-R1 and OpenAI-OSS. Despite their similarity, co-activation prevents the model from converging to a single stable behavioral mode: it produces molecular bond distributions that fluctuate across samples and deviate from those characteristic of either OSS or R1. Consistent with this instability, the self-correlation of the jointly activated model does not exceed 0.8. 225 226 ##### This structural chaos leads to a significant decline in the performance of the model. 227 228 As shown in Fig. 11 (e), joint activation also causes a marked drop in performance relative to either chain alone. This seemingly paradoxical effect indicates that structural compatibility, rather than mere statistical correlation, governs whether reasoning systems can coexist. The interference pattern suggests that the underlying cognitive architecture is rigid: without careful alignment, attempts to merge such systems yield fragmented, low-utility outputs instead of enhanced capability. 229 230 231 232 | Model | GSM8K | MATH-500 | AIME2024 | AIME2025 | AMC2023 | OlympiadBench | AVG | 233 | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | 234 | LLaMA-3.1-8B-Base [^9] | 7.58 | 3.20 | 0.00 | 0.00 | 4.22 | 1.19 | 2.70 | 235 | + 20K Qwen-Distill-Data | 62.47 | 29.40 | 0.00 | 0.00 | 12.81 | 6.81 | 18.58 | 236 | + 20K OSS-Distill-Data | 75.89 | 54.20 | 4.38 | 6.46 | 37.34 | 23.85 | 33.69 | 237 | + 20K QwQ-Distill-Data | 64.53 | 32.20 | 2.92 | 0.42 | 16.72 | 8.89 | 20.95 | 238 | + 20K OSS-Mole-Syn | 67.85 | 35.20 | 1.83 | 0.83 | 20.53 | 11.11 | 22.89 | 239 | + 20K QwQ-Mole-Syn | 66.41 | 35.00 | 2.08 | 0.63 | 20.16 | 10.37 | 22.44 | 240 | Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct [^9] | 75.89 | 35.20 | 4.17 | 1.04 | 23.59 | 12.00 | 25.32 | 241 | + 20K Qwen-Distill-Data | 76.50 | 39.80 | 4.38 | 1.04 | 25.63 | 19.70 | 27.84 | 242 | + 20K OSS-Distill-Data | 79.00 | 60.80 | 10.83 | 7.71 | 47.03 | 30.22 | 39.27 | 243 | + 20K QwQ-Distill-Data | 82.41 | 60.80 | 4.38 | 8.33 | 32.97 | 25.48 | 35.73 | 244 | + 20K OSS-Mole-Syn | 83.24 | 51.80 | 4.79 | 1.04 | 32.50 | 21.04 | 32.40 | 245 | + 20K QwQ-Mole-Syn | 84.31 | 50.20 | 5.21 | 1.67 | 32.34 | 20.00 | 32.29 | 246 247 Table 2: Performance comparison across six benchmarks. Moreover, Figures 12 (b-d) show that these gains persist over extended RL training, demonstrating durable benefits from synthesized Long CoT structures. This effective use under RL supports their practical utility across diverse cognitive tasks. 272 273 274 275 ## 7 Function: Shaping Function of Each Bond in Long CoT Structure 276 277 Further, we analyze the shaping function of each bond in Long CoT structure. 320 Figure 14: The reasoning behavior distribution of summarized QwQ traces. 321 322 ## 8 Deteriorated Molecular Structure Cannot Be Easily Restored 323 324 ##### How Current Private LLMs Protect Their Long CoT from Distillation? 325 326 Exposing reasoning traces allows LLMs to imitate both answers and procedures. Common defenses always consider compressing intermediate steps. We quantify this by distilling from Gemini-2.5-Pro-Thinking and Claude-4-Sonnet. Table 3 shows that beyond $\sim$ 45% token reduction versus QwQ-32B rationales, distillation causes accuracy drops, showing compression can disrupt Long CoT structure. 327 328 ##### Summarization break reasoning bond distributions to prohibit distillation. 329 330 To further validate the effectiveness of summarization, we summarized Long-CoT traces from QwQ and R1. Table 4 shows that training on compressed trajectories yields weaker performance than training on full traces and reduces distillation effectiveness by 2%. In Figure 14, summarization shifts reasoning behavior distributions and creates a gap between observable outputs and internal error-bounded transitions, limiting trace inversion and behavioral cloning. However, compression can also protect model architecture and embedded inductive priors from unauthorized imitation. 331 332 333 334 ## 9 Related Work 335 336 Chain-of-Thought (CoT) elicits intermediate rationales, improving multi-step reasoning on math and logic tasks. Scaling short CoT to Long CoT is difficult: coherence often degrades, and cold-start gains frequently require targeted training or high-quality trajectories [^8] [^11]. A common approach distills stepwise solutions from strong teacher models into weaker students [^12] [^13]. Outcomes hinge on reasoning quality: strong reasoning models transfer useful behaviors [^14], whereas weaker instruction models may mimic format without robust Long CoT capability [^7] [^15]. 337 338 Long CoT training elicits three behaviors: deep reasoning, self-reflection, and self-exploration [^16] [^8] [^5]. Work has studied their roles; [^17] used self-reflection to revise earlier steps, and [^18] combined reflection and exploration to improve robustness. Early studies framed CoT as sequences of these behaviors, emphasizing step-level imitation and local coherence [^1] [^3] [^19]. Later work used tree- or graph-structured reasoning to capture branching and revisitation [^20] [^21] [^22] [^23]. 339 340 Although trees or graphs represent individual Long CoT traces by modeling behaviors as nodes, they do not capture the overall distribution of logical behaviors. In contrast, our approach models Long CoT as a molecular-like structure, with edges encoding stable distributions of reasoning behaviors, to test how their arrangement and interactions support effective learning. 341 342 ## 10 Conclusion 343 344 This study provides a mechanistic account of Long CoT learning, conceptualized as molecular-like reasoning structures emerging through Self-Reflection, Deep-Reasoning, and Self-Exploration bonds. We propose a semantic isomer framework through behavior-transition distributions, offering insight into the stability and failure modes of Long CoT learning. Building on these, our Mole-Syn leverages distribution transfer graphs to construct robust Long CoT structures, thereby improving performance and enhancing the stability of RL. 345 346 ## Limitations 347 348 While our approach achieves strong performance on several reasoning benchmarks, it still has several limitations: First, limited by cost and scale constraints, our analysis relies on a limited set of teacher models and student backbones, which may introduce bias in observed statistical patterns of Long CoT toward specific architectures or training recipes. Second, we focus on offline distillation and supervised fine-tuning, leaving open how well the method scales in realistic online or interactive settings with RL-like feedback. We can only approximately visualize the geometric characteristics of the inferred bond in information and semantic spaces. However, accurately delineating a universal Long CoT macromolecular structure remains an important future direction. Finally, our behavior analysis relies on an automatically labeled dataset. Even though we provide an initial robustness check, label noise or bias will inevitably appear on estimated distributions. 349 350 ## References 351 352 ## 11 General Experimental Setting 353 354 ##### Target Model. 355 356 Unless otherwise specified, we start from a generic instruction-tuned LLM (e.g., Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct [^9]). The model is standard pre-trained and supervised fine-tuned, but is not specifically optimized for long chain-of-thought reasoning. 357 358 ##### Data Source. 359 360 We randomly sample 20K–35K high-quality Long CoT queries from OpenThoughts-3 [^24] as the primary training corpus. The dataset provides multi-step reasoning traces, averaging over 20 steps per example, and covers diverse mathematical and logical problem types. 361 362 ##### Evaluation Benchmarks. 363 364 We evaluate on 6 challenging mathematical reasoning benchmarks that require multi-step logic: 365 366 - GSM8K [^25]: Grade-school math problems requiring multi-step calculations. 367 - MATH-500 [^26]: High-school and early college-level problems across major math topics. 368 - AMC 2023 [^27]: High-school competition problems in algebra, geometry, and combinatorics. 369 - AIME 2024 [^28]: Invitational-level problems with integer final answers. 370 - AIME 2025 [^29]: Invitational-level problems with integer final answers. 371 - OlymBench [^30]: A comprehensive Olympiad-level benchmark. 372 373 Unless stated otherwise, (Overall) Accuracy is the mean accuracy across all benchmarks above. 374 375 ##### Inference and Metrics. 376 377 For evaluation, we use the same sampling temperature as in reinforcement learning, $=0.6$, to reduce the SFT–RL mismatch. We report Avg@1 accuracy for GSM8K, MATH-500, and OlymBench. For smaller test sets (AMC 2023 and AIME 2024/2025), we report Avg@16 accuracy. We instruct the model to output the final answer in $\backslash$ boxed{ $\cdot$ } format to simplify extraction. We then parse boxed answers and match them to reference solutions using standard answer-matching tools (e.g., math-verify). Except for specifically specified variables, all model training settings are the same. 378 379 ## 12 Detailed Experimental Settings for Preliminary Study 380 381 In this appendix, we detail the experimental setup for the preliminary study on cold-start Long CoT. We compare 3 data construction pipelines. For all pipelines, we fine-tune the model for 1 epoch with a learning rate of $2e-5$ and a global batch size of $128$, using a max sequence length of $16K$ or $32K$ tokens (we select the better-performing setting between these two lengths). We use Qwen2.5 [^31] and Llama3.1 [^9] as backbones to cold-start Long CoT across multiple model sizes. 382 383 ![Refer to caption](https://arxiv.org/html/2601.06002v2/x15.png) 384 385 Figure 15: The full failure result of ICL from weak instruction-following LLMs and Human-annotated reasoning traces to acquire Long CoT structures, compared to successful distillation from strong reasoning LLMs. 386 387 ##### Setting 1: Distillation from Strong Reasoning LLMs. 388 389 To construct a high-quality synthetic dataset, we use a reasoning LLM as the teacher. Specifically, we distill Long CoT reasoning traces from DeepSeek-R1-671B-0528 [^8], QwQ-32B [^32], OpenAI-OSS-120B [^33]. 390 391 ##### Setting 2: Distillation from Weak Instruction LLMs (ICL-Distill). 392 393 To simulate surface imitation via in-context learning in instruction-tuned LLMs, we use a standard instruction model (e.g., Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct) that is not optimized for deep reasoning. We randomly select 1-shot exemplar (an R1-generated Long CoT trace) in the prompt, and generate solutions for the same problems as in Setting 1. 394 395 ##### Setting 3: Fine-tuning on Human-Annotated Traces. 396 397 We utilize 50 R1-generated reasoning traces and 50 human-written step-by-step solutions for supervised fine-tuning to compare against human-annotated reasoning traces. The data are collected from [^7]. 398 399 ## 13 Reasoning Bond in Long CoT 400 401 In this section, we provide detailed experimental settings for analyzing reasoning bonds in Long CoT. 402 403 ### 13.1 Mathematical Definition & Analysis of Reasoning Bonds 404 405 #### 13.1.1 Reasoning Behavior Definition. 406 407 Given an input query $x$, a model generates an output text $y$ containing intermediate reasoning followed by a final answer. We segment $y$ into $T$ step-level units (“steps”) using standard delimiters (e.g., line breaks or bullet markers), following prior work [^34] [^19]. This yields a Long-CoT trajectory 408 409 $$ 410 \tau\coloneqq(u_{1},\ldots,u_{T}), 411 $$ 412 413 where each $u_{t}$ is a textual step. 414 415 To analyze the geometry of $\tau$, we map each step $u_{t}$ to a vector $h_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$. Concretely, we encode $u_{t}$ with a fixed reference encoder and obtain token hidden states from a fixed layer (e.g., the penultimate layer). We then average token hidden states to form a step embedding $h_{t}$, producing an embedding sequence $(h_{1},\ldots,h_{T})$. 416 417 ##### Behavior space and labeled transitions. 418 419 We model Long-CoT as a sequence of step-to-step transitions. For each $t\in\{1,\ldots,T-1\}$, define the directed transition (edge) 420 421 $$ 422 e_{t}\coloneqq(u_{t}\rightarrow u_{t+1}). 423 $$ 424 425 Let the behavior label set be 426 427 $$ 428 \mathcal{B}\coloneqq\{\mathcal{N},\mathcal{D},\mathcal{R},\mathcal{E}\}, 429 $$ 430 431 where $\mathcal{N}$ denotes Normal Operation, $\mathcal{D}$ Deep Reasoning, $\mathcal{R}$ Self-Reflection, and $\mathcal{E}$ Self-Exploration. An automated classifier (Appendix C.1) assigns a label $b_{t}\in\mathcal{B}$ to each transition $e_{t}$, yielding a labeled transition sequence $(e_{t},b_{t})_{t=1}^{T-1}$. 432 433 We formalize a behavior-graph framework for Long CoT, in which molecular-inspired ‘bonds’ correspond to behavior-labeled edges whose distributions can be estimated, compared, and transferred across models. 434 435 ##### Definition 1 (Deep Reasoning: 𝒟\\mathcal{D}). 436 437 A transition $e_{t}=(u_{t}\rightarrow u_{t+1})$ is labeled $\mathcal{D}$ if the primary intent of $u_{t+1}$ is to extend the reasoning chain via non-trivial inference (e.g., multi-step causal, deductive, or analogical reasoning). Operationally, $\mathcal{D}$ typically introduces at least one of: (i) new latent assumptions, (ii) intermediate logical variables/nodes, or (iii) derivations that go beyond direct computation or restatement. 438 439 ##### Definition 2 (Self-Reflection: ℛ\\mathcal{R}). 440 441 A transition $e_{t}=(u_{t}\rightarrow u_{t+1})$ is labeled $\mathcal{R}$ if $u_{t+1}$ explicitly comments on, audits, or regulates the model’s own reasoning process. This includes expressing uncertainty, revising the solution strategy, identifying or correcting mistakes, or re-examining earlier steps (i.e., tracing back to prior logical nodes). 442 443 ##### Definition 3 (Self-Exploration: ℰ\\mathcal{E}). 444 445 A transition $e_{t}=(u_{t}\rightarrow u_{t+1})$ is labeled $\mathcal{E}$ if $u_{t+1}$ intentionally branches into alternative hypotheses or candidate solution paths. Operationally, $\mathcal{E}$ raises new possibilities or sub-questions and keeps multiple paths active rather than committing to a single convergent chain. 446 447 ##### Remark (Normal Operation; 𝒩\\mathcal{N}). 448 449 Any transition not meeting the criteria for $\mathcal{D}$, $\mathcal{R}$, or $\mathcal{E}$ is labeled $\mathcal{N}$. This category covers routine progression such as straightforward calculation, paraphrasing, formatting, or direct execution of an already-chosen plan. 450 451 ##### Note: 452 453 It should be noted that an edge linking logical nodes does not merely connect the step $s_{t}$ to the next step $s_{t+1}$, but also adds edges to previously related nodes. 454 455 #### 13.1.2 Attention Energy Definition of Reasoning Bonds. 456 457 We now replace the molecular analogy with a direct analysis of attention patterns. For a given Transformer layer and head, let $q_{i},k_{j}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{k}}$ denote the query and key vectors of the $i$ -th and $j$ -th tokens, respectively. The attention weight $\alpha_{ij}$ from token $i$ to token $j$ is 458 459 $$ 460 s_{ij}=\frac{q_{i}^{\top}k_{j}}{\sqrt{d_{k}}}, 461 $$ 462 463 $$ 464 \alpha_{ij}=\frac{\exp\left(\frac{q_{i}^{\top}k_{j}}{\sqrt{d_{k}}}\right)}{\sum_{\ell}\exp\left(\frac{q_{i}^{\top}k_{\ell}}{\sqrt{d_{k}}}\right)}. 465 $$ 466 467 Following the standard Gibbs–Boltzmann parametrization, we define the *attention energy* 468 469 $$ 470 E_{ij}\triangleq-s_{ij}=-\frac{q_{i}^{\top}k_{j}}{\sqrt{d_{k}}}. 471 $$ 472 473 Then, substituting Eq. (8) into Eq. (7) yields 474 475 $$ 476 \alpha_{ij}=\frac{\exp(-E_{ij})}{\sum_{\ell}\exp(-E_{i\ell})}, 477 $$ 478 479 which is a Boltzmann distribution over targets $j$ with inverse temperature fixed to $1$.3 That is, the attention weight is $E_{ij}$ Gibbs–Boltzmann distribution (temperature is taken to be 1). In this view, lower $E_{ij}$ corresponds exactly to higher attention weight $\alpha_{ij}$, i.e., stronger dependency from $i$ to $j$. 480 481 To relate this to Long CoT behaviors, we use the edge-level labeling procedure from Appendix C.3. Each reasoning transition (edge) in a trajectory is classified as one of three behaviors: Deep Reasoning, Self-Reflection, or Self-Exploration (plus Normal Operation as a local baseline). For each labeled edge $b$, we aggregate the token-level attention weights between the source and target steps into a single scalar logit, and convert it to an energy value $E_{b}$ using Eq. (8). This yields three random variables $E_{\mathcal{D}},E_{\mathcal{R}},E_{\mathcal{E}}$ corresponding to Deep, Reflection, and Exploration edges, respectively. 482 483 #### 13.1.3 Attention-Energy Ordering of Reasoning Bonds 484 485 To analyze ordering among attention energies for different reasoning bonds, model queries, and keys with Rotary Positional Embedding (RoPE) [^35]. In an autoregressive Transformer, attention weights are a softmax of pre-softmax logits; define an attention energy as the negative logit so that higher attention corresponds to lower energy (Boltzmann/Gibbs form). 486 487 ##### RoPE model 488 489 RoPE can be written as a position-dependent block-diagonal rotation on (pairs of) coordinates. Model this head’s queries/keys as 490 491 $$ 492 q_{i}=R(i)u_{i},\qquad k_{j}=R(j)v_{j}, 493 $$ 494 495 where $R(t)\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{k}\times d_{k}}$ is deterministic and orthogonal. Then 496 497 $$ 498 s_{ij}=\frac{u_{i}^{\top}R(i)^{\top}R(j)v_{j}}{\sqrt{d_{k}}}=\frac{u_{i}^{\top}R(i-j)v_{j}}{\sqrt{d_{k}}}, 499 $$

551	$$

559	$$

565	$$

614

617	$$

619	#### 13.1.4 Low-energy edges dominate path aggregation.
620	
621	##### Step-level dependency graph.
622	
623	Let a model-produced chain-of-thought be partitioned into reasoning steps. Represent these steps as nodes in a directed graph $G=(V,B)$. For two steps $u,v\in V$, include a directed edge $b=(u\to v)\in B$ if step $v$ attends to step $u$ with average attention weight above a fixed threshold. (Thus, edges point from an attended-to step to the attending step.)
624	
625	##### Step-level edge energy.
626	
627	Assume token-level energies $E_{ij}$ are defined for token pairs $(i,j)$. For an edge $b=(u\to v)$, define the set of cross-step token pairs
628	
629	$$
630	\mathcal{C}(u\to v)\;=\;\{(i,j):i\in\text{tokens}(u),\;j\in\text{tokens}(v)\}.
631	$$
632	
633	Define the step-level edge energy as the mean token-level energy across these pairs:
634	
635	$$
636	E_{b}\;\equiv\;E_{u\to v}\;=\;\frac{1}{|\mathcal{C}(u\to v)|}\sum_{(i,j)\in\mathcal{C}(u\to v)}E_{ij}.
637	$$
638	
639	##### Reasoning paths and path energy.
640	
641	A reasoning path $p$ from a source step $s$ to a target step $t$ is a sequence of edges
642	
643	$$
644	p=(b_{1},\dots,b_{L}),\quad b_{\ell}=(u_{\ell}\to u_{\ell+1}),\quad u_{1}=s,\quad u_{L+1}=t.
645	$$
646	
647	Define the path energy as the additive cost
648	
649	$$
650	\mathcal{E}(p)\;=\;\sum_{\ell=1}^{L}E_{b_{\ell}}.
651	$$
652	
653	##### Soft-min (effective) energy over all paths.
654	
655	Let $\mathcal{P}(s\to t)$ denote the set of all paths from $s$ to $t$ in $G$. Following the standard log-sum-exp (soft-min) construction, define the effective energy
656	
657	$$
658	\mathcal{E}^{\star}(s\to t)\;=\;-\log\sum_{p\in\mathcal{P}(s\to t)}\exp\bigl(-\mathcal{E}(p)\bigr).
659	$$
660	
661	Equivalently, each path receives an (unnormalized) Gibbs weight $\exp(-\mathcal{E}(p))$, so lower-energy paths contribute more strongly to the aggregate dependence from $s$ to $t$.
662	
663	##### Low-energy edges define effective constraints.
664	
665	Consider two paths $p$ and $p^{\prime}$ from $s$ to $t$ of equal length $L$. Assume they are identical except at a single position $\ell^{\ast}$, where $p$ uses edge $b_{\ell^{\ast}}$ and $p^{\prime}$ uses $b^{\prime}_{\ell^{\ast}}$. If $E_{b_{\ell^{\ast}}}\leq E_{b^{\prime}_{\ell^{\ast}}}-\delta$ for some $\delta>0$, then
666	
667	$$
668	\frac{\exp\bigl(-\mathcal{E}(p)\bigr)}{\exp\bigl(-\mathcal{E}(p^{\prime})\bigr)}=\exp\bigl(\mathcal{E}(p^{\prime})-\mathcal{E}(p)\bigr)\;\geq\;\exp(\delta).
669	$$
670	
671	Thus, holding all other edges fixed, replacing a higher-energy edge by a lower-energy edge amplifies the relative influence of that path by at least a factor $\exp(\delta)$ in the attention-induced dependency distribution.
672	
673	##### Proof.
674	
675	Because $p$ and $p^{\prime}$ differ only at $\ell^{\ast}$,
676	
677	$$
678	\mathcal{E}(p)-\mathcal{E}(p^{\prime})=E_{b_{\ell^{\ast}}}-E_{b^{\prime}_{\ell^{\ast}}}.
679	$$
680	
681	The assumption $E_{b_{\ell^{\ast}}}\leq E_{b^{\prime}_{\ell^{\ast}}}-\delta$ implies
682	
683	$$
684	\mathcal{E}(p)\leq\mathcal{E}(p^{\prime})-\delta\quad\Rightarrow\quad\mathcal{E}(p^{\prime})-\mathcal{E}(p)\geq\delta.
685	$$
686	
687	Exponentiating yields
688	
689	$$
690	\frac{\exp\bigl(-\mathcal{E}(p)\bigr)}{\exp\bigl(-\mathcal{E}(p^{\prime})\bigr)}=\exp\bigl(\mathcal{E}(p^{\prime})-\mathcal{E}(p)\bigr)\geq\exp(\delta),
691	$$
692	
693	which proves the claim.
694	
695	##### Analysis.
696	
697	Proposition 13.1.4 shows that low-energy edges act as effective constraints: they bias the model toward reusing specific multi-step dependency patterns, because any path that swaps in a lower-energy edge gains multiplicative weight in the induced path distribution. If edges labeled as Deep Reasoning consistently exhibit lower energies than alternative behaviors, then multi-hop dependencies that rely more heavily on Deep Reasoning edges will dominate the effective aggregation from premises to conclusions, stabilizing long chain-of-thought structure without invoking an external chemical analogy.
698	
699	#### 13.1.5 Long CoT process is looking for a more stable reasoning structure.

5	## 从“被世界控制的人”，到“真正独立的创造者”
6	
7	如果认真研究 Dan Koe 的内容，你会发现，他真正讨论的，从来不只是赚钱、自媒体、效率或者个人品牌。这些东西只是表层。他真正想讨论的问题，其实是：**人在现代世界里，如何重新夺回自己的意识。** 这也是为什么，他推荐的内容跨度会极大。有些讨论灵性，有些讨论意识，有些讨论心理结构，有些讨论专注，有些讨论创造力，有些讨论商业与营销。表面上，它们像是不同领域，但如果真正把这些思想串联起来，你会发现，它们其实都在解释同一件事：**现代人，为什么会逐渐失去真正的自我，以及人又如何一步步完成意识进化。**
8	
9	现代社会最危险的地方，并不是贫穷，而是越来越多的人，开始失去“真正思考”的能力。人们每天都在接收信息，刷短视频、看新闻、切换注意力、不断被新的刺激吸引。表面上，人知道得越来越多，但实际上，**人正在越来越难形成完整意识。** Dan Koe 后来慢慢意识到，现代世界真正的问题，可能根本不是“信息不够”，而是：**人的意识，正在被系统性切碎。**
10	
11	短视频、社交媒体、算法推荐、无限信息流、即时反馈，这些东西最危险的地方，并不只是浪费时间，而是它们会不断打断人的意识连续性。于是人开始越来越难长时间专注、越来越难深度思考、越来越难阅读复杂内容，也越来越难形成长期认知结构。人会逐渐习惯快速刺激、情绪冲击、短周期满足与即时反馈，最后，大脑会慢慢退化成一种“只能对刺激做反应”的状态。而 Dan Koe 认为：**一个无法长期思考的人，最终会慢慢失去真正的自由。**
12	
13	很多人以为，自由是财富自由、时间自由或者地理自由。但 Dan Koe 后来发现，更深层的自由，其实是：**意识自由。** 也就是说，你是否真正拥有控制注意力、控制情绪、长期专注以及独立思考的能力。因为如果这些东西无法被自己控制，那么所谓的“自我”，可能只是一个幻觉。
14	
15	于是这里开始出现一个极其重要的转折：**“你”与“你的思想”，并不是同一个东西。** 人的大脑，会不断自动产生焦虑、恐惧、比较、欲望与自我否定。很多人默认：“这些想法就是我。” 但真正的问题在于：**如果这些东西无法被你控制，那它们为什么会被称为“你”？** 于是 Dan Koe 开始重新理解，大部分人的人生，其实并不是“主动活着”，而是在不断重复自己的心理程序。过去经历形成的恐惧、社会评价形成的焦虑、环境塑造的欲望、长期积累的情绪惯性，这些东西会持续自动运行。于是人看似在生活，实际上却只是被自己的心理结构推动。
16	
17	而当 Dan Koe 继续向下思考时，他又发现了另一个更深的问题：很多人以为的“自己”，其实根本不是自己。从小开始，社会就在不断训练人：被认可才有价值、被喜欢才算成功、必须符合标准、必须获得认同、必须拥有社会身份。于是，人会逐渐形成一种“社会化人格”。很多人并不是在活出真正的自己，而是在扮演一个被社会接受的人格。有人拼命赚钱，有人拼命证明自己，有人拼命维持形象，有人拼命追求身份，但这些行为背后真正驱动他们的，很多时候并不是热爱，而是恐惧。恐惧不被认可，恐惧自己不够好，恐惧失去价值，恐惧被忽视。
18	
19	于是现代人开始越来越依赖点赞、数据、外部评价与社会反馈。最后，一个人的价值感，完全建立在外界之上。而这时候，人已经不再真正自由，因为：**他的情绪控制权，已经交给了外部世界。**
20	
21	Dan Koe 后来越来越相信，真正强大的人，都拥有一种能力：**长时间保持完整意识。** 他们能够长时间专注、深度思考、长周期创造、稳定输出，并且不被外界持续干扰。而这时候，他开始重新理解，为什么很多真正厉害的人，都会进入一种极度沉浸状态。在那里，人会忘记时间、忘记自我、完全投入、思维高度统一。于是，创造力开始提升，理解能力开始提升，精神状态开始稳定。
22	
23	Dan Koe 慢慢意识到：**人生质量，本质上取决于意识质量。** 而不是获得多少娱乐、拥有多少消费、接收多少刺激。因为低质量意识，会不断制造焦虑、内耗、分裂与混乱；而高质量意识，则会逐渐形成深度、稳定、清晰与创造力。
24	
25	后来，Dan Koe 开始进一步意识到：人与人真正的差距，并不是财富、学历或者天赋，而是：**理解世界的维度不同。** 低维度的人，只能看到表面现象，他们容易情绪化、非黑即白、被群体推动、被短期刺激控制。而高维度的人，则开始慢慢拥有系统思维、长周期视角、多层因果理解以及自我反思能力。于是，他们不再只是“对事情做反应”，而开始理解事情为什么会发生。
26	
27	而这时候，成长的含义也开始发生变化。因为成长不再只是：获得更多信息，而是：**升级理解现实的能力。**
28	
29	Dan Koe 最终慢慢推导出一个核心结论：未来真正强大的人，不会只是信息最多的人、最忙的人，或者最会迎合系统的人。因为 AI 会快速压缩普通知识、重复技能以及信息优势。未来真正稀缺的，会变成：**深度思考能力。** 因为只有真正能够长期保持高质量意识的人，才可能理解复杂世界、构建独立认知、长周期创造，并输出真正有价值的东西。
30	
31	于是，Dan Koe 最终把灵性、哲学、心理学、深度工作、创造力、商业与互联网个人品牌，全部统一成了一件事：**意识进化。** 因为未来真正的竞争，最终都会变成：**谁能长期保持更高质量的意识状态。** 而那些真正完成意识升级的人，**会慢慢从“被世界塑造的人”，变成“主动塑造世界的人”。**

1	# X 上的 Tropical Value：“Why Palantir Makes New Hires Read a Theater Improvisation Book ” / X
2	
3	https://x.com/tropicalvalue/status/2057859376497701334?s=20
4	
5	Keith Johnstone's Impro is on Palantir's onboarding reading list. It has nothing to do with software, national security, or AI. That's the point.
6	
7	The book is about improvisational theater. Its author, Keith Johnstone, spent decades teaching actors how to stop blocking and start creating. The lessons he extracted along the way — about status, spontaneity, and what education does to raw talent — are among the most precise diagnostics of organizational behavior I've read. [$PLTR](https://x.com/search?q=%24PLTR&src=cashtag_click) clearly agrees.
8	
9	Reading it through the lens of company building, the message is uncomfortable: most of what makes a "good candidate" on paper is exactly what makes someone difficult to work with in practice.
10	
11	**The talent problem isn't what you think**
12	
13	Johnstone's most counterintuitive observation is that talent is not normally distributed the way intelligence is. "Intelligence is proportional to population, but talent appears not to be related to population numbers." You can't recruit for it at scale using standard proxies.
14	
15	Worse, formal education actively suppresses it. "The dullness was not an inevitable consequence of age, but of education." The students most damaged by this process, the ones hardest to unlock, are not the failures. They are "the star performers at bad high schools. Instead of learning how to be warm and spontaneous and giving, they've become armoured and superficial, calculating and self-obsessed."
16	
17	This is a direct challenge to every credential-driven recruiting process in Silicon Valley. The polished candidate who knows how to perform competence is often the one least capable of actual creative output. The armor is the problem. "To actually create something means going against one's education."
18	
19	What Palantir actually screens for is whether someone has preserved the imaginative responsiveness that education systematically trains out. "I began to think of children not as immature adults, but of adults as atrophied children."
20	
21	**Yes-sayers vs. blockers**
22	
23	The most operationally useful framework in the book is the binary between acceptors and blockers.
24	
25	"Those who say 'Yes' are rewarded by the adventures they have, and those who say 'No' are rewarded by the safety they attain."
26	
27	In improvisation, blockers kill scenes. In organizations, they kill momentum. Johnstone's observation is that blocking is a skill. "Bad improvisers block action, often with a high degree of skill. Good improvisers develop action." High-status players block because they're afraid of being humiliated. They'd rather kill the idea than be seen to fail with it.
28	
29	This maps cleanly onto organizational dysfunction. The person who says "that won't work" three seconds after you propose something is not being rigorous, they are most likely just protecting their status. The person who says "yes, and—" and develops the action is the one you want in the room.
30	
31	Palantir's deployment model — putting engineers directly inside customer organizations, often in chaotic, ambiguous situations — selects hard for acceptors. You cannot be a blocker in that environment. There's no script for FDEs.
32	
33	**Status is the operating system**
34	
35	The chapter on status dynamics is the sharpest management reading I've encountered outside of explicit leadership literature. The core insight: "Things said are not as important as the status played."
36	
37	Every interaction in an organization is a status transaction. Most people are running these transactions unconsciously and inconsistently. A manager who can read them — and who understands that high-status security manifests as relaxation, not aggression — has a meaningful edge.
38	
39	"When the highest-status person feels most secure he will be the most relaxed person." The corollary is that leaders who micro-manage, dominate airtime, or punish failure publicly are broadcasting insecurity, not authority. The status play undermines itself.
40	
41	The book's "ten golden rules for people who are Number 1" are worth reading twice. Rule six stands out: "You must reward your immediate subordinates by permitting them to enjoy the benefits of their ranks." Retention is a status problem before it's a compensation problem.
42	
43	**What good leadership looks like**
44	
45	Johnstone's model of the teacher (which translates directly to the manager) is radically non-hierarchical in one specific way: he accepts blame for failure as a tool for liberating performance. "I play low status, and I will explain that if the students fail they are to blame me." By removing the threat of personal failure from the learner, you remove the defense mechanism that suppresses their best output.
46	
47	The parallel in team management is creating an environment where people's first instinct is execution rather than self-protection. That requires the leader to absorb downside risk publicly — to be the one who falls on the sword when an experiment doesn't work. Most leaders do the opposite.
48	
49	The goal, as Johnstone frames it, is helping people "abandon control while at the same time they exercise control." That is the highest-leverage thing a manager can do: build enough safety that the team stops blocking themselves.
50	
51	**The real reason it's on the reading list**
52	
53	Palantir is not a normal software company and it has never pretended to be. The things it needs from its people — comfort with ambiguity, the ability to walk into a hostile room and read what's actually happening, the willingness to develop action in real time without a playbook — are not teachable via technical onboarding.
54	
55	Impro is on the list because it names the underlying capabilities more precisely than any management book does, and because it forces a reckoning with a hard truth: the selection and development of genuinely creative, high-agency people requires dismantling the exact habits that made them look attractive on paper in the first place.
56	
57	"The real avant-garde are not imitating what other people are doing, or what they did forty years ago, they're solving the problems that need solving."
58	
59	That's the job description. The book explains why it's hard to hire for it.

# Dan Koe 意识进化论

> [!abstract]- AI 摘要
> Dan Koe 将灵性、哲学、心理学、深度工作、创造力与商业统一为"意识进化"——现代人正在被系统性切碎意识，真正的自由是意识自由，未来竞争取决于谁能长期保持高质量意识状态。

---

## 扫读

> [!tip] 💡 一句话
> 人生质量本质上取决于意识质量，而现代社会正在系统性地将人的意识切碎。

> [!important] 📌 关键结论
> - 更深层的自由不是财富自由或时间自由，而是意识自由——控制注意力、情绪、长期专注和独立思考的能力
> - "你"与"你的思想"不是同一个东西，大多数人并非主动活着，而是在重复自己的心理程序
> - AI会压缩知识技能的优势，未来真正稀缺的是深度思考能力

> [!quote] 🎬 可行动项
> - 审视自己的"社会化人格"：哪些行为是被恐惧驱动（怕不被认可），而非真正热爱？
> - 保护意识连续性：减少碎片化信息摄入，训练长时间专注一件事的能力

---

## 精读

### 论证链

```
现代社会系统性地切碎人的意识
      ↓
论点1：碎片化信息流破坏意识连续性 → 人越来越难长时间专注和深度思考
论点2：大脑退化到"只能对刺激做反应"的状态 → 失去真正的自由
      ↓
证据层：
  ① 短视频、算法推荐、即时反馈不断打断注意力，抑制深度认知结构形成
  ② 社会化人格使人依赖外部评价（点赞、数据、社会反馈），情绪控制权交给外界
  ③ 低质量意识制造焦虑、内耗、分裂；高质量意识产生深度、稳定、清晰与创造力
      ↓
核心转折："你"与"你的思想"不是同一个东西——大脑的焦虑/恐惧/欲望是自动程序
      ↓
AI时代的分水岭：AI压缩普通知识和重复技能，深度思考能力成为唯一稀缺品
      ↓
结论：意识进化 = 从"被世界塑造的人"变为"主动塑造世界的人"
```

### 关键引述

> "现代社会最危险的地方，并不是贫穷，而是越来越多的人，开始失去'真正思考'的能力。"

> "人生质量，本质上取决于意识质量。"

> "未来真正的竞争，最终都会变成：谁能长期保持更高质量的意识状态。"

> "那些真正完成意识升级的人，会慢慢从'被世界塑造的人'，变成'主动塑造世界的人'。"

### 局限与盲区

- 本文未覆盖：未讨论如何具体训练意识连续性或提升意识质量，缺乏可操作的实践方法；也未涉及经济压力、身体健康等底层制约因素对意识自由的影响
- 隐含假设：假设每个人都有条件追求意识进化——但许多人生存压力已经耗尽全部认知资源，意识自由可能是马斯洛金字塔上层的奢侈品
- 可能的反例：有些高创造力的人（如某些艺术家、创业者）恰恰是在混乱、碎片化、高刺激的环境中产生突破性创意的，深度专注并非唯一路径

# Palantir 即兴戏剧管理哲学

> [!abstract]- AI 摘要
> Palantir 要求新员工阅读即兴戏剧书籍《Impro》，因为标准招聘筛选出的"优秀候选人"往往是最难合作的人。教育的本质是压制创造力，组织管理的核心是地位心理学：真正的高地位表现为放松而非攻击性。

---

## 扫读

> [!tip] 💡 一句话
> 教育系统批量生产"装甲化"的明星学生，而真正有创造力的组织需要那些保留了原始想象力与自发性的人。

> [!important] 📌 关键结论
> - 纸面上"最优秀的候选人"通常是创造力最弱的人——教育教会了他们表演能力而非创造能力
> - 组织中的人分为两类：推动行动的"Yes-sayers"和用高超技能扼杀创意的"Blockers"
> - 地位是组织的操作系统：真正有安全感的高地位者是放松的，微观管理、垄断发言、公开惩罚都是不安全感的信号

> [!quote] 🎬 可行动项
> - 在团队会议上观察阻断行为：谁说"这不行"比谁说"让我们试试"更频繁？那些快速否定的人可能只是在保护自己的地位
> - 作为管理者，主动吸收失败风险（"如果失败怪我"），移除团队成员的自我防卫机制

---

## 精读

### 论证链

```
教育系统系统性地压制人的创造力与自发性
      ↓
论点1：天赋不按人口正态分布 → 标准招聘无法规模化筛选真正有创造力的人
论点2：明星学生变得"装甲化、肤浅、精于算计"，非失败者的受损最严重
      ↓
证据层：
  ① "儿童的迟钝不是年龄的必然结果，而是教育的产物"
  ② "要真正创造东西意味着违背自己的教育"
  ③ Palantir筛选的是：谁保留了教育系统训练掉的想象力响应能力
      ↓
组织行为映射：即兴戏剧的两类人
  · Yes-sayers → 推动行动，获得冒险 → 组织动量
  · Blockers → 扼杀创意，获得安全 → 组织功能障碍
      ↓
地位动力学：高地位 = 放松（非攻击性），低地位安全感缺失表现为微观管理与控制
      ↓
领导力实践：管理者吸收失败风险 → 建立心理安全 → 团队停止自我阻断
      ↓
结论：选择与发展真正有创造力、高自主性的人，需要拆除让他们在纸面上看起来优秀的那些习惯
```

### 关键引述

> "大多数让一个人在纸面上看起来是'好候选人'的素质，恰恰是让他们在实践中难以合作的东西。"

> "说'是'的人被他们获得的冒险所奖励，说'不'的人被他们获得的安全所奖励。"

> "当一个地位最高的人感到最安全时，他会是最放松的人。"

> "真正的先锋不是在模仿别人在做什么，或者四十年前做了什么——他们在解决需要解决的问题。"

### 局限与盲区

- 本文未覆盖：未讨论如何在实践中具体识别"Yes-sayers"并有效面试筛选；也未涉及即兴戏剧方法的潜在风险（如过度"say yes"可能导致缺乏批判性评估）
- 隐含假设：假设所有"阻断"行为都是负面的——但某些情境下，有原则的拒绝和批判性审视是必要的风险管理
- 可能的反例：许多成功的组织（如某些顶级律所、金融机构）恰恰依赖于严格的审查流程和怀疑文化，完全开放的"Yes-and"文化可能不适合高风险、零容错的领域

45	## 具有结构性
46	
47	结构性防止你用一个混乱的问题进入复杂行业。很多人问问题时，会把客户、产品、渠道、成本、竞争、利润、组织能力混在一起，最后答案也会变得松散。
48	
49	所谓结构度，就是它能不能被拆成一棵清晰的逻辑树。
50	
51	比如一个公司为什么能赚钱，不能只问“它怎么赚钱”。应该拆成：
52	
53	- 收入来自哪里？
54	- 成本主要在哪里？
55	- 毛利是否健康？
56	- 获客成本是否可控？
57	- 用户是否复购？
58	- 哪个环节有规模效应？
59	- 哪个环节有定价权？
60	- 风险被谁承担？
61	
62	当一个问题能自然展开成这些互斥又相对穷尽的变量，它就更接近一个好问题。
63	
64	## 3C 战略框架
65	
66	3C 分别是 Customer、Company、Competitor，也就是客户、公司和竞争对手。很多问题之所以问得浅，是因为只看了公司自己，没有看客户为什么需要，也没有看竞争对手如何反应。
67	
68	比如“创始人如何做 Twitter 爆款内容”这个问题，如果只从 Company 角度看，就是创始人该怎么写内容；但如果加入 Customer，就要问目标受众是谁，他们为什么会关注、转发、信任；如果加入 Competitor，就要问同类创始人、同类产品、同类观点在争夺什么心智位置。
69	
70	这时候问题就会从“怎么写爆款”变成：
71	
72	> 创始人如何通过内容，在目标客户心智里建立一个区别于竞争对手的问题解释权？
73	
74	这就是 3C 框架带来的升维。
75	
76	## 价值链和利润池分析
77	
78	很多问题看起来在问增长、流量、趋势，本质上却应该问利润、权力和价值分配。一个行业真正值得研究的不是“谁最热闹”，而是：
79	
80	比如 AI 应用公司第一年数据很好，但平台期死掉。表面问题是增长停滞，深层问题是价值链位置不稳：如果公司的核心能力只是调用底层模型，再包装一个 UI，那么它在产业链里没有掌握控制点。一旦大模型平台或 SaaS 巨头集成同类功能，它的利润空间就会被压缩。
81	
82	## 极端场景和关键成功因素
83	
84	一个问题是否足够高级，往往要看它有没有压力测试。
85	
86	比如“这个行业未来怎么样”很普通；但如果问：
87	
88	> 如果未来三年价格战导致毛利率下降 30%，同时获客成本不再下降，哪些企业还能活下来？
89	
90	这就是一个更好的问题。因为它把行业放进极端场景里，逼迫我们识别真正的关键成功因素。
91	
92	真正的壁垒不是顺风时看起来强，而是在逆风、价格战、政策变化、技术替代、大厂进入时还能支撑公司活下来。
93

117

119	
120	## 完整的回答如下
121	
122	```text
123	创始人在 Twitter 上做爆款内容，不能从“什么内容容易火”开始，而要从“什么内容能放大我的商业判断”开始。
124	
125	创始人的身份决定了你不是普通内容博主。你发内容的最终目的，不应该只是获得点赞、转发和粉丝，而是让正确的人更快理解你的行业判断、产品价值和可信度。换句话说，创始人的爆款不是娱乐型爆款，而应该是商业型爆款。
126	
127	商业型爆款有三个标准。
128	
129	第一，它能吸引目标人群，而不是泛人群。如果你做 AI 产品，你的内容应该吸引创业者、产品经理、开发者、企业客户、投资人或某个垂直行业用户，而不是吸引一群只喜欢热闹观点的人。如果内容爆了，但来的人和你的业务无关，这条内容对商业模式没有太大价值。
130	
131	第二，它能建立信任，而不是只制造情绪。Twitter 上很多内容靠冲突、讽刺、极端观点获得传播，但创始人不能只追求这种传播。因为创始人的内容会反向影响公司形象。你要让别人觉得你有判断力、有行业经验、有产品理解、有长期主义，而不是只会写观点段子。
132	
133	第三，它能自然连接到你的业务。好的创始人内容不一定要硬广，但它应该让用户看完之后更理解：你为什么做这个产品，你解决什么问题，你为什么比别人更懂这个问题。
134	
135	比较适合创始人的 Twitter 爆款内容，有五类。
136	
137	第一类是反常识判断。结构是：“大多数人以为 A，其实真正决定结果的是 B。”比如：“很多 AI 产品失败不是因为模型不够强，而是因为没有进入用户工作流。”这种内容容易传播，因为它打破了默认理解。
138	
139	第二类是问题重定义。结构是：“你以为这是 X 问题，其实这是 Y 问题。”比如：“创始人做内容不是流量问题，而是信任成本问题。”这类内容能体现你的认知深度。
140	
141	第三类是行业机制拆解。解释一个行业为什么增长、为什么亏钱、为什么平台期死掉、为什么某些公司有定价权。这类内容吸引的人质量更高，因为它不是情绪消费，而是认知消费。
142	
143	第四类是方法论框架。把一个复杂问题拆成三层、四步、五个变量。Twitter 用户喜欢转发能帮他们表达专业判断的框架。比如：“判断一个 AI 产品是否有真 PMF，看 5 个指标：90 日留存、工作流嵌入、预算归属、模型毛利、平台替代风险。”
144	
145	第五类是真实经营现场。创始人可以写真实的产品取舍、客户反馈、销售失败、招聘判断、融资反思、增长实验。这类内容不一定最爆，但最容易建立信任。因为它证明你不是纸上谈兵，而是在真实经营里形成判断。
146	
147	创始人做 Twitter 爆款，可以用一个基本公式：
148	
149	目标人群的真实痛点
150	→ 一个反常识判断
151	→ 背后的行业机制
152	→ 一个清晰的方法论
153	→ 和你的产品/公司能力自然连接
154	例如，不要写：
155	
156	如何用 AI 提高效率？
157	
158	这太泛。
159	
160	可以写：
161	
162	大多数公司用 AI 提效失败，不是因为员工不会用工具，而是因为公司没有把流程拆成可被 AI 接管的任务节点。AI 转型真正要改的不是工具，而是工作流。
163	
164	这类内容更适合创始人，因为它有观点、有机制、有方法论，也能自然连接到 AI 产品、咨询服务、企业培训或自动化工具。
165	
166	所以，创始人在 Twitter 上做爆款内容的核心，不是追热点，而是持续输出一个领域里的高密度判断。你要让市场逐渐形成一种印象：这个人长期理解某个问题，而且他的公司可能真的能解决这个问题。
167	
168	一句话结论：
169	
170	创始人的 Twitter 爆款，不是最大化流量，而是把公司的核心商业判断包装成可传播、可信任、可转化的公共表达。
171	```
172	
173	**5\. 问题升维**
174	
175	![图像](https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HI--TKEbwAAb5O2?format=png&name=large)
176	
177	```text
178	这个问题要从“如何做爆款内容”升维到“如何构建创始人的商业分发系统”。
179	
180	Twitter 本质上是一个公共注意力市场。平台负责分发，但平台不会自动帮你沉淀商业价值。你真正要争夺的不是流量，而是目标人群心智中的一个位置。
181	
182	从商业结构看，创始人内容至少参与了四个环节：
183	
184	第一，认知环节。别人是否知道你在解决什么问题。
185	
186	第二，教育环节。别人是否理解这个问题为什么重要。
187	
188	第三，信任环节。别人是否相信你有能力解决这个问题。
189	
190	第四，转化环节。别人是否愿意进一步关注、咨询、试用、购买、合作、投资或加入。
191	
192	爆款只解决第一环节的一部分：让更多人看到你。但如果内容没有进入教育、信任和转化环节，它只是一次平台流量，不是商业资产。
193	
194	所以，创始人做 Twitter 内容的高阶理解应该是：
195	
196	通过持续输出行业判断，获得某个问题的解释权；通过解释权建立信任；通过信任降低商业模式里的获客成本、销售成本、招聘成本和融资沟通成本。
197	
198	这比“做爆款”重要得多。
199	
200	真正优秀的创始人账号，不是每条都爆，而是长期围绕一个清晰主题积累认知资产。例如：
201	
202	你长期解释 AI 产品为什么必须进入工作流
203	你长期解释创始人内容为什么是信任基础设施
204	你长期解释某类客户的真实痛点
205	你长期解释一个行业的利润池和定价权变化
206	当这些判断持续出现，市场会逐渐把你和某个问题绑定。这个绑定关系，才是内容对商业模式的长期价值。
207	
208	因此，升维后的问题不是：
209	
210	创始人如何在 Twitter 上做爆款内容？
211	
212	而是：
213	
214	创始人应该持续输出哪一类行业判断，使目标客户在理解问题时自然采用我的框架，并因此更容易信任我的产品或服务？
215	
216	这才是创始人内容的本质：不是追逐平台热度，而是争夺问题解释权。
217	```
