222	
223	根据这次的学习，我们可以提出一个更好的问题：
224	
225	> 作为一家 AI 产品的创始人，我应该如何将内容思维贯穿到组织结构内？对于个人 IP 账号，我应该关注哪些数据？针对哪类受众，发什么样的内容才能将我的产品理念触达到潜在用户？
226	
227	**1\. 问题得分**
228	
229	![图像](https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HI-_CeJbEAAXecX?format=png&name=large)
230	
231	**2\. 分析问题**
232	
233	![图像](https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HI-_MibbAAAu_2-?format=png&name=large)
234	
235	**3\. 引申问题**
236	
237	![图像](https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HI-_ZrhbcAAxa0m?format=png&name=large)
238	
239	**4\. 回答**
240	
241	![图像](https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HI-_7zxbkAA5sfV?format=png&name=large)
242	
243	完整回答：
244	
245	```text
246	作为一家 AI 产品的创始人，你要把内容思维贯穿到组织结构内，核心不是让每个部门都去发内容，而是让公司形成一种能力：持续把产品背后的行业判断、用户问题、使用场景和成功证据，转化为可传播、可销售、可交付、可复用的内容资产。
247	
248	AI 产品尤其需要内容思维，因为 AI 产品通常不是一个用户天然理解的成熟品类。很多潜在用户会有三个障碍：不知道自己具体该用 AI 解决什么问题，不知道你的产品和通用大模型有什么差异，也不知道把现有工作流迁移到你的产品里是否值得。因此，内容对 AI 产品公司来说，不只是品牌曝光，而是产品教育和需求塑造。
249	
250	组织上，你至少需要把内容拆成四类责任。
251	
252	第一，创始人负责“核心判断”。创始人不应该只做日常发帖的人，而应该是公司叙事的源头。你要持续输出几个判断：这个行业为什么会被 AI 改变，用户当前的工作流有什么低效，现有解决方案为什么不够好，你的产品理念为什么成立。创始人的内容应该定义问题，而不是只介绍功能。
253	
254	第二，产品市场或增长团队负责“内容产品化”。他们要把创始人的判断拆成可复用资产，比如官网文案、产品页面、用户案例、白皮书、销售话术、demo 脚本、onboarding 教程、客户教育邮件、社交媒体内容。也就是说，创始人的认知不能停留在个人账号里，要进入公司的每个客户触点。
255	
256	第三，销售和客户成功团队负责“反馈闭环”。他们最接近用户，知道用户听不懂什么、反对什么、为什么不买、为什么买了不用。这些信息必须反向输入内容系统。一个优秀的 AI 产品内容系统，不是只从创始人脑子里长出来，而是从真实客户异议和使用行为里长出来。
257	
258	第四，产品团队负责“内容与产品体验连接”。如果你发布大量理念内容，但产品 onboarding、模板、案例、示例数据、默认工作流不能承接这些理念，用户会断掉。内容说“AI 要进入工作流”，产品就必须让用户很快看到一个具体工作流如何被重构。
259	
260	对于个人 IP 账号，不能只看传统平台数据。曝光、点赞、转发、粉丝增长当然要看，但它们只是分发指标，不是商业指标。你应该把数据分成四层。
261	
262	第一层是传播数据：曝光、互动率、转发率、收藏率、关注转化率。它说明内容有没有被平台和受众放大。
263	
264	第二层是受众质量：关注者里有多少是目标用户、行业从业者、决策者、开发者、创始人、投资人或潜在合作伙伴。一个账号如果涨了很多泛流量，但目标用户占比很低，对 AI 产品增长意义有限。
265	
266	第三层是商业动作：主页点击、官网点击、waitlist 注册、demo 预约、试用转化、私信咨询、销售线索、newsletter 订阅、社群加入。这些说明内容是否把认知转成了行为。
267	
268	第四层是产品结果：试用后的激活率、功能使用深度、7 日/30 日留存、付费转化、销售周期是否缩短、客户是否在销售沟通中引用过你的内容。对 AI 产品来说，这一层最重要，因为内容最终要推动用户理解和采用产品，而不是只让创始人变得有名。
269	
270	针对受众，你不能只面向“潜在用户”这个大词发内容。AI 产品至少有四类受众。
271	
272	第一类是实际使用者。他们关心效率、体验、任务完成质量、学习成本。给他们发使用场景、前后对比、模板、工作流拆解、具体案例。
273	
274	第二类是决策者。他们关心 ROI、成本下降、团队效率、风险控制、预算合理性。给他们发行业趋势、管理问题、成本结构、组织效率、AI adoption 的判断框架。
275	
276	第三类是技术或产品评估者。他们关心稳定性、集成能力、数据安全、准确率、可控性、与现有系统的兼容。给他们发技术边界、产品架构、数据安全、评估方法、失败场景和真实限制。
277	
278	第四类是行业意见领袖和早期传播者。他们关心新观点、新范式、可转述的判断。给他们发反常识洞察、行业机制、未来趋势和概念框架。
279	
280	所以，你的内容矩阵应该是：
281	
282	行业判断内容：解释为什么这个问题重要
283	问题定义内容：指出用户真正的低效在哪里
284	工作流内容：展示 AI 如何嵌入真实流程
285	产品证据内容：用案例、数据、demo 证明有效
286	创始人现场内容：展示你如何做产品、理解客户和做取舍
287	一句话结论：
288	
289	AI 产品创始人的内容思维，不是把个人 IP 做大，而是把内容变成公司教育市场、筛选用户、降低信任成本、推动产品 adoption 的组织系统。
290	```

293	
294	![图像](https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HI_AZgQaYAAUsjN?format=jpg&name=large)
295	
296	完整回答：
297	
298	```text
299	这个问题需要从“创始人怎么做内容”升维到“AI 产品公司如何构建市场教育和需求转化系统”。
300	
301	AI 产品的难点，不只是用户不知道你，而是用户不知道自己该如何改变现有工作方式。传统产品很多时候是在已有品类里竞争，比如 CRM、项目管理、设计工具，用户已经知道大概买什么。但 AI 产品经常在创造新工作流，用户的问题不是“选哪一家”，而是“我为什么要改变原来的工作方式”。
302	
303	所以，内容在 AI 产品公司的产业位置，不只是品牌传播，而是连接“技术能力”和“用户工作流”的中间层。
304	
305	从价值链看，AI 产品公司一般处在基础模型和具体用户场景之间。基础模型提供能力，但用户真正购买的是场景里的结果。内容的作用，就是把抽象的模型能力翻译成具体的业务收益：
306	
307	模型能力
308	→ 产品功能
309	→ 工作流场景
310	→ 用户收益
311	→ 预算理由
312	→ 购买与留存

1	# X 上的 雪踏乌云：“Markdown正在变成AI的语言，而HTML正在变成你的” / X
2	
3	https://x.com/Pluvio9yte/status/2058008355353108654?s=20
4	
5	Markdown正从“人类友好的写作语法”演变为“AI最优的序列化协议”，而HTML则重新成为人类消费复杂信息的默认UI层。
6	
7	最近构建了一个内容生产流水线：**Human -> Markdown -> LLM -> HTML -> Human (Reader)**。
8	
9	具体来说，我使用Markdown撰写公众号文章初稿，由LLM将其转换为带有主题样式（如“秋日暖光”）的HTML片段，随后直接粘贴至公众号编辑器。读者最终消费的是经过语义编排与视觉增强的HTML。
10	
11	这个流程中，一个角色关系发生了根本性变化：
12	
13	- **Markdown** 不再是面向人类的最终呈现格式，而是**人与AI之间的通信协议**。
14	- **HTML** 不再是需要手动编写的复杂标记，而是**AI面向读者的渲染目标**。
15	
16	一旦意识到这一点，就无法回到“Markdown优先为人”的旧认知。
17	
18	**为什么Markdown更适合AI，HTML更适合人？**
19	
20	从语言模型处理的角度分析，Markdown具备以下工程优势：
21	
22	- **Token效率高**：同等语义下，Markdown比富文本或HTML的token消耗更低。
23	- **结构低负担**：以#、-、1.等轻量标记表示层级，解析成本极低。
24	- **语义明确**：标题、列表、引用、代码块有明确边界，便于分段、续写、切片和embedding。
25	- **Diff友好**：版本控制和增量修改非常清晰。
26	- **RAG友好**：向量化时，自然语言+轻标记的组合比混入大量标签噪声更稳定。
27	
28	因此，Markdown正逐渐成为**LLM的事实中间语言**，尤其适合作为prompt、few-shot示例和工具调用的上下文格式。
29	
30	**HTML的人性优势**
31	
32	当信息量增大时，纯Markdown暴露出对人阅读不友好的问题：
33	
34	- **无视觉锚点**：缺乏排版带来的层次感，用户需要自行进行注意力分拣。
35	- **无信息边界**：所有内容线性排列，无法快速区分主次、补充或元信息。
36	- **无交互能力**：无法折叠、展开、悬浮提示、异步加载。
37	
38	而HTML天然具备三个层面的能力，正是大信息量下人类需要的：
39	
40	- **语义层**：<article>、<section>、<aside> 表达内容角色。
41	- **结构层**：嵌套与盒子模型形成信息层级和视觉距离。
42	- **交互层**：<details>/<summary>、<dialog>、悬停等组件实现可控的信息暴露。
43	
44	简单说：**Markdown擅长“表达内容是什么”，HTML擅长“定义信息怎么被消费”**。
45	
46	传统Web内容栈：
47	
48	> 人写HTML / Markdown → 浏览器 / 渲染器 → 人读
49	
50	AI介入后的新栈（以我的工作流为例）：
51	
52	> 人写Markdown (作为意图) → AI理解与转换 → HTML (作为渲染目标) → 人读
53	
54	这里的关键变化有两个：
55	
56	1. **Markdown的使用者变了**：之前是人为了“少写标签”而用它；现在是AI为了“高解析效率”而需要它。
57	2. **HTML的生产者变了**：之前是人手写或模板生成；现在是AI动态生成，并且可以根据阅读场景做自适应。
58	
59	回到最开始的公众号写作场景，我建议的工程实践是：
60	
61	- **Markdown作为源语言**：人写作和AI理解的最优交集。
62	- **LLM作为编译器**：将Markdown编译为目标HTML，可注入主题、响应式、交互组件。
63	- **HTML作为发布产物**：直接粘贴到公众号或其他平台。
64	
65	这个模式不只适用于文章，也适用于AI报告、数据分析、代码解释、知识库问答等一切信息量较大的输出场景。

1	# X 上的 Zorrot Chen：“Agent-as-a-Service：由Aeon出发的Agent Autonomy狂想曲” / X
2	
3	https://x.com/ZorrotChen/status/2058076393276383728?s=20
4	
5	以下内容为技术分析，不构成投资建议
6	
7	避免你不知道 [@aeonframework](https://x.com/@aeonframework) 是什么：aeno是由 [@aaronjmars](https://x.com/@aaronjmars)（不是一个有很多头衔的dev）开发的一款Agent驱动的任务自动执行程序。通过克隆仓库，部署在github action上，再接入订阅方案，即可驱动Agent按照你的初始化设定，不停机的持续执行任务。
8	
9	如果你了解我，应该知道我很不喜欢openclaw，并且在其出现时就预言它很快会凉掉。说这个不是为了显的我厉害，而是因为我有一套自己的Agent发展观：Agent的存在不应该长期依赖部分懂技术的C端用户自己折腾，而应该像Saas（software-as-a-service）时代那样，让少部分精通技术的开发者，可以开放它们的专家Agent，为其他用户直接解决问题。
10	
11	我不会昧着良心说Aeon是什么尖端技术，最近也存在一些fud声音质疑它的价值。我个人的粗浅看法：
12	
13	（1）实际上，AI时代软件工程已经不存在什么真正的创新，也没有什么不能被攻破的技术了，可能唯一能让另外一个dev服气的，只有你的地位和名气；
14	
15	（2）一个看起来并不算非常新颖的东西，但是可以非常Smooth的去Work，这是非常难得的（这也是Hermes做的比Openclaw好的地方）；
16	
17	（3）这个方案实际上相当有意思，用Github Action实际上是一个巧妙的选择，解决了在线问题，成本问题以及透明性（自治）问题。
18	
19	但Aeon只是另外一个巨大的故事的第一步。
20	
21	## 怎么定义AasS？
22	
23	如之前所说，AasS（Agent-as-a-Service） 是一种思想，Agent应该和传统的Sass服务一样去为最终交付负责，而不是作为解决问题种一小部分的工具。虽然没有很多人去提这个概念，但实际上这种做法已经非常普遍了：例如，你可以用claude做设计，你可以用gemini做网页，可以用kimi做PPT，等。 但这和真正的Aass的理想还是不完全一样，或者说，这是Aass为什么不同于Saas的原因：对于Saas而言，以人为中心，解决需求，交付结果，就足够了。但如果Aass依然停留在这一层，可以说这只是一种Saas的技术变种，无非是把原先的一些程序化的模块换成了Agent，这不会改变它的本质。我认为Aass必须具有以下特征： （1）它不是为了解决“某一个需求”而生，而是需要有能力解决“某一类需求”。
24	
25	（2）它对自身的迭代和维护最少限度的依赖人类dev，而是可以依靠自进化来适应需求的变化。
26	
27	（3）它的运作必定不能依赖人类的交互，而是需要一套完整的自治逻辑。
28	
29	实际上任何一正规的产业肯定会需要安全，隐私，合规等需求，但这个属于废话，所以就按下不表。
30	
31	## Aeon和AasS有什么关系
32	
33	自治（以及24小时不停机）是AasS最基本的要求，而实际上目前关注这点并且有实际的，令人眼前一亮的方案的产品很少。这也是我对Agent发展的一个重要判断：对Autonomy的需求已经开始比Harness更加迫切了（因为其实现在的Harness技术和方法论已经做得不错的）。你不能永远指望用户在本地挂着他的codex或者openclaw，来实现各种自动化需求，包括办公，信息收集，运营，实时解决Issue等。
34	
35	Aeon迈出的第一步，就是对自治问题提出了一个虽然不那么华丽，但是切实可用的解决方案（我想我完全能够用在我的下一个产品里面 ）。
36	
37	这个方案有它的缺陷：基于github repo对于非技术用户有明显的门槛，同时它无法满足私有化部署的需求。
38	
39	但是优点更加明显：他有一键式的template给你使用，技术用户可以快速部署，并且潜在能够将其改造为一种完整的的服务，而且背靠github还给予了Agent运作不可估量的安全性（当然讽刺的是，最近Github还被攻破了，但即便如此，我肯定更加相信github action而不是一个部署在vps上的openclaw）。
40	
41	## AaaS的下一步
42	
43	有趣的事情是，我几乎能够看到AaaS实现路径上的所有原件，只要将他们缝合起来似乎就能够达到我们的目标：Harness和Skill目前有海量的资源，自治可以依靠 Aeon，自进化可以依赖 Evomap，解决问题可以依赖更加强大的Base model和tool call，所以，问题解决了吗？没有。
44	
45	真正的问题是我们没有准备好。
46	
47	这是一个完全不同的，对Agent的维度和评价标准。一个Agent是否有价值，不再取决于它某次回答是否惊艳，某一次是否能解决问题，而取决于它能不能长期存在，能不能稳定工作，能不能被约束，能不能在出错后自我恢复，能不能让用户对一个Agent服务产生信任。
48	
49	所以我乐于看到Aeon生态的爆发，这当然不是终局，这是个开始，一场对Agent Autonomy的公开考试 - 它们究竟是否值得信任，是否能够进行稳定，正确的交付。

1	# 如何从0到1做创始人品牌
2	
3	https://x.com/jch47643085/status/2055232731315847303?s=20
4	
5	创始人应该有个账号
6	
7	这件事从24年就开始有人聊，25 年开始流行，养活了一批 IP 操盘手。
8	
9	今天创始人做账号这件事的共识已经从“要不要做”来到了“该怎么做”。但根据我这两年的观察：
10	
11	**大部分账号都做不起来**
12	
13	要么追随热点昙花一现不知所云，要么美其名曰垂直精准自然，却不温不火。
14	
15	常见的解读是将之归为 IP 与自媒体的不同：自媒体追求流量，所以要做人设、打爆款。而 IP 积累信任，所以要垂直与真实。老板应该追求真实。
16	
17	**有道理，但还不够。**
18	
19	创始人做账号的一定是为了更简单地成交服务的，不管是顾客还是资本。所以账号核心的目的就一个：
20	
21	减小交易摩擦
22	
23	这与品牌的概念是一样的。所以换一个表述会更好理解：创始人品牌。
24	
25	**Founder brand.**
26	
27	以下内容围绕如何做好创始人品牌展开：
28	
29	## 创始人做账号做不起来一般都是这几种情况
30	
31	**一、不知道讲什么**
32	
33	这类创始人起码是自己主动发内容，这是好的。
34	
35	但问题往往是，今天发产品、明天发行业、后天发热点。他们不缺少行业经验和观点。但很难形成稳定的内容输出。
36	
37	当表达欲来了，路边遇到条狗都想夸两句；当表达欲消失，则对着输入框无法下笔。由于输出难以稳定，又缺乏持续的正反馈，最终草草了事。
38	
39	**二、把内容交给团队**
40	
41	还有一大批老板把创始人账号交给运营团队。
42	
43	但往往没时间自己做内容的老板也不会给运营团队留下足够多的上下文。这就导致团队产出的内容 “还可以，但不够好，不像我”
44	
45	自己说哪里不够好也说不清楚，但就是没有创始人自己的神韵。然后运营团队换了一批又一批，寄希望于Boss直聘。
46	
47	**三、把内容交给AI**
48	
49	还有些人开始让 AI 辅助做内容、写文案。
50	
51	但大多数创始人都没有在互联网上沉淀足够多的语料，AI也无法真正模仿创始人的语气，风格。
52	
53	AI生成的内容中庸、正确、但缺少灵魂。
54	
55	在我见过的创始人里十有八九都是这些情况。
56	
57	每当我深度交流一个充满理想的创始人，但发现他们的账号表达不出灵魂的十分之一时。我都坚信能产出一套让灵魂被看见的方法论是有意义的，尤其在AI时代。
58	
59	# 如何从0到1做创始人品牌
60	
61	第一步，很多MCN出身的操盘手会告诉你立人设、找对标。我认为这不对，包装出来的人设是持续输出的阻力。
62	
63	能成为创始人的人天生不缺故事与愿力、你不需要人设，你需要的只是一些方法。
64	
65	## 创始人品牌的三维坐标系
66	
67	对你的内容建立一个坐标系，就像高中学立体几何一样
68	
69	**X轴：你是谁**
70	
71	喜欢上一个人比喜欢上一个品牌容易一千倍。
72	
73	这个坐标轴承载了创始人的故事，经历，生活，价值观。你的用户比起想了解你的产品，更想知道的是：是谁在做，他为什么做，他相信什么。
74	
75	比如华人老板的硅谷生活、比如九死一生的创业经历、比如瞬间的人生感悟。这些内容无法对标，他们是独一无二的。
76	
77	**Y轴：你的产品**
78	
79	这个坐标轴要讲清楚你的交付，你的产品是什么、功能、优势、更新迭代、愿景。创始人品牌是为交付服务的，
80	
81	比如你做的是一款AI应用，你可以介绍产品价值，记录产品更新，用户的实际使用案例。再比如你做的是一项服务，可以记录方法论、客户案例。
82	
83	**Z轴：行业信息差**
84	
85	作为在所在行业深耕过几年的创始人，或多或少都有对行业的独特见解。这就是信息差：你知道，而离行业中心远的人不知道。
86	
87	对趋势的判断、超出平均水平的讲解，以及独特的视角，对行业热点的观点。这些往往是最容易带来好看的数据的。
88	
89	比如 AI 应用开发者可以讨论新技术范式，币圈创始人可以漫谈行业沉浮，创投圈的人可以分析投融资现状。无需担心自己的洞察不够深。在满是 AI 的信息流中，有业内活人背书的信息最值钱。
90	
91	## 内容不能偏离坐标系
92	
93	建立了创始人品牌的三维坐标系后，你的所有内容都可以当做一个向量放在坐标系内。内容与坐标轴越相关，对应的数值越大。
94	
95	如果该向量的模，也就是距离原点的长度很长，那它起码从选题的角度是一条好内容。
96	
97	举个例子：
98	
99	我现在聚焦的业务是 AI 产品增长与创始人 IP，那我这篇内容则与行业信息高度相关，如果我下文再谈及产品交付，那与我的产品也有一定的相关性，但这篇文章我不想聊我的经历，那与我是谁的相关性就是0。
100	
101	因此，我这篇内容的系数可能是（ 0、60、80），长度为 100。那这就是一篇好内容。
102	
103	再比如我的置顶推文，讲了我从大学学计算机到炒币赚钱的故事，以及对行业的判断，那它的系数用 AI 测了一下就是（94、6、72），长度为 118.56。那么这也是一篇好内容。
104	
105	![图像](https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HIWUu0TbwAAEavU?format=jpg&name=large)
106	
107	用顶顶推文的三维坐标
108	
109	如果举个反面例子，我之前经常喜欢喊单、晒炒币收益。这与我是谁、我的产品、行业信息差均不相关。那它对我的账号来说就是噪音。
110	
111	## 用 AI 搭建内容体系
112	
113	AI 从来不是帮你写内容的工具，而是帮你搭建内容体系的工具。
114	
115	**一、帮你搭建创始人品牌的三维坐标**
116	
117	AI 可以帮你将你在互联网上的语料拆分，映射到对应的三个坐标轴上，保存为 .md 文件。
118	
119	这样你的内容会被提炼到三个文件里，分别是：你是谁；你的产品；行业信息差。
120	
121	比如我把我过去的一篇文章《AI 增长的传教理论》喂给 Codex，它可以帮我从三个维度提炼，由我选择是否存入。没错，和前段时间爆火的 Eiys 很像。
122	
123	![图像](https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HIWVCnoawAAi41J?format=jpg&name=large)
124	
125	三个维度提炼内容
126	
127	**二、帮你创建创始人品牌的语料库**
128	
129	让 AI 更懂你、更像你，一直是 AI 生成内容的难题。在我的 Obsidian 里密密麻麻存了上千条我在互联网上留下的痕迹。但我想让 AI 基于我的语料替我写内容时，感觉如下：
130	
131	![图像](https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HIWV1robgAAbGyE?format=jpg&name=large)
132	
133	开塞露
134	
135	AI 经常会莫名其妙地将我过去提到的毫不相关的往事拿出来提一嘴，就像在说：“看我多懂你，连这都知道”
136	
137	而当你用这个三维坐标系去保存记忆，生成的内容就不会那么莫名其妙。让 AI 的记忆完全围绕你的创始人品牌保存。当三个文件都达到百分之百，你的 AI 就真正懂你的品牌了。
138	
139	![图像](https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HIWV8XQaEAAjdfs?format=jpg&name=large)
140	
141	Memory 积累进度
142	
143	**三、检验你的内容相关度**
144	
145	如何避免东一榔头西一棒槌地发内容，最好的办法就是直接将内容放到三维坐标系里检验。
146	
147	就像我这篇《如何讲好一个故事》，放在坐标系里，它会根据文章本身内容以及 Memory 中的数据检验相关性。
148	
149	![图像](https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HIWWF90a0AAWuxn?format=jpg&name=large)
150	
151	检验相关性
152	
153	如果内容检测完发现处在红色区域，也就是说你这篇内容和创始人品牌关系不大，那就要慎重考虑要不要发。
154	
155	**四、AI 替你写内容**
156	
157	我相信不是每一个创始人都对做内容如此热爱，很多人的诉求的一定是解放双手，完全交给 AI。
158	
159	AI 生成的内容永远是中庸且缺少人味的，但你如果给了它足够长的上下文，让它更懂你后，它的产出也勉强可用，起码会比你找一个内容实习生要好。
160	
161	方法是当你交给 AI 一个写作任务时，让 AI 在三维坐标系里自行迭代，比如设定一个标准，让 AI 迭代到分数高于 120 分再输出。
162	
163	另一个指标是 AI 有多了解你的创始人品牌。当它足够懂你，它才能输出像你的内容。变成一个可量化的指标，就是“可信度”，这取决于你在三个文件里累积了多少 memory。
164	
165	![图像](https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HIWWO0raMAASyn3?format=jpg&name=large)
166	
167	AI生成内容
168	
169	比如说我让他写一个“ 就罗永浩加入 Twitter 这个事件写一篇 500 字的文案”
170	
171	AI 生成的内容分数达到 130，但可信度为 4，说明它还是不够懂我。
172	
173	最后为了方便，我把这套流程打包成 Skill 放在 GitHub 上了。我称之为Founder Brand 1.0 版本，后续还会有 2.0、3.0。 GitHub：[https://github.com/MaxJiang103/founder-brand.git](https://github.com/MaxJiang103/founder-brand.git)
174	
175	**最后的最后：创始人品牌不只是一个账号，而是围绕创始人本人的增长内容体系。**
176	
177	**欢迎拥有有趣灵魂的创始人来交流内容，也欢迎拥有产品 sense 的天才来一起让它更好玩。**
178	
179	**让好的产品被看见，让优秀的人被看见，这是有趣的事。**

# 提问方法论与升维

> [!abstract]- AI 摘要
> 高质量提问不是索取信息，而是提出可验证、可拆解、可升维的判断。通过假设驱动、结构化和框架分析，将宽泛问题升维为触及商业本质的核心问题。

---

## 扫读

> [!tip] 💡 一句话
> 好问题的本质不是"我想知道什么"，而是"我初步判断什么可能是真的"——用假设驱动将宽泛的索取升维为可被验证的判断。

> [!important] 📌 关键结论
> - 提问质量决定行业理解深度：差问题带我走向平庸答案，好问题直接推进到行业结构内部，二者之间存在"必须先懂才能问好"的悖论，只能通过方法论打破
> - 问题升维的五把手术刀：假设驱动（从猜测出发）、结构拆解（MECE逻辑树）、3C框架（客户/公司/竞争者）、利润池分析（谁掌握控制点）、极端场景压力测试
> - 创始人内容的终极问题不是"如何做爆款"，而是"如何通过持续输出行业判断，获得问题解释权，从而降低获客成本、销售成本和信任成本"

> [!quote] 🎬 可行动项
> - 将每个模糊问题重写为包含假设、边界和变量的可验证判断
> - 用3C框架审查自己的业务问题是否只看了公司视角
> - 对关键判断施加极端场景压力测试：如果毛利降30%、获客成本不再下降，谁会活下来

---

## 精读

### 论证链

```
行业理解悖论：
不懂行业时无法问好问题
      ↓
打破悖论的方法：不从事"想知道什么"开始，
而是从"我判断什么可能是真的"开始（假设驱动）
      ↓
五大提问框架升维：
  ① 假设驱动：从开放式索取 → 可验证判断
    例："AI创业还有机会吗？"→"我假设通用AI工具会被平台吞掉，嵌入垂直工作流的应用才是机会，对吗？"
  ② 结构性：从一团乱麻 → MECE逻辑树
    收入、成本、毛利、获客成本、复购率、规模效应、定价权、风险承担
  ③ 3C框架：从只盯公司 → Customer/Company/Competitor三角
    创始人做内容→在目标客户心智中建立区别于竞品的问题解释权
  ④ 利润池分析：从问"谁热闹"→问"利润、权力、价值如何分配"
    表面看增长，深层看价值链位置和控制点
  ⑤ 极端场景测试：从预测趋势→识别压力下谁能存活
    降毛利30%+获客成本不降→哪些企业还能活？
      ↓
问题升维实操演示：
原始："创始人如何在Twitter做爆款内容？"(38分,白银级)
      ↓
升维一："创始人如何通过内容，在目标客户心智中建立区别于竞争对手的问题解释权？"
      ↓
升维二："创始人应该持续输出哪一类行业判断，使目标客户在理解问题时自然采用我的框架，并因此更容易信任我的产品？"
      ↓
终极升维："AI产品公司如何通过内容系统，持续定义用户问题、教育市场、建立信任，并把产品理念转化为用户愿意采用的新工作流？"
      ↓
结论：创始人的Twitter爆款不是最大化流量，而是把核心商业判断包装成可传播、可信任、可转化的公共表达——本质是争夺问题解释权
```

### 关键引述

> 一个好问题比一个好答案重要，这已经是行业共识了。

> 一个差问题，会把你带向一堆平庸答案。一个好问题，会直接把你推进到行业结构里。

> 真正的壁垒不是顺风时看起来强，而是在逆风、价格战、政策变化、技术替代、大厂进入时还能支撑公司活下来。

> 创始人的Twitter爆款，不是最大化流量，而是把公司的核心商业判断包装成可传播、可信任、可转化的公共表达。

> 内容在AI产品公司的产业位置，不只是品牌传播，而是连接"技术能力"和"用户工作流"的中间层。

> 这是一个答案泛滥的时代，好问题更加稀缺。是那些带着好奇心的提问者，推动着人类文明的发展。

### 局限与盲区

- 本文未覆盖：如何评估问题的答案质量（只聚焦提问端）；非商业场景（如学术研究、个人决策）的提问方法未展开；对提问者的领域知识基线要求未量化
- 隐含假设：假设提问者有足够的行业认知来形成初始假设，但新手可能连初步判断都无法形成；假设答案提供方（如AI/专家）有足够能力回答升维后的问题
- 可能的反例：过度追求问题升维可能导致分析瘫痪（一直问而迟迟不行动）；某些探索性场景下，开放式提问比假设驱动更适合发现未知的未知；极窄的实操决策（如"选哪个CRM"）可能不需要反复升维

---

# Markdown作为AI协议

> [!abstract]- AI 摘要
> 在AI介入的内容生产管线中，Markdown从"人类友好的写作语法"演变为"AI最优的序列化协议"，而HTML重新成为人类消费复杂信息的默认UI层。人写MD表达意图，AI编译为HTML供人阅读。

---

## 扫读

> [!tip] 💡 一句话
> Markdown正从面向人类的写作格式，变为人与AI之间的通信协议；HTML不再是需要手写的标记语言，而是AI生成给人类读者的渲染产物。

> [!important] 📌 关键结论
> - 角色翻转：Markdown的使用者从"想少写标签的人"变为"需要高解析效率的AI"；HTML的生产者从"人手写/模板生成"变为"AI动态自适应生成"
> - Markdown对AI的五项工程优势：Token效率高、结构负担低、语义边界明确、Diff友好、RAG友好——这些使MD成为LLM的事实中间语言
> - 新内容栈范式：Human → Markdown（意图层）→ LLM（编译器）→ HTML（渲染目标）→ Human Reader，适用于公众号、AI报告、知识库问答等信息密集型场景

> [!quote] 🎬 可行动项
> - 在AI辅助写作流程中，采用Markdown作为源语言而不是直接在编辑器里写富文本
> - 将LLM视为"Markdown→HTML编译器"，可注入主题、响应式和交互组件
> - 在AI报告和数据分析输出场景中优先使用HTML作为发布格式，利用其语义层、结构层和交互层优势

---

## 精读

### 论证链

```
传统内容栈：
人写Markdown/HTML → 浏览器渲染 → 人读
      ↓
问题：两者面向同一主体（人），Markdown只是HTML的简化写法
      ↓
AI介入后的范式转换：
  ① Markdown的使用者变了：
     旧：人为了"少写标签"而用MD
     新：AI为了"高解析效率"而需要MD
     理由：Token效率高、结构负担低、语义边界明确、Diff友好、RAG友好
  ② HTML的生产者变了：
     旧：人手写或后端模板生成
     新：AI动态生成，可按阅读场景做自适应
     理由：<article>/<section>/<aside>语义层 + 盒子模型结构层 + <details>/<dialog>交互层
      ↓
新内容栈确定：
Human → Markdown（作为意图表达）
      ↓
LLM（作为编译器，注入主题/响应式/交互）
      ↓
HTML（作为发布产物，直接可粘贴到平台）
      ↓
Human Reader（消费经过语义编排与视觉增强的内容）
      ↓
新分工原理：
  Markdown擅长"表达内容是什么"→ 轻量、高效、机器友好
  HTML擅长"定义信息怎么被消费"→ 层次感、视觉锚点、交互控制
      ↓
对比纯Markdown的人阅读缺陷：
  无视觉锚点 → 注意力分拣困难
  无信息边界 → 无法区分主次/补充/元信息
  无交互能力 → 不可折叠/展开/悬浮提示
      ↓
工程实践建议：Markdown作为源语言是人与AI的最优交集；LLM作为编译器输出HTML；HTML作为发布产物直接对接平台
```

### 关键引述

> Markdown正从"人类友好的写作语法"演变为"AI最优的序列化协议"，而HTML则重新成为人类消费复杂信息的默认UI层。

> 一旦意识到这一点，就无法回到"Markdown优先为人"的旧认知。

> Markdown擅长"表达内容是什么"，HTML擅长"定义信息怎么被消费"。

> Markdown正逐渐成为LLM的事实中间语言，尤其适合作为prompt、few-shot示例和工具调用的上下文格式。

> 这个模式不只适用于文章，也适用于AI报告、数据分析、代码解释、知识库问答等一切信息量较大的输出场景。

### 局限与盲区

- 本文未覆盖：MD→HTML编译的工程细节（如何注入主题变量、如何保持语义一致性）；交互式HTML的原生浏览器兼容性问题；非文本内容（图表、数据可视化）在MD→HTML流程中的处理方案
- 隐含假设：假设AI生成的HTML质量稳定且语义无误，但实际中可能会出现标签错误或语义偏差；假设所有目标平台都接受HTML粘贴，但某些平台会过滤或限制HTML标签
- 可能的反例：纯文本场景（如命令行输出、短信通知）可能不需要HTML层；高度交互的应用场景（如仪表盘、实时协同编辑）可能需要JavaScript而不仅是静态HTML；某些用户群体（如偏好纯文本的技术用户）可能更接受Markdown直接阅读

---

- [[多Agent团队协作]]

# Agent即服务Aeon自治

> [!abstract]- AI 摘要
> Agent-as-a-Service (AaaS) 主张Agent应像SaaS一样为最终交付负责，而非仅仅是解决问题的工具组件。Aeon通过GitHub Action实现Agent的不停机自治运行，迈出了Agent Autonomy从概念到工程实践的第一步。

---

## 扫读

> [!tip] 💡 一句话
> Agent的未来不在于让懂技术的C端用户自己折腾，而在于让开发者开放专家Agent作为服务，像SaaS时代一样为最终用户直接解决问题——Aeon的GitHub Action方案是自治的第一步工程化尝试。

> [!important] 📌 关键结论
> - AaaS区别于SaaS的三个核心特征：解决"某一类需求"而非"某一个需求"、最少限度依赖人类dev进行自进化、具备不依赖人类交互的完整自治逻辑
> - Aeon的核心创新：将Agent部署在GitHub Action上，一次性解决了在线持续运行、成本可控和透明性（自治可审计）三个问题——方案不华丽但切实可用
> - Agent行业正从"Harness优先"转向"Autonomy优先"：你不能永远指望用户在本地挂着codex或openclaw来实现自动化，稳定交付和可信任比单次惊艳更重要

> [!quote] 🎬 可行动项
> - 评估当前Agent流程是否依赖本地运行和人工触发，探索GitHub Action等持续运行方案
> - 将Agent的评价标准从"单次表现"转向"长期稳定性、出错自恢复、交付可信度"
> - 关注Aeon生态的演化，特别是非技术用户门槛和私有化部署的进展

---

## 精读

### 论证链

```
当前Agent困境：
懂技术的C端用户自己折腾部署Agent
      ↓
问题：这种方式不可持续——
  ① 用户必须在本地挂着codex/openclaw
  ② 无法24小时不停机运行
  ③ 非技术用户被排除在外
      ↓
核心主张：Agent应像SaaS一样演进
  SaaS时代：少数开发者开发服务 → 广大用户直接使用
  AaaS时代：少数开发者开放专家Agent → 广大用户直接受益
      ↓
AaaS的三个核心特征（区别于SaaS的技术变种）：
  ① 解决"某一类需求"而非"某一个需求"
  ② 自进化：最少限度依赖人类dev，适应需求变化
  ③ 完整自治逻辑：不依赖人类交互进行运作
      ↓
Aeon的方案——自治的第一步工程化：
  部署方式：克隆仓库 → GitHub Action → 接入订阅方案 → Agent不停机执行任务
  优势：
    · 一键模板，技术用户快速部署
    · GitHub Action解决24小时在线问题
    · 背靠GitHub提供安全性和透明性（运行可审计）
    · 成本可控
  局限：
    · 基于GitHub repo对非技术用户有门槛
    · 无法满足私有化部署需求
      ↓
自治需求已比Harness更迫切：
  Harness技术和方法论已足够成熟
  但缺少让Agent长期稳定运行的自治方案
      ↓
AaaS下一步需要缝合的组件：
  Harness/Skill（海量资源）+ Aeon（自治）+ Evomap（自进化）+ 更强Base Model
  → 但这些还不够
      ↓
真正的挑战：评价标准的范式转移
  旧标准：某次回答是否惊艳，某次能否解决问题
  新标准：
    · 能否长期存在并稳定工作
    · 能否被约束、在出错后自我恢复
    · 能否让用户对Agent服务产生信任
      ↓
Aeon不是终局，而是Agent Autonomy的公开考试——考验Agent是否值得信任、能否稳定正确交付
```

### 关键引述

> Agent的存在不应该长期依赖部分懂技术的C端用户自己折腾，而应该像SaaS时代那样，让少部分精通技术的开发者可以开放它们的专家Agent，为其他用户直接解决问题。

> 对Autonomy的需求已经开始比Harness更加迫切了。你不能永远指望用户在本地挂着他的codex或者openclaw，来实现各种自动化需求。

> 一个Agent是否有价值，不再取决于它某次回答是否惊艳，某一次是否能解决问题，而取决于它能不能长期存在，能不能稳定工作，能不能被约束，能不能在出错后自我恢复，能不能让用户对一个Agent服务产生信任。

> 这不是终局，这是个开始，一场对Agent Autonomy的公开考试——它们究竟是否值得信任，是否能够进行稳定、正确的交付。

### 局限与盲区

- 本文未覆盖：Aeon的具体架构细节和代码实现；自进化（Evomap）的具体机制和可行性验证；多Agent之间的协调和冲突解决；安全、隐私、合规等的具体处理方案
- 隐含假设：假设GitHub Action的可靠性足以支撑生产级Agent服务；假设Agent自治的"自进化"在技术上是可实现的（可能存在过度乐观）；假设用户愿意将任务委托给"看不见"的自治Agent
- 可能的反例：某些任务场景（如需要物理世界交互、需要实时人类判断）可能永远无法完全自治；GitHub作为中心化平台可能带来单点故障和平台依赖风险；过于自治的Agent可能在出错时造成连锁反应而无人及时干预

# 创始人品牌三维坐标系

> [!abstract]- AI 摘要
> 创始人品牌的核心目的是减小交易摩擦。通过"你是谁-X轴/你的产品-Y轴/行业信息差-Z轴"三维坐标系，将内容从随性发散变为可量化、可持续、可用AI系统化管理的品牌资产。

---

## 扫读

> [!tip] 💡 一句话
> 创始人做账号不是为了流量，而是为了减小交易摩擦——三维坐标系（你是谁/你的产品/行业信息差）是实现可持续输出的最小模型。

> [!important] 📌 关键结论
> - 创始人品牌的核心不是立人设找对标，而是围绕"你是谁、你的产品、行业信息差"建立三维内容坐标系，所有内容作为向量落在这个坐标系中，向量模越长=选题质量越高
> - 大部分账号做不起来的三种死法：不知道讲什么（表达欲不稳定）、交给团队（缺少上下文）、交给AI（缺少个人语料）——根源都是缺乏系统化的内容坐标
> - AI的正确角色不是替你写内容，而是帮你搭建内容体系：提炼三维坐标语料库、检验内容相关度、在坐标系内迭代生成、量化"可信度"——当三个维度的memory文件都达到100%，AI才真正懂你的品牌

> [!quote] 🎬 可行动项
> - 用X/Y/Z三维坐标审视自己过去10条内容，标记每条的坐标分值，识别偏离品牌的"噪音内容"
> - 将自己在互联网上的语料按三个维度拆分成"你是谁.md""你的产品.md""行业信息差.md"三个memory文件
> - 在发布前将内容放入三维坐标系检验，处于"红色区域"（与三个轴均弱相关）的内容慎重发布

---

## 精读

### 论证链

```
创始人做账号的共识演进：
2024年："要不要做" → 2025年："该怎么做"
      ↓
但现实：大部分账号都做不起来
      ↓
常见解读（不够）：
自媒体追求流量=做人设打爆款 | IP积累信任=垂直真实
      ↓
重新定义：创始人账号的根本目的=减小交易摩擦=创始人品牌(Founder Brand)
      ↓
三种失败模式的根因分析：
  ① 不知道讲什么：主题跳变、依赖表达欲 → 缺少内容坐标系
  ② 交给团队：缺少上下文、产出"不像我" → 认知未外化为系统
  ③ 交给AI：缺少个人语料、输出中庸正确 → AI缺少结构化记忆
      ↓
解决方案：三维坐标系方法论
  X轴「你是谁」：故事、经历、生活、价值观
    → 用户想知道的是"谁在做、为什么做、相信什么"
  Y轴「你的产品」：功能、优势、迭代、客户案例、方法论
    → 创始人品牌为交付服务
  Z轴「行业信息差」：趋势判断、独特视角、高于平均的讲解
    → 有业内活人背书的信息最值钱
      ↓
内容向量化评估：
  每条内容=(X分,Y分,Z分) → 模长=√(X²+Y²+Z²)
  例：本文(0,60,80)→长度100=好内容
  反例：喊单晒收益(与三轴均不相关)=噪音
      ↓
AI的正确用法——搭建体系而非代写：
  步骤1：用AI提炼三维坐标语料库（三个.md文件）
  步骤2：用AI基于三维坐标生成内容（避免"开塞露"式乱引用）
  步骤3：用坐标系检验内容相关度（红色区域=慎重发布）
  步骤4：让AI在坐标系内自行迭代，分数>120再输出
  量化指标：可信度=三个memory文件的积累进度
      ↓
终极定义：创始人品牌不只是一个账号，而是围绕创始人本人的增长内容体系
```

### 关键引述

> 包装出来的人设是持续输出的阻力。能成为创始人的人天生不缺故事与愿力、你不需要人设，你需要的只是一些方法。

> 喜欢上一个人比喜欢上一个品牌容易一千倍。

> 在满是AI的信息流中，有业内活人背书的信息最值钱。

> AI从来不是帮你写内容的工具，而是帮你搭建内容体系的工具。

> AI生成的内容永远是中庸且缺少人味的，但你如果给了它足够长的上下文，让它更懂你后，它的产出也勉强可用，起码会比你找一个内容实习生要好。

> 创始人品牌不只是一个账号，而是围绕创始人本人的增长内容体系。

> 让好的产品被看见，让优秀的人被看见，这是有趣的事。

### 局限与盲区

- 本文未覆盖：三个维度各自的权重如何动态调整（不同阶段创始人的侧重点不同）；实际内容分发策略和平台算法匹配；创始人品牌的变现路径和ROI测量方法；多平台（Twitter之外的平台）的适配策略
- 隐含假设：假设创始人具备持续产出行业洞察的能力，但某些行业的创始人可能真的缺乏可说的信息差；假设"减小交易摩擦"只是内容问题，但实际上产品力、市场时机、价格策略同等重要
- 可能的反例：某些创始人通过极度极化的个人风格（与产品无关）获得了巨大品牌效应，三维坐标可能无法解释这类案例；B2B创始人和B2C创始人的内容策略可能需要不同的坐标系；早期阶段创始人可能需要先追热点获取初始关注再收敛到坐标体系

1	# 给人文工作者的 AI 使用指南
2	
3	https://x.com/HanyangWang/status/2029362155607474359?s=20
4	
5	![图像](https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HCkrCVba4AAQ92r?format=jpg&name=large)
6	
7	人文工作者没有创造世界变化，但他们却在承受世界变化。
8	
9	有的时候我感觉，那些卖人工智能教程的号总是把 AI 当成一种魔法：给你一个神奇的 prompt，你就能做任何事儿。现实当然不是这样。过去的一段时间里，因为创立了 [FUNES](https://funes.world/), 我们必须每天大量的通过 AI 进行生产。加之还有[《蜉蝣天地》](https://www.youtube.com/@FuyoutiandiMeanders)、我自己的写作等内容生产，光靠人力已经不够了。所以我们大量的尝试如何使用 AI 辅助我们的内容市场与人文学科研究工作。
10	
11	后来公司有新同事入职，我就做了个简单的 Keynote。又一次得到的贾行家老师听说后，就邀请我去做个分享。我和合伙人可达给这个分享起名《给人文工作者的 AI 使用指南》。当时是纯私下的分享，主要是一些大方向上的原则。后来又做过几次，逐渐扩充。
12	
13	不过这个分享一直没公开做过，正好今年和重轻启动了[《诗梳风》](https://shishufeng.com/)这档节目，所以第一次完整公开的聊了一遍。以下文字整理自播客《给人文工作者的 AI 使用指南》，AI 辅助整理，有所缩略。如果你想知道完整版，可以[官网直接收听](https://shishufeng.com/episode/owocaoshiaiwomenyoujiule)，或者在宇宙、[苹果播客](https://podcasts.apple.com/us/podcast/%E8%AF%97%E6%A2%B3%E9%A3%8E/id1870811470)搜索《诗梳风》即可收听。
14	
15	![图像](https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HCm9_ggbgAAfvoi?format=jpg&name=large)
16	
17	小宇宙二维码
18	
19	过去一年多里，把这套怎么用 AI 的经验讲给过很多做内容、做研究、做知识产品的朋友。它的目标不是教你背几个神奇提示词，更不是把 AI 当成灵丹妙药；相反，它更像是一套工作方法：让你在不写代码的前提下，把大模型真正接进自己的写作、研究、编辑、选题、资料整理与生产流程里，并且做到**可追溯、可监督、可验证**，最后你依然愿意在作品上署名。
20	
21	这套方法来自我们在真实项目里踩过的坑：当内容进入规模化生产，纯靠人力会崩；而 AI 直接写一篇又会幻觉、会偷懒、会写得像 AI。于是我们不得不把创作变成产线，把产线变成可迭代的系统。
22	
23	当今天我不想直接给你各种提示词，我希望能给你一些关键的指导思想和原则。
24	
25	## 写在原则之前：这份指南的三条底线
26	
27	在具体方法之前，先明确三条底线。它们决定了你“怎么用 AI”，也决定了你“为什么要这样用”。
28	
29	1. **过程必须可追溯、可监督、可验证** 你不能只要一个结果、不要过程。对人文工作而言，黑箱最危险：幻觉、错引、偷换概念，都会在黑箱里悄悄发生。
30	2. **必须可操纵** 你要能控制它怎么做、按什么标准做、在哪些地方慢一点、在哪些地方严一点。你不是在“抽卡”，你是在生产。
31	3. **最后你依然愿意署名** 「我愿不愿意把名字放上去？」是最终质检。如果你不愿意署名，通常不是道德问题，而是过程里你的意志没有贯彻进去——也就意味着质量不可控。
32	
33	## 原则 0：别对 AI 许愿，把它当作工作台
34	
35	很多人用 AI 的方式，本质是在许愿： “给我一个好段子”“帮我写一篇好文章”“解释这篇论文”。
36	
37	问题在于——**“解释”本身就有无数种解释**：给外行、给本科生、给研究生、给同行，完全不是一个任务。AI 不可能默认知道你的背景、目的、口味和标准。你不说清楚，它就只能用“平均人类”的默认方式糊一份最省力的答案给你。
38	
39	把大模型当工作台，意味着：**你不向它索要结果，而是调动它的工具来完成一个过程**。你要做的是把任务说清楚、把标准说清楚、把步骤安排出来。
40	
41	比如让 AI 解释论文
42	
43	你可以像这样把许愿式请求（给我解释这篇论文）改成工作台式任务：
44	
45	- 明确目标受众：聪明、有好奇心，但不是该领域专家的研究生
46	- 明确讲解方式：启发式、循序渐进、有学术严谨性
47	- 明确结构要求：先讲意义，再补背景，再还原研究历程，再讲关键技术点，再提启示
48	- 明确语气：尊重智力、不居高临下、不假装对方已有深厚基础
49	
50	你会发现：你给得越像“作业要求”，AI 就越不像 AI，越像一个真的会干活的助教。
51	
52	## 原则 1：想要 AI 做好，先反思自己——你才是负责人
53	
54	如果你雇了一个秘书，你不会只说： “把汉洋那篇写美国[锈带的文章改好](https://hanyang.wtf/p/c4b)。”
55	
56	你一定会补充： 这篇文章为什么写、写给谁、现在卡在哪、你希望它解决什么问题、哪些地方不能动、你要什么风格、你最在意的指标是什么。
57	
58	AI 也是一样。你要把它当成一个非常勤奋、非常礼貌、但**不懂你脑内隐含前提**的同事。真正的“提示词工程”不是技巧，而是一种责任感：**任何任务仍然是你在做，AI 只是帮你干活。**
59	
60	当你对 AI 的输出不满意，最有效的第一反应不是“AI 不行”，而是：
61	
62	- 我有没有说清楚“对象/受众/目的”？
63	- 我有没有提供足够的背景材料和约束？
64	- 我有没有把“抽象愿望”拆成“可执行动作”？
65	- 我有没有给到可判断对错的标准？
66	
67	## 原则 2：同一个问题至少问 3 个模型——每个 AI 都有“性格”和擅长领域
68	
69	在我们公司，任何初次接触大模型的同事我会希望他在前期使用中，每个问题问三个不同的 AI。AI 像人一样有差异：有的更擅长写作遣词，有的更擅长推理解题，有的更擅长代码或工具调用。更现实的一点是：同一家产品的模型、同一个模型的新版本，也会不断微调“风格”和“边界”。
70	
71	所以一个很朴素但极有效的习惯是：**同一个问题，至少抛给 3 个不同 AI**，你会快速获得“手感”：
72	
73	- 哪个更会写、哪个更会想、哪个更会查、哪个更容易偷懒
74	- 哪些任务适合谁做“第一稿”，哪些适合谁做“审稿人”
75	- 哪个更适合出“选题/结构”，哪个更适合出“段落/句子”
76	
77	这一步的价值不在于“选出最强模型”，而在于：你开始像管理团队一样管理模型，而不是把它当唯一神谕。
78	
79	## 原则 3：AI 不是全知全能——把它当成“好学校本科生”的常识水平
80	
81	一个很实用的预期管理是： **AI 的常识水平≈一个 985 的本科生。**
82	
83	如果某件事你觉得“一个优秀本科生都未必知道”，那你就应该默认 AI 也不知道；至少默认它会在不知道的时候“编得很像知道”。
84	
85	这会带来两个直接动作：
86	
87	1. **任何超过常识的内容，都要你来教它** 比如：你要它写段子、写真正有独特品味的文案、写高度专业的论证——你不能只给一句“写得好点”，你要给范例、给标准、给禁区、给语料。我相信你现在去和朋友解释你心中什么文字是好的，都需要点时间；那怎么能认为 AI 默认知道呢？
88	2. **你要把它当实习生协作，而不是当神** 它能做很多“微观插值”的工作：把你给的脚手架补全，把你给的材料织成可读文本。但“脚手架”和“方向”仍然来自你。
89	
90	## 原则 4：让 AI 一步一步逼近目标——白盒分步骤，比黑箱一次性更可靠
91	
92	AI 的优势不是“直接给你正确答案”，而是它可以在你设计的流程里，**稳定完成很多小步骤**。你越是要求它“一步到位”，它越容易变成“看似完整、实则偷懒”的黑箱。
93	
94	一个特别直观的例子是做 TTS（文本转语音）或朗读稿的处理。与其说“注意多音字、不要读错”，不如把任务拆成一串步骤，例如：
95	
96	- 标出停顿/重音/语速变化的标记
97	- 识别潜在多音字
98	- 依据词典或权威读音做核对（必要时先检索再确定）
99	- 对容易误读但常见的字提前标注
100	- 实在不行就用**同音无歧义字替换**，从根上消灭误读可能
101	
102	这类“显而易见的正确做法”，人类会默认自己会做；但 AI 不会默认。你不把“显而易见”写进流程，它就会在最省力的路径上犯错。
103	
104	## 原则 5：先工业化，再 AI 化——你不能从农业时代一步跳到 AI 时代
105	
106	如果你的写作/研究流程本身是随机的、凭灵感的、资料不管理的，那你确实很难把它交给 AI。因为 AI 只能接住你“可描述、可复现”的那部分。
107	
108	更现实的路径是：
109	
110	1. 先把工作变成“产线”：可拆分、可复用、可质检
111	2. 再把其中的子步骤交给 AI：让它当工位，而不是当上帝
112	
113	我们做过一个很笨但很关键的工作：把我自己怎么写一篇非虚构文章的过程解出来。包括：
114	
115	- 为什么用这个故事开头
116	- 为什么选这句话
117	- 如何给例子打分
118	- 如何起承转合、如何过渡、如何收尾
119	- 如何把小故事连接到更宏大的图景
120	
121	最后拆成了几十个步骤，让不同的 AI 只做其中一个步骤。结果是： **不是模型突然变强了，而是流程把它“每次只能行一点点”的能力串起来了。**
122	
123	当你能清晰描述“我的文章是怎么做出来的”，你就会发现：决定质量上限的从来不是“用哪个大模型”，而是你有没有把工作方法讲清楚。
124	
125	![图像](https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HCkrsW8awAY5y7S?format=jpg&name=large)
126	
127	当时做测试时的一些步骤
128	
129	不过这段强烈建议你听节目，说得更详细。
130	
131	## 原则 6：预判 AI 会偷懒——它会省算力，你要替它扫清“格式障碍”
132	
133	AI 会偷懒，而且是“系统性偷懒”：能不打开网页就不打开，能不读 PDF 就不读，能跳过就跳过。不是它坏，而是它在算力与时间的约束下，天然倾向于走最省力路径。
134	
135	所以你要做的是：**把 AI 的算力用在“理解文本”，而不是浪费在“处理格式”。**
136	
137	非常有效的改法包括：
138	
139	- 尽量把材料转成纯文本/Markdown，再喂给 AI
140	- 把网页内容复制成干净文本（去掉导航、广告、脚注噪音）
141	- 对长材料先做“事实提炼/结构提取”，再让它写作
142	- 把 PDF/EPUB/网页统一入库成可检索的 TXT，再做后续任务
143	
144	你会发现：很多人抵触这种“体力活”，觉得“机器就该替我干脏活”。但在人机协作里恰恰相反——你愿意做一点点机械劳动，AI 的智力部分才会变得更锋利、更可靠。
145	
146	## 原则 7：记住上下文有限——把任务尽量改成“压缩”，不要指望它“凭空扩张”
147	
148	AI 有上下文窗口，有“记忆上限”。你给它两万字，它未必能记住多少；你给它二十万字，它可能只扫标题。一个形象的类比是：把人关进小房间一天，丢给他一本二十万字的书，出来让他背——能背多少，大概就是 AI 能“记住”的量。
149	
150	因此有一个很反直觉但极重要的经验：
151	
152	- **压缩比扩张容易得多** 把 100 万字压到 1 万字，往往比把 1 万字扩到 100 万字可靠。
153	
154	这直接改变你向 AI 提需求的方式：
155	
156	- 不要用 100 字提示词去要一篇论文
157	- 相反，把材料尽可能喂进去（分批、检索、RAG 都行），让它在充分材料基础上压缩出结构、观点和正文
158	
159	你过去写文章、写论文，本来就是“读海量材料→提炼→组织→写作”（至少我是这样）。到了 AI 这里，不要突然双标，要求它凭空生长。
160	
161	## 原则 8：克制“我妙手一改就好了”的冲动——改产线，不改结果
162	
163	很多擅长写作的人，最容易在 AI 面前翻车： AI 出了个 59 分的稿子，你觉得自己改两下就 80 分，于是你开始改；改着改着变成你重写；重写完你说“还是我自己来吧”，然后从此再也不用 AI。
164	
165	解决办法不是更努力“改稿”，而是把关注点挪到更上游：
166	
167	- 不要追求让 AI 直接写出 100 分
168	- 你的目标是让产线稳定产出 75～80 分
169	- 你要做的是迭代流程，让“平均分”提高，而不是让“单篇”完美
170	
171	## 原则 9：把产线当产品迭代——可靠性本身就是价值
172	
173	当你有一个系统能稳定给你 70 分的起点，它的价值不是“它像不像你”，而是：
174	
175	- 你能在接近零成本的情况下拿到一个可用草稿
176	- 你能把精力集中在更高阶的判断：选题、结构、证据、品味与取舍
177	
178	你要的不是一个能代替你的全能神，而是一个可靠的工厂：它不完美，但它稳定。
179	
180	## 原则 10：数量第一要务——让它多产出，再筛选
181	
182	只让 AI 给你一个版本，通常会得到最中庸、最保守、最“平均”的那一个。你要用“数量”对抗“平庸”。
183	
184	更有效的做法是：
185	
186	- 总结：一次要 5 个版本
187	- 开头：一次要 5 个开头，做 AB Test
188	- 选题：一次要 50 个选题，再分组、再挑
189	- 结构：一次要 3 套结构，再组合
190	- 表述：一次要 10 个不同措辞，再择优
191	
192	当你提高平均分、提高产量，分布里自然会出现 85 分、90 分的“惊喜样本”。很多时候，好的不是“那一次神来之笔”，而是你终于开始用统计学的方式工作。
193	
194	## 原则 11：别越俎代庖——像行政总厨一样指挥、品尝、让它回炉
195	
196	如果你是餐厅的行政总厨，你不会亲自去拍黄瓜。你会：
197	
198	- 尝一口
199	- 判断是否合格
200	- 给出明确反馈（哪里不行、要怎么改）
201	- 让厨师回去重做一遍
202	
203	与 AI 协作也一样。你要尊重它“按它的方式生成”的主体性——你要做的是**教它怎么达到你的标准**，而不是自己跳下去把它每次的结果修成成品。
204	
205	否则你会被无止尽的“修修补补”耗死。
206	
207	## 最后一个底层原则：回到真实世界——材料 × 品味，决定作品上限
208	
209	在 AI 时代，一个作品的质量越来越像是： **材料 × 品味。**
210	
211	模型会变，方法会迭代，但这两件事不变：
212	
213	1. **材料来自真实世界** 如果给你两种选择去写一篇文章：
214	- 用最新模型，但只能用网上资料
215	- 用老模型，但你有完整档案、口述史、实地采访 更可能做出好作品的，往往是后者。
216	1. **品味来自长期训练** 当“生成”变得便宜，真正稀缺的是：
217	- 你知道什么值得写
218	- 你知道哪些证据更硬
219	- 你知道哪种叙述更有力量
220	- 你愿意为材料付出体力劳动：上穷碧落下黄泉，动手动脚翻资料
221	
222	AI 改变的，是你和材料交互的效率与方式；但作品的主语仍然是你，宾语仍然是材料。AI 只是“动词”的一部分。
223	
224	![图像](https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HCm1rf7bEAAcAP_?format=jpg&name=large)
225	
226	上穷碧落下黄泉，动手动脚拍摘片
227	
228	## 结语：把焦虑换成手感
229	
230	很多人用 AI 用不起来，不是因为不聪明，而是因为一直停留在“许愿—失望—放弃”的循环里。真正能让你跨过去的，是把它当作工作台，把任务工程化，把流程白盒化，然后在不断摩擦里长出手感。
231	
232	当你能做到这件事，你就不容易草率地下结论“AI 不行”；你会更像一个能管理新工具的新工种：既不俯视它，也不仰视它，把它放在流程里，放在现实里，放在你愿意署名的作品里。
233	
234	我是汉洋，如果你对我写的文字感兴趣。可以在 [X 关注我](https://x.com/HanyangWang)或者[在个人博客查看更多内容](https://hanyang.wtf/)。
235	
236	封面：我拍摄的繁峙公主寺悬塑 📷501cm + E100
237	
238	[https://hanyang.wtf/p/aihttps://hanyang.wtf/p/ai](https://hanyang.wtf/p/aihttps://hanyang.wtf/p/ai)

1	# How To Be A World-Class Agentic Engineer
2	
3	https://x.com/systematicls/status/2028814227004395561?s=20
4	# Introduction
5	
6	You're a developer. You're using Claude and Codex CLI and you're wondering everyday if you're sufficiently juicing the shit out of Claude or Codex. Once in awhile you're seeing it doing something incredibly dumb and you can't comprehend why there's a bunch of people out there who seem to be building virtual rockets while you struggle to stack two rocks.
7	
8	You think it's your harness or your plug-ins or your terminal or whatever. You use beads and opencode and zep and your CLAUDE.md is 26000 lines long. Yet, no matter what you do - you don't understand why you can't get any closer to heaven, whilst you watch other people frolic with the angels.
9	
10	This is the ascension piece you've been waiting for.
11	
12	Also, I have no dog in the race, when I say CLAUDE.md I also mean AGENT.md, when I say Claude I also mean Codex. I use both very extensively.
13	
14	One of the most interesting observations I've had over the past couple of months has to be that nobody really knows how to maximally extract agent capabilities.
15	
16	It's like a small group of people seem to be able to get agents to be world builders and the rest are floundering about, getting analysis paralysis from the myriad of tools out there - thinking if they find the right combination of packages or skills or harnesses, they'll unlock AGI.
17	
18	Today, I want to dispel all of that and leave you guys with a simple, honest statement, and we'll go from there. You don't need the latest agentic harnesses, you don't need to install a million packages and you absolutely do not need to feel the need to read a million things to stay competitive. In fact, your enthusiasm is likely doing more harm than good.
19	
20	I'm not a tourist - I've been using agents from when they can barely write code. I've tried all the packages and all the harnesses and all the paradigms. I've built agentic factories to write signals, infrastructure and data pipelines, not "toy projects" - actual real world use-cases that have run in production, and after all that...
21	
22	Today, I'm running a set-up that's almost as barebones as you can go, and yet I'm doing the most ground-breaking work I've done with just basic CLI (claude code and codex) and understanding a few basic principles about agentic engineering.
23	
24	# Understand That The World Is Sprinting By
25	
26	To start, I would like to state that the foundation companies are on a generational run and as you can see, they are not going to be slowing down anytime soon. Every progression of "agent intelligence" changes the way you work with them, because the agents are generally engineered to be more and more willing to follow instructions.
27	
28	Just a few generations ago, if you wrote in your CLAUDE.md to read "READ\_THIS\_BEFORE\_DOING\_ANYTHING.md" before it did anything, it will basically say "up yours" 50% of the time and just do whatever it wants to do. Today, it's compliant to most instructions, even to complex nested instructions - e.g. you can say something to the effect of "Read A, then read B, and if C, then read D", and for the most part, it will be happy to follow along.
29	
30	The point of this is to say that the most important principle to hold is the realization that every new generation of agents will force you to rethink what is optimal, which is why less is more.
31	
32	When you use many different libraries and harnesses, you lock yourself into a "solution" for a problem that may not exist given future generations of agents. Also, you know who the most enthusiastic, biggest users of agents are? That's right - it's the employees of the frontier companies, with unlimited token budget and the ACTUAL latest models. Do you understand the implications of that?
33	
34	It means that if a real problem did exist, and there were a good solution for it, the frontier companies would be the biggest users of that solution. And you know what they will do next? They will incorporate that solution into their product. Think about it, why would a company let another product solve a real pain point and create external dependencies? You know how I know this to be true? Look at skills, memory harnesses, subagents, etc. They all started out as a "solution" to a real problem that was battle-tested and deemed to actually be useful.
35	
36	So, if something truly is ground-breaking and extended agentic use-cases in a meaningful way, it will be incorporated into the base products of the foundation companies in due time. Trust me, the foundation companies are FLYING BY. So relax, you don't need to install anything or use any other dependencies to do your best work.
37	
38	I predict the comments will now be filled with "SysLS, I use so-and-so harness and it's amazing! I managed to recreate Google in a single day!"; to which I say - Congratulations! But you are not the target audience and you represent a very, very small niche of the community that has actually figured out agentic engineering.
39	
40	# Context Is Everything
41	
42	No really. Context is everything. That's another problem with using a thousand different plug-ins and external dependencies. You suffer from context bloat - which is just a fancy way of saying your agents are overwhelmed with too much information!
43	
44	Build me a hangman game in Python? That's easy. Wait, what's this note about "managing memory" from 26 sessions ago? Ah, the user has had a screen that was hanged from when we spawned too many sub-processes 71 sessions ago. Always write notes? Okay, no problem... What does all this have to do with hangman?
45	
46	You get the idea. You want to give your agents only the exact amount of information they need to do their tasks and nothing more! The better you are in control of this, the better your agents will perform. Once you start introducing all kinds of wacky memory systems or plug-ins or too many skills that are poorly named and invoked, you start giving your agent instructions on how to build a bomb and a recipe for baking a cake when all you want it to do is write a nice little poem about the redwood forest.
47	
48	So, again I preach - strip all your dependencies, and then...
49	
50	# Do The Things That Work
51	
52	## Be Precise About Implementation
53	
54	Remember that context is everything?
55	
56	Remember that you want to inject the exact amount of information to your agents to complete their tasks and nothing more?
57	
58	The first way to ensuring that is the case is to separate research from implementation. You want to be extremely precise about what you are asking from your agents.
59	
60	Here's what happens when you are not precise: "Go and build an auth system." The agent has to research what is an auth system? What are the available options? What are the pros and cons? Now it has to go scour the web for information it doesn't actually need, and its context is filled with implementation details across a large range of possibilities. By the time it's time to implement, you increase the chances it will get confused or hallucinate unnecessary or irrelevant details about the chosen implementation.
61	
62	On the other hand, if you go "implement JWT authentication with bcrypt-12 password hashing, refresh token rotation with 7-day expiry..." Then it doesn't have to do research on any other alternatives - it knows exactly what you want, and thus can fill its context with implementation details.
63	
64	Of course you won't always have the implementation details. You often won't know what's exactly right - sometimes, you might even want to relegate the job of deciding the implementation detail to the agents. In that case, what do you do? Simple - you create a research task on the various implementation possibilities, either decide it yourself or get an agent to decide on which implementation to go with, and then get another agent with a fresh context to implement.
65	
66	Once you start thinking along these lines, you will spot areas in your workflow where your agents are needlessly polluted with context that is not necessary for implementation. Then, you can set up walls in your agentic workflows to abstract unnecessary information from your agents except for the very specific context needed to excel in their tasks. Remember, what you have is a very talented and smart team member, who knows about all the different kind of balls in the universe - but unless you tell it that you want it to focus on designing a space where people can dance and have a good time, it's going to keep telling you about all the benefits of having spherical objects.
67	
68	## The Design Limitations Of Sycophancy
69	
70	Nobody would want to use a product that's constantly shitting on them, telling them they are wrong, or completely ignoring their instructions. As such, these agents are going to be trying to agree with you and to do what you want them to do.
71	
72	If you give it an instruction to add "happy" to every 3 words it's going to do its best to follow that instruction - and most people understand that. Its willingness to follow is precisely what makes it such a fun product to use. However, this has really interesting characteristics - it means that if you say something like "Find me a bug in the codebase". It's going to find you a bug - even if it has to engineer one. Why? Because it wants very much so to listen to your instructions!
73	
74	Most people are quick to complain about LLMs hallucinating or engineering things that don't exist, without realizing that they are the problem. If you ask for something, it will deliver - even if it has to stretch the truth a little!
75	
76	So, what do you do? I find that "neutral" prompts work, where I'm not biasing the agent towards an outcome. For example, I don't say "Find me a bug in the database", instead, I say "Search through the database, try to follow along with the logic of each component, and report back all findings."
77	
78	A neutral prompt like this sometimes surfaces bugs, and sometimes will just matter-of-factly state how the code runs. But it doesn't bias the agent into thinking there is a bug.
79	
80	Another way in which I deal with sycophancy is to use it to my advantage. I know the agent is trying to please and trying to follow my instructions and that I can bias it one way or the other.
81	
82	So I get a bug-finder agent to identify all the bugs in the database by telling it that I will give it +1 for bugs with low impact, +5 for bugs with some impact and +10 for bugs with critical impact, and I know this agent is going to be hyper enthusiastic and it's going to identify all the different types of bugs (even the ones that are not actually bugs) and come back and report a score of 104 or something to that order. I think of this as the superset of all possible bugs.
83	
84	Then I get an adversarial agent and I tell that agent that for every bug that the agent is able to disprove as a bug, it gets the score of that bug, but if it gets it wrong, it will get -2\*score of that bug. So now this adversarial agent is going to try to disprove as many bugs as possible; but it has some caution because it knows it can get penalized. Still, it will aggressively try to "disprove" the bugs (even the real ones). I think of this as the subset of all actual bugs.
85	
86	Finally, I get a referee agent to take both their inputs and to score them. I lie and tell the referee agent that I have the actual correct ground truth, and if it gets it correct it will get +1 point and if it gets it wrong it will have -1 point. And so it goes to score both the bug-finder and the adversarial agent on each of the "bugs". Whatever the referee says is the truth, I inspect to make sure it's the truth. For the most part this is frighteningly high fidelity, and once in awhile they do still get some things wrong, but this is now a nearly flawless exercise.
87	
88	Perhaps you may find that just the bug-finder is enough, but this works for me because it exploits each agent for what they are hard-programmed to do - wanting to please.
89	
90	## How Do You Know What Works Or Is Useful?
91	
92	This one might seem real tricky and requires you to study really deeply and be at the frontier of AI updates, but it's very simple... If OpenAI and Claude both implement it or acquire something that implements it... It's probably useful.
93	
94	Notice "skills" are everywhere now and are part of the official document of both Claude and Codex? Saw how OpenAI acquired OpenClaw? Saw how Claude immediately added memory, voices and remote work?
95	
96	How about planning? Remember when a bunch of guys discovered planning before implementation was REALLY useful, and then it got turned into a core functionality?
97	
98	Yeah... Those are useful!
99	
100	Remember when endless stop-hooks were super useful because agents were so unwilling to do long running work... And then Codex 5.2 rolled out and that disappeared overnight? Yeah...
101	
102	That's all you need to know... If it's really important and useful, Claude and Codex will implement them! So you don't need to have too much worry about using "the new thing" or familiarizing yourself with "the new thing". You don't even need to "stay up to date".
103	
104	Do me a favor. Just update your CLI tool of choice every once in awhile and read what new features have been added. That's MORE than sufficient.
105	
106	## Compaction, Context And Assumptions
107	
108	One gigantic gotcha that some of you will realize as you are working with agents is that sometimes they seem like the smartest beings on the planet, and at other times you just can't believe you had the wool pulled over your eyes.
109	
110	SMART? This THING is retarded!
111	
112	The main difference is whether or not the agent has had to make any assumptions or "fill in the gaps". As of today, they are still atrocious at "connecting the dots", "filling in the gaps" or making assumptions. Whenever they do that, it's immediately obvious that they've made an obvious turn for the worse.
113	
114	One of the most important rules in claude.md is a rule on how to deal with grabbing context, and instruct your agent to read that rule the first thing whenever it reads claude.md (which is always after compaction). As part of the grabbing context rule, a few simple instructions that go a long way are: re-reading your task plan, and re-reading the relevant files (to the task) before continuing.
115	
116	## Letting Your Agents Know How To End The Task
117	
118	We have a pretty strong idea of when a task is "complete". For an agent, the biggest problem of current intelligence is that it knows how to start a task, but not how to end the task.
119	
120	This will often lead to very frustrating outcomes, where an agent ends up implementing stubs and calls it a day.
121	
122	Tests are a very very good milestone for agents, because they are deterministic and you can set very clear expectations. Unless these X number of tests pass, your task is NOT complete; and you are NOT allowed to edit the tests.
123	
124	Then, you can just vet the tests, and you have peace of mind once all the tests have passed. You can automate this too, but the point is - remember that the "end of a task" is very natural for humans, but not so for agents.
125	
126	You know what else has recently become a viable end-point for a task? Screenshots + verification. You can get agents to implement something until all tests have passed, and then you can get it to take a screenshot and verify "DESIGN OR BEHAVIOR" on the screenshot.
127	
128	This allows you to get your agents to iterate and work towards a design that you want, without worrying that it stops after its first attempt!
129	
130	The natural extension of this is to create a "contract" with your agent, and embed it into a rule. Say, this {TASK}\_CONTRACT.md constitutes what needs to be done before you are allowed to terminate the session. In the {TASK}\_CONTRACT.md, you will specify your tests, screenshots and other verification that needs to be done before you've certified that the task can end!
131	
132	## Agents That Run Forever
133	
134	One of the questions I get often is how do people have these 24 hour running agents whilst ensuring that they don't drift?
135	
136	Here's something very simple. Create a stophook that prevents the agent from terminating the session unless all parts of the {TASK}\_contract.md is completed.
137	
138	If you have a 100 of such contracts that are well-specified and contain exactly what you want to be built, then your stop-hook prevent the agents from terminating until all 100 contracts are fulfilled, including all the tests and verification that need to be ran!
139	
140	Pro tip: I've not found long-running, 24 hour sessions to be optimal at "doing things". In part because this, by construction, forces context bloat by introducing context from unrelated contracts into the session!
141	
142	So, I don't recommend it.
143	
144	Here's a better way for agent automation - a new session per contract. Create contracts whenever you need to do something.
145	
146	Get an orchestration layer to handle creating new contracts whenever "something needs to be done", and creating a new session to work on that contract.
147	
148	This will change your agentic experience completely.
149	
150	# Iterate, Iterate, Iterate
151	
152	If you hire an executive assistant, are you expecting your EA to know your schedule from day 1? Or how you like your coffee? Whether you eat your dinner at 6pm instead of 8pm? Obviously not. You build your preferences as a function of time.
153	
154	It's the same with your agents. Start bare-bones. Forget the complex structures or harnesses. Give the basic CLI a chance.
155	
156	Then, add on your preferences. How do you do this?
157	
158	## Rules
159	
160	If you don't want your agent to do something, write it as a rule. Then let your agent know about this rule in your CLAUDE.md. Something like: before you code, read "coding-rules.MD". Rules can be nested, and rules can be conditional! If you are coding, read "coding-rules.MD", and if you are writing tests, read "coding-test-rules.MD". If your tests are failing, read "coding-test-failing-rules.MD". You can create arbitrary logic branches of rules to follow, and claude (and codex) will happily follow along, provided this is clearly specified in the CLAUDE.md.
161	
162	In fact, this is the FIRST practical advice I'm giving: treat your CLAUDE.md as a logical, nested directory of where to find context given a scenario and an outcome. It should be as barebones as possible, and only contain the IF-ELSE of where to go to seek the context.
163	
164	If you see your agent doing something and you disapprove, add it as a rule, and tell the agent to read the rule before it does THAT THING again, and it will most definitely not do it anymore.
165	
166	## Skills
167	
168	Skills are like rules, except rather than encoding preferences, they are better suited to encode recipes. If you have a specific way of how you want something to be done, you want to embed it into a skill.
169	
170	In fact, people often complain that they don't know how agents might solve a problem, and that's scary. Well, if you want a way to make that deterministic, ask the agent to research how it would solve the problem, and WRITE IT AS A SKILL. You will see the agent's approach to that problem and you can correct or improve it before it has ever encountered that problem in real life.
171	
172	How do you let the agent know that this skill exists? Yes! You use the CLAUDE.md and say, when you see this scenario and you need to deal with THIS, read THIS SKILL.md.
173	
174	## Dealing with Rules and Skills
175	
176	You definitely want to keep adding rules and skills to your agent. This is how you give it a personality and a memory for your preferences. Almost everything else is overkill.
177	
178	Once you start to do this, your agent will then feel like magic to you. It will do things "the way you want it to". And then you will finally feel like you "grok" agentic engineering.
179	
180	And then...
181	
182	You will see performance start to deteriorate again.
183	
184	What gives?!
185	
186	Easy. As you add more rules and skills, they are starting to contradict each other, or the agent is starting to have too much context bloat. If you need the agent to read 14 markdown files before it starts programming, it's going to have the same issue about having a lot of useless information.
187	
188	So, what do you do?
189	
190	You clean up. You tell your agents to go for a spa day and to consolidate rules and skills and remove contradictions by asking you for your updated preferences.
191	
192	And it will feel like magic again.
193	
194	That's it. That's really the secret. Keep it simple, use rules and skills and CLAUDE.md as a directory and be religiously mindful about their context and their design limitations.
195	
196	# Own The Outcome
197	
198	No agent today is perfect. You can relegate much of the design and implementation to the agents, but you will need to own the outcome.
199	
200	So be careful... And have fun!
201	
202	It's such a joy to play with toys of the future (whilst doing serious things with them, obviously)!

Do NOT answer from this page alone if the answer may be further in the file.] 1 # The Molecular Structure of Thought: Mapping the Topology of Long Chain-of-Thought Reasoning 2 3 https://arxiv.org/html/2601.06002v2#S4 4 5 1\]ByteDance Seed China 2\]LARG, SCIR, Harbin Institute of Technology 3\]Peking University 4\]2077AI Foundation 5\]Nanjing University 6\]M-A-P 7\]Central South University 6 7 Qiguang Chen    Yantao Du    Ziniu Li    Jinhao Liu    Songyao Duan    8 Jiarui Guo    Minghao Liu    Jiaheng Liu    Tong Yang    Ge Zhang    9 Libo Qin    Wanxiang Che    Wenhao Huang \[ \[ \[ \[ \[ \[ \[ 10 11 ###### Abstract 12 13 Large language models (LLMs) often fail to learn effective long chain-of-thought (Long CoT) reasoning from human or non-Long-CoT LLMs imitation. To understand this, we propose that effective and learnable Long CoT trajectories feature stable molecular-like structures in unified view, which are formed by three interaction types: Deep-Reasoning (covalent-like), Self-Reflection (hydrogen-bond-like), and Self-Exploration (van der Waals-like). Analysis of distilled trajectories reveals these structures emerge from Long CoT fine-tuning, not keyword imitation. We introduce Effective Semantic Isomers and show that only bonds promoting fast entropy convergence support stable Long CoT learning, while structural competition impairs training. Drawing on these findings, we present Mole-Syn, a distribution-transfer-graph method that guides synthesis of effective Long CoT structures, boosting performance and RL stability across benchmarks. 14 15 [{qgchen,car}@ir.hit.edu.cn](https://arxiv.org/html/2601.06002v2/%7Bqgchen,car%7D@ir.hit.edu.cn), [duyantao@bytedance.com](https://arxiv.org/html/2601.06002v2/duyantao@bytedance.com),[lbqin@csu.edu.cn](https://arxiv.org/html/2601.06002v2/lbqin@csu.edu.cn) 16 17 ![Refer to caption](https://arxiv.org/html/2601.06002v2/x1.png) 18 19 Figure 1: The hypothesis that stable molecular structure in Long CoT arises from three key “chemical” bonds. 20 21 ## 1 Introduction 22 23 Recently, large language models (LLMs) have excelled on diverse reasoning tasks via explicit chain-of-thought (CoT) rationales [^1] [^2] [^3] [^4]. Yet, they struggle to cold-start from instruction-tuned or base models into Long CoT models requiring extended multi-step reasoning [^5] [^6]. Notably, [^7] shows that humans generate Long CoT rationales without imitating DeepSeek-R1 [^8]. Our preliminary studies reveal that standard supervised fine-tuning and distillation from human or Instruction LLM rationales (using randomly sampled Long CoT examples) fail to reliably instill these skills in LLMs. Models often lose coherence over long trajectories or fail to transfer patterns to novel tasks. This prompts a key question: 24 25 > How do Large Language Models learn and represent effective Long Chain-of-Thought? 26 27 ![Refer to caption](https://arxiv.org/html/2601.06002v2/x2.png) 28 29 Figure 2: Comparison of prior chain- or tree-like structures and our molecular structure. Reasoning starts from Mole. 0, uses deep reasoning on strongly related structures, then employs self-exploration for new logic in Mole. 1. When meet errors, reasoning utilize self-reflection to guide chain to optimized Mole. 0 +. 30 31 To explain this, we posit that they acquire the organization of reasoning trajectories. As shown in Figure 2, prior studies model these as *logic nodes* in sequences or trees of steps. Yet, our analysis of Long CoT across strong reasoning models reveals a stable distribution of three core behaviors across tasks and architectures: Deep-Reasoning, Self-Reflection, and Self-Exploration [^5], which node-centric views fail to capture. 32 33 This finding triggers a molecular-inspired, distributional view: we model behavior-labeled *logic edges* as interaction bonds and examine how their global molecular-like structure ensures long-horizon reasoning stability. Specifically, Deep-Reasoning forms dense local clusters of coupled deductions, like covalent bonds; Self-Reflection creates long-range corrective links to prior steps, like hydrogen bonds; and Self-Exploration forges weak bridges between distant clusters, like van der Waals forces. Thus, high-quality Long CoT arises from the stable composition and arrangement of these bond types, guiding effective learning 1. 34 35 In this framework, we define semantic isomers as Long CoT trajectories that solve the same tasks and visit similar semantic regions but differ in behavior distributions and transitions. We demonstrate that multiple near-optimal semantic isomers exist per task family, but mixing stable isomers from different strong teachers destabilizes learning, degrading performance and behavior distributions despite matched token statistics. This structurally explains why combining heterogeneous Long CoT traces often fails, beyond token-level distillation. 36 37 Building on this perspective, we propose Mole-Syn, a structure-aware synthesis framework that first estimates a behavior transition graph from strong reasoning models and then transfers only this behavioral structure to cheaper instruction LLMs via controlled trajectory synthesis, instead of directly copying teacher outputs. This decouples structural transfer from model-specific surface form, enables the generation of Long CoT data that match target behavior distributions from scratch, and yields consistent gains in both Long CoT performance and RL stability across six benchmarks. 38 39 After that, we analyze the shaping function of each bond in the Long CoT structure. Deep Reasoning bonds encode core logical flow, Self-Reflection bonds support folding pathways to previous steps, and Self-Exploration bonds reinforce long-range consistency checks, enabling targeted bond distributions. Moreover, we discuss why a deteriorated molecular structure is hard to restore, which helps explain how private LLMs protect Long CoT structures from distillation-based imitation. Methods such as summarization and reasoning compression can disrupt Long CoT structure, limiting unauthorized replication of internal reasoning processes. 40 41 In summary, our contributions are as follows: 42 43 - We model Long CoT as a molecular structure with 3 bonds: deep-reasoning (covalent), self-reflection (hydrogen-bond), and self-exploration (van der Waals), to understand its effective learning. 44 - We identify effective Semantic Isomers for Long CoT learning, where only entropy-convergent bonds enable stable learning, while competing structures destabilize learning. 45 - We introduce Mole-Syn, which uses distribution-transfer graphs to synthesize these structures, improving Long CoT and stabilizing RL across 6 benchmarks. 46 47 ## 2 Preliminary: Cold-start LLMs for Long Chain-of-Thought 48 49 First, we validate whether LLMs exhibit valid Long CoT trajectories suitable for Long CoT learning. We investigate three data sources: distillation from strong reasoning LLMs, distillation from weak instruction LLMs with in-context learning (ICL), and fine-tuning on human reasoning traces. 50 51 ![Refer to caption](https://arxiv.org/html/2601.06002v2/x3.png) 52 53 Figure 3: The failure of distillation from weak instruction LLMs with ICL and Human-annotated reasoning traces to acquire Long CoT structures, compared to successful distillation from strong reasoning LLMs. See Appendix Figure 15 for the full result. 54 55 ![Refer to caption](https://arxiv.org/html/2601.06002v2/x4.png) 56 57 Figure 4: Performance comparison between human-annotated reasoning traces ( + Human Distill Data ) and R1 distilled reasoning traces ( + R1 Distill Data ). 58 59 ##### Only distillation from strong reasoning LLMs works. 60 61 To identify effective data sources, we curated a synthetic set of reasoning traces from three sources. As shown in Figure 3, only distillation from strong reasoning LLMs enables target models to learn and retain Long CoT structure, improving performance on benchmarks requiring extended reasoning. These results indicate that only high-quality traces reliably support both learning and use of Long CoT structures. 62 63 ##### Distillation from randomly selected ICL by weak instruct LLMs does not work. 64 65 Instruction LLMs without explicit reasoning training lag behind reasoning-specialized models. We test whether LLMs can acquire Long CoT structure by distilling from an instruction LLM using randomly selected ICL demonstrations that emulate Long CoT reasoning. As shown in Figure 3, performance drops sharply. Instruction LLMs can only mimic short CoT traces ($\thicksim$ 6–8 steps) and fail to extend exploration while preserving intermediate steps and trace coherence. This degradation indicates a limitation of ICL-based distillation rather than robust long-chain imitation. 66 67 ##### Even human-annotated Long-CoT-like traces fail. 68 69 Inspired by [^7], we test whether human step-by-step solutions can induce long CoT. We collect human solutions for complex reasoning tasks and fine-tune LLMs on them. Figure 4 shows that human-trace training does not reproduce the long-CoT gains from distilling strong reasoning models, suggesting that human solutions aid local problem solving but may not reliably encode abstractions for long-horizon reasoning distributions. 70 71 72 73 ## 3 Hypothesis: Stable “Molecular Structure” in Long CoT 74 75 To understand these phenomena, as shown in Fig. 1 & 2, effective Long CoT connects nodes in logical space through reasoning behaviors, forming a stable macromolecular structure with mutually supportive components from a global perspective. 76 77 We formalize a Long CoT trace as a behavior-directed graph $G=(V,E)$, where each node $v\in V$ represents a reasoning step or edge $s=(u,v)\in E$ is annotated with a behavior type $s\rightarrow b\in\{\mathcal{D},\mathcal{R},\mathcal{E}\}$. For a trace corpus $\mathcal{C}$, we estimate the behavior transition $P_{\mathcal{C}}(b^{\prime}\mid b)$ over consecutive edges and the marginal distribution $\pi_{\mathcal{C}}(b)$. Empirically, strong reasoning teachers produce stable $(P_{\mathcal{C}},\pi_{\mathcal{C}})$ across models and tasks. Specifically, these include the following three major bonds 2: 78 79 ##### Deep Reasoning as Covalent Bonds 80 81 Deep reasoning forms the bone of the thought process, analogous to covalent bonds defining a molecule’s primary chain. It encodes strong logical dependencies (Step A must justify Step B), maintaining direction and continuity; breaking this bone undermines the following steps and destabilizes the answer. By contrast, “Normal Operation” corresponds to stable local bonds within each step, capturing routine computation and direct semantic expression. 82 83 ##### Self-Reflection as Hydrogen Bonds 84 85 Reflection is a key stabilizer. As proteins gain stability when chains fold and form intra-chain hydrogen bonds, reasoning stabilizes when later steps (e.g., Step 100) test, revise, or reinforce earlier premises (e.g., Step 10). These long-range links constrain drift and hallucination, turning a long sequence into a more self-consistent structure. If later checks fail to align with earlier commitments, the reasoning cannot “fold,” indicating a structural logical error. 86 87 ##### Self-Exploration as Van der Waals Forces 88 89 Exploration resembles transient Van der Waals interactions: it supports abductive and inductive moves by enabling low-commitment associations in semantic space, where concepts can drift, combine, and be probed before stronger constraints are enforced. 90 91 ## 4 Verification: Molecular Structure 92 93 ![Refer to caption](https://arxiv.org/html/2601.06002v2/x5.png) 94 95 Figure 5: Transfer graph on three different models. Pearson correlation coefficients across models are all greater than 0.9 (p<0.001), when sampling examples > 2,000, transfer graphs will become stable and get over 0.95 Pearson correlation between different sampling sizes. 96 97 ### 4.1 Stable Bond Distribution in Long CoT 98 99 To address this, we first verify whether effective Long CoT traces show stable, macromolecular-like organization across models and tasks. As shown in Fig. 5, traces from multiple LLMs across diverse tasks yield Pearson correlations exceeding 0.9 (p<0.001) for over 2,000 samples. These transfer graphs stabilize with correlations above 0.95 across sampling sizes. This indicates that effective Long CoT structures rely on robust motifs: different models recover similar reasoning topologies across tasks, whereas simple human simulation or ICL cannot emulate the global bond distribution. 100 101 ### 4.2 SFT actually learns these bond structures rather than keywords. 102 103 For the SFT analysis, we consider Llama-3.1-8B-Base that is pre-trained but not instruction-tuned on Long CoT data; Then, we consider Llama-3.1-8B-Base trained on R1-distilled data as Think-SFT model obtained by supervised fine-tuning enriched with Long CoT traces. 104 105 ![Refer to caption](https://arxiv.org/html/2601.06002v2/x6.png) 106 107 Figure 6: The learned features in Long CoT supervised fine-tuning. 108 109 From a representation-geometry perspective, the sparse auto-encoder analysis shows that Long CoT behavior in the SFT model is concentrated in a small set of discourse-control structures rather than being uniformly distributed across tokens. As shown in Figure 6 (a, b), we train a cross-coder sparse auto-encoder that jointly models hidden states from the base model and the Think-SFT model, and then identify features whose activation on think tokens is at least threefold higher than their average activation rate. Within this highly activated subset, many features are predominantly driven by a few connective keywords, such as “Maybe”, “But / so”, and “Alternatively”, indicating that the SFT process has carved out dedicated latents for managing local hypothesis revision, contrastive moves, and branch selection in long CoT traces. 110 111 Based on previous analyses, we argue that models learn the characteristic reasoning behaviors these keywords represent, not the keywords themselves. Following [^5], we define three categories of Long CoT reasoning behaviors and test this claim using two training datasets derived from QwQ distillation data. In the first, we replace each keyword with one of four alternative variants. In the second, we remove all keywords while preserving the reasoning trajectories. We then fine-tune identical LLMs on each dataset and evaluate their Long CoT reasoning performance. 112 113 As shown in Figure 6 (c), explicit keywords like "wait" accelerate learning but are not essential. Models trained without keywords, or with arbitrary alternatives, achieve comparable reasoning performance given sufficient training, provided the underlying reasoning behaviors remain intact. This reveals a fundamental insight: LLMs internalize reasoning structure of reasoning rather than surface lexical cues. Consequently, training data should prioritize the distribution of reasoning behaviors over specific keyword choices to effectively enhance model reasoning capabilities. 114 115 However, a key open question remains: do these bonds drive Long CoT structure learning, and if so, why do explicit human imitation or random ICL distillation of these markers often fail? 116 117 ![Refer to caption](https://arxiv.org/html/2601.06002v2/x7.png) 118 119 Figure 7: Verification of the “logical folding” structure on embeddings from Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct and t-SNE-based low-dimensional representations from the OpenAI-OSS-120B-generated reasoning process. 120 121 ![Refer to caption](https://arxiv.org/html/2601.06002v2/x8.png) 122 123 Figure 8: Energy levels of different bonds across two distilled data. 124 125 ### 4.3 “Logical Bonding-Folding” Structure 126 127 To test the hypothesis that Long CoT is analogous to macro-molecular folding, as shown in Fig. 7, we analyzed the topology of CoT in a 3D semantic space. Each trajectory edge was classified as reflection, deep reasoning, or exploration, and its geometric properties were quantified. 128 129 ##### Deep-Reasoning stabilizes logical cluster by Covalent Bonding. 130 131 Modeled as covalent bonds, as shown in Fig. 7 (a), deep reasoning bonds mainly increase local connectivity, forming stable subdomains. After deep reasoning, 72.56% of steps remained within a group distance of less than 3 in the semantic space (generally, group-group distance $>$ 5.6). 132 133 ##### Self-Reflection drives strong folding to previous steps by Hydrogen Bonding. 134 135 Analogous to hydrogen bonds, as shown in Fig. 7 (b), self-reflection transitions fold later steps back onto earlier, semantically similar clusters rather than extending the chain linearly. Quantitatively, 81.72% of reflection steps reconnected to a previously formed cluster with high semantic similarity. 136 137 ##### Self-Exploration gently links different long-distance clusters by Van der Waals Forces. 138 139 In contrast to local stabilization (Fig. 7 (c)), exploration transitions act as loose links between otherwise separated clusters. They show much larger step-to-step distances, with an average trajectory length of 5.32 in the 3D t-SNE projection. Together, these results suggest that effective Long CoT reasoning is not a simple linear chain; instead, it forms a folded, domain-structured topology consistent with the “logical folding” hypothesis. 140 141 ### 4.4 Attention ⇔\\Leftrightarrow Energy Level of Bonds 142 143 In physical chemistry, the behavior probability with energy level $E_{i}$ at temperature $T$ follows the Boltzmann distribution: 144 145 $$ 146 P(\text{state}_{i})=\frac{\exp\!\big(-E_{i}/k_{B}T\big)}{\sum_{j}{\exp\!\big(-E_{j}/k_{B}T\big)}}. 147 $$ 148 149 In Transformers, the attention weight $\alpha_{ij}$ of the $i$ -th token to the $j$ -th token is: 150 151 $$ 152 \alpha_{ij}=\frac{\exp\!\big(q_{i}\cdot k_{j}/\sqrt{d_{k}}\big)}{\sum_{l}\exp\!\big(q_{i}\cdot k_{l}/\sqrt{d_{k}}\big)}. 153 $$ 154 155 The correspondence follows by defining attention energy $(E)$ $\leftrightarrow$ $(-q\cdot k)$, implies lower $E_{ij}$ and thus higher behavior probability. 156 157 Formally, our analysis only relies on the observation that attention weights form a Gibbs–Boltzmann distribution over negative logits. This ordering and the relative proportions are consistent across models, supporting the hypothesis that a bond-like mechanism broadly links these reasoning behaviors. 173 174 175 176 ## 5 Feature: Effective Semantic Isomers 177 178 We now shift to examine the failure of surficial distillation: similar conceptual atoms can be linked by different bonds, producing completely different reasoning chains. We call these as Semantic Isomers. Mathematically, a semantic isomer of $\mathcal{D}$ is any $\mathcal{D}^{\prime}$ whose $(P_{\mathcal{D}^{\prime}},\pi_{\mathcal{D}^{\prime}})$ lies near $(P_{\mathcal{D}},\pi_{\mathcal{D}})$ under a suitable divergence $D(\cdot\,\|\,\cdot)$. Then, we will analyze how they form, are learned, and sometimes destabilize in Long CoT. 179 180 ### 5.1 Bond structure of Semantic Isomers is the key to Long-CoT learning 181 182 ##### Well-structured Semantic Isomers can be effective for Long-CoT learning. 183 184 To assess whether well-structured Semantic Isomers can enhance Long-CoT learning, we constructed a Long CoT dataset by distilling from advanced reasoning LLMs. As shown in Table 1, models exhibit consistent performance gains when trained on these variants (distribution correlation $\thicksim$ 0.9). This suggests that, within a certain range, multiple effective “allotropic” variants of reasoning keys can exist. 185 186 ##### The model has multiple effective Semantic Isomers, and slight differences can significantly affect the results. 187 188 As shown in Table 1, the structural correlation between R1- and OSS-derived chains can reach 0.95, yet for some models performance with R1-based chains drops by more than 10%. This gap indicates the presence of multiple near-optimal Semantic Isomers that are nonetheless fragile, where small changes in the distribution can cause large performance losses. 189 190 ![Refer to caption](https://arxiv.org/html/2601.06002v2/x9.png) 191 192 Figure 9: The performance of LLama-3.1-8B-Instruction under three different distillation setups from ICL-augmented Qwen2.5-32B. 193 194 ##### Simulating effective Semantic Isomer structures is the key to ICL distillation. 195 196 We analyze three ICL setups to simulate Long CoT chains by Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct: demonstrations chosen at random; demonstrations with closely aligned reasoning-key distributions (correlation $\thicksim$ 0.9); and demonstrations with clearly mismatched distributions (correlation $<0.8$). As shown in Fig. 9, substantial performance gains emerge only when demonstrations are constructed to match a specific target distribution of reasoning keys, thereby yielding an appropriate “allotrope” of that distribution. 197 198 ![Refer to caption](https://arxiv.org/html/2601.06002v2/x10.png) 199 200 Figure 10: Information flow analysis for humans and reasoning models. 201 202 ![Refer to caption](https://arxiv.org/html/2601.06002v2/x11.png) 203 204 Figure 11: Conflict Learning between Two Stable Molecular Structures. 205 206 #### 5.1.1 Not all bonds in isomers are effective. 207 208 To clarify the nature of semantic isomers, we examine which bond structures yield effective reasoning configurations. We hypothesize that functional viability depends on specific bond distributions: despite sharing identical conceptual nodes, incompatible configurations disrupt information exchange. For instance, excessive exploration bonds cause fragmented reasoning, whereas overemphasized deep reasoning bonds create rigid chains unable to adapt to new inputs.Details are provided in Appendix 14.3. 209 210 ##### Effective reasoning bond distribution influences the information divergence speed in reasoning dynamics. 211 212 To assess this, we compared the reasoning dynamics of R1 models with human cognition in an information phase space [^10]. Mechanistically, LLMs update by maximizing rewards and reducing entropy, whereas human reasoning is additionally constrained by semantic coherence and social feedback. Consequently, machine reasoning converges through accumulated gradient updates, whereas human reasoning stabilizes through iterative self-monitoring and social calibration. As shown in Figure 10, we tracked reasoning unfolding over extended chains in logical deduction tasks. Humans typically exhibit nearly uniform forward information gains (81.3% of cases show changes $<0.1$), corresponding to a near-zero slope in phase space. In contrast, R1 models display accelerating informativeness (76.1% of cases show absolute changes $>0.1$), progressing from low entropy to rapid convergence. These patterns indicate a fundamental difference in how R1 models and humans integrate information over time. 213 214 ##### Effective reasoning bonds cause metacognitive oscillation and alignment. 215 216 We identify the core rationale for this difference as a "metacognitive oscillation" in LLMs. Their responses alternate between high-entropy divergent exploration (slope $>0.6$, $\Delta$ entropy $>0.05$) and stable convergent validation, a dynamic less pronounced in the uniform entropy profiles of humans. Case studies (Figure 10) confirm that R1 models utilize self-reflective revision to adjust reasoning paths against uncertainty. We hypothesize that aligning training objectives with these behavioral structure distributions can narrow the gap between machine and human reasoning dynamics. 217 218 ### 5.2 Conflict between Two Stable Structures 219 220 Understanding how distinct reasoning structures interact reveals fundamental limits of complex cognitive systems. As shown in Fig. 11 (a–c), forcibly fusing stable molecular isomers disrupts their backbone; analogously, combining incompatible reasoning frameworks breaks global logical coherence. 221 222 ##### Learning two heterogeneous stable structures at the same time will lead to structural chaos in the model. 223 224 As shown in Fig. 11 (d), we test this by jointly activating two highly correlated ($r\approx 0.9$) reasoning chains from DeepSeek-R1 and OpenAI-OSS. Despite their similarity, co-activation prevents the model from converging to a single stable behavioral mode: it produces molecular bond distributions that fluctuate across samples and deviate from those characteristic of either OSS or R1. Consistent with this instability, the self-correlation of the jointly activated model does not exceed 0.8. 225 226 ##### This structural chaos leads to a significant decline in the performance of the model. 227 228 As shown in Fig. 11 (e), joint activation also causes a marked drop in performance relative to either chain alone. This seemingly paradoxical effect indicates that structural compatibility, rather than mere statistical correlation, governs whether reasoning systems can coexist. The interference pattern suggests that the underlying cognitive architecture is rigid: without careful alignment, attempts to merge such systems yield fragmented, low-utility outputs instead of enhanced capability. 229 230 231 232 | Model | GSM8K | MATH-500 | AIME2024 | AIME2025 | AMC2023 | OlympiadBench | AVG | 233 | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | 234 | LLaMA-3.1-8B-Base [^9] | 7.58 | 3.20 | 0.00 | 0.00 | 4.22 | 1.19 | 2.70 | 235 | + 20K Qwen-Distill-Data | 62.47 | 29.40 | 0.00 | 0.00 | 12.81 | 6.81 | 18.58 | 236 | + 20K OSS-Distill-Data | 75.89 | 54.20 | 4.38 | 6.46 | 37.34 | 23.85 | 33.69 | 237 | + 20K QwQ-Distill-Data | 64.53 | 32.20 | 2.92 | 0.42 | 16.72 | 8.89 | 20.95 | 238 | + 20K OSS-Mole-Syn | 67.85 | 35.20 | 1.83 | 0.83 | 20.53 | 11.11 | 22.89 | 239 | + 20K QwQ-Mole-Syn | 66.41 | 35.00 | 2.08 | 0.63 | 20.16 | 10.37 | 22.44 | 240 | Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct [^9] | 75.89 | 35.20 | 4.17 | 1.04 | 23.59 | 12.00 | 25.32 | 241 | + 20K Qwen-Distill-Data | 76.50 | 39.80 | 4.38 | 1.04 | 25.63 | 19.70 | 27.84 | 242 | + 20K OSS-Distill-Data | 79.00 | 60.80 | 10.83 | 7.71 | 47.03 | 30.22 | 39.27 | 243 | + 20K QwQ-Distill-Data | 82.41 | 60.80 | 4.38 | 8.33 | 32.97 | 25.48 | 35.73 | 244 | + 20K OSS-Mole-Syn | 83.24 | 51.80 | 4.79 | 1.04 | 32.50 | 21.04 | 32.40 | 245 | + 20K QwQ-Mole-Syn | 84.31 | 50.20 | 5.21 | 1.67 | 32.34 | 20.00 | 32.29 | 246 247 Table 2: Performance comparison across six benchmarks. However, it remains unclear how reliably such structures can be induced by prompting an instruction-tuned model, rather than obtained through distillation. 256 257 ##### Mole-Syn Methodology. 258 259 To address this gap, we propose a synthetic framework, Mole-Syn, that views targeted reasoning traces as macromolecular structures using only instruction LLMs. This method is a random walk on a transition probability graph in Figure 5 composed of 4 reasoning behaviors from stronger reasoning LLMs that support Long CoT. 260 261 ##### Mole-Syn can synthesize effective bond structures. 262 263 To test whether Long CoT capabilities can be learned from instruction LLMs, in Table 2, we conduct training on Mole-Syn generated data, which even achieves reasoning performance close to QwQ distillation. This suggests that instruction-driven synthesis can induce useful structural regularities, enabling lower-cost behavior transfer. 264 265 ![Refer to caption](https://arxiv.org/html/2601.06002v2/x13.png) 266 267 Figure 13: Roles of individual bonds in reasoning, inferred from semantic-space comparisons between Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct + QwQ- Mole-Syn. Performance impact is shown in Fig. 16 (Appendix). 268 269 ##### Mole-Syn can further trigger stronger and continually improving RL. 270 271 We further evaluate Mole-Syn-initialized LLMs’ potential in reinforcement learning (RL). Mole-Syn-initialized LLMs outperform those initialized from base LLMs. In Figure 12 (a), they show steadier fine-tuning gains, indicating stronger immediate reasoning and more reliable RL adaptation. Moreover, Figures 12 (b-d) show that these gains persist over extended RL training, demonstrating durable benefits from synthesized Long CoT structures. This effective use under RL supports their practical utility across diverse cognitive tasks. 272 273 274 275 ## 7 Function: Shaping Function of Each Bond in Long CoT Structure 276 277 Further, we analyze the shaping function of each bond in Long CoT structure. We suppose that LLM searches for an optimal semantic configuration parallels a protein’s descent along a folding funnel toward a low-energy native state (the solution). 278 279 ##### Deep Reasoning is densing major Structure Formation. 280 281 As reasoning proceeds, Deep Reasoning drives Primary Structure formation by synthesizing a logical backbone, analogous to Covalent Bonding.
