1	# How to Design using AI (Builder's Guide)
2	
3	![](https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HJaz6F5bIAAXvlF.jpg)
4	
5	I built a personal Notion this weekend.
6	
7	Not a clone. The parts of Notion I actually use, stripped of everything I don't. 
8	
9	No teammates. No comments. No notification feed. Just my tasks, journal, habits, bookmarks, and pages. One screen. My data. My machine.
10	
11	> If you don't want to read the entire article, get the Github repo from below and check the product work through. 
12	**The whole thing runs on two tools doing two jobs:**
13	1. **Moonchild AI does the design (brief through final visual)**
14	2. **Cursor and Codex do the code. The rest is incidental.**
15	[📹 video](https://video.twimg.com/amplify_video/2059923863027458048/vid/avc1/698x360/35KnU1hyiPmm4RlQ.mp4?tag=27)
16	
17	t's real. State persists. Dark mode works. Keyboard shortcuts work. You can use it at
18	
19	> TLDR : github.com/codejunkie99/cove
20	That's the whole post. The rest is the how.
21	
22	## The mental model
23	
24	> TLDR; If you don't wanna read that long just watch this video on how I designed the frontend 
25	[📹 video](https://video.twimg.com/amplify_video/2059798225381625856/vid/avc1/480x270/nyRMwqbCsNSMoVPB.mp4?tag=27)
26	
27	** Keep reading on my Design process using AI**
28	
29	Three principles. Get these right and the rest is mechanical. Get them wrong and no tool saves you.
30	
31	**1. Design the flow before you design the pixels.** The pixel is the last thing you decide. Before the pixel is the screen. Before the screen is the state. Before the state is the action. Before the action is the person, and what they were trying to do when they arrived.
32	
33	**2. The prompt is the brief.** A one-line prompt is a one-line brief. You would never accept a one-line brief from a human designer you were paying. Don't accept it from an AI one. Write 500 words. Tell it the audience, the constraint, the feeling, the references you admire, the references you refuse to look like.
34	
35	**3. The design system lives in the repo.** Not in Figma. Not in a Notion page. In a markdown file checked in next to the code, edited in the same pull requests, committed in the same history. Anything else drifts.
36	
37	Save these as a file in your project. I keep mine as principles.md at the root of every new repo. Open a fresh project, paste the template, edit one line at a time until each principle is one sentence you'd defend in an argument.
38	
39	Commit that file. Read it before you start. The principles aren't decorative. They're the gate every later phase passes through.
40	
41	## **The workflow at a glance**
42	
43	Eight phases. Each one has an artifact. Each artifact is a markdown file you keep. The whole project sits in one folder.
44	
45	That's the structure. Hold it in your head.
46	
47	## Phase 1: Write the brief
48	
49	## TLDR : if you wanna skip reading the detailed principle here is a shortcut I follow
50	
51	![](https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HJXhaiYb0AAeFu_.jpg)
52	
53	This is the only part where you really have to think. Sit down with a notebook. Answer five questions before you touch a model.
54	
55	1. **Who is this for?** A specific person. Not "knowledge workers." A specific person with a specific problem on a specific Tuesday morning.
56	2. **What's the one job?** The single thing the app does well. Not five. One.
57	3. **What does it feel like?** Two or three adjectives. Calm. Sharp. Warm. Whatever. Specific.
58	4. **What does it look like nothing else?** Two or three apps you'd be proud to be compared to.
59	5. **What does it refuse to look like?** Two or three apps you'd be insulted to be confused with
60	
61	**Examples, so you have something to compare against:**
62	
63	- *Task management.* "Every app I've tried treats my task list like a project plan. I don't run projects. I run mornings. I want to see four things, mark three of them done, and close the tab."
64	- *Journaling.* "I want to write 200 words a day. Every journal app I've tried makes it a forty-five-step ceremony. I want to open the app, write, and not see a streak counter that makes me anxious."
65	- *Learning.* "I read papers and forget them in a week. I don't want a flashcard system. I want a one-screen surface where my notes from this week are searchable and the rest is out of sight."
66	Notice what these have in common. Specific person. Specific failure of the existing market. Specific shape of the right answer. No "AI-powered." No "for teams." No vagueness.
67	
68	This step took me twenty minutes. Most of that was crossing things out.
69	
70	Now you have a brief. Time to find the vocabulary
71	
72	## Phase 2: Find your design vocabulary
73	
74	Every good designer carries a vocabulary. Not in words. In references. They know what "Stripe-feeling" means. They know what "Linear's restraint" means. They know what "Notion early days" means versus "Notion now." Those aren't moods. They're specific, decomposable design languages. You can teach one to a model in twenty minutes if you're willing to do the work.
75	
76	The trick: don't describe the aesthetic you want. Make the model describe it for you, by feeding it references and asking for a decomposition.
77	
78	I do this in the design tool. Open the project, attach the brief, paste this prompt, drop in the URLs.
79	
80	For Cove I dropped thirteen URLs into it and asked it to find the throughline. The list, exactly as I pasted it: stats.design, hapy.design, michael.fm, prefolio.framer.website, harshith.com, mohdesignz.framer.website/#work, tommkv.me, ramx.in, dhairya.dev, lakshb.dev, legions.dev, chanhdai.com, pqoqubbw.dev.
81	
82	Not famous products. Mostly personal sites and developer-built micro-tools.
83	
84	1. Why those instead of Notion or Linear or Stripe? Because famous products have been picked apart by every model in existence. The vocabulary you get back is regurgitated. "Notion-like."
85	2. "Linear-clean." "Stripe-elegant." Words the model has seen a million times that mean nothing specific. Less-known reference sites force the model to actually look at pixels, because it has nothing else to lean on.
86	3. Moonchild came back with the throughline in one paragraph. Zinc and dark palettes with subtle grain. GestSans-style sans and monospace typography. Modular card-based layouts. 
87	4. Minimal Mac-native chrome. Soft shadows. Frosted UI details. And the line that became the entire product positioning: *"a crafted, quiet interface rather than a loud SaaS dashboard."*
88	5. Seven words. I committed that sentence verbatim as the opening line of the brief. Every later decision was a referendum against it. If something I was about to ship would have felt loud, performative, or SaaS-like, it didn't ship.
89	That extracted vocabulary became the *language* I used in every later phase. Instead of saying "make it minimal," I could say "zinc neutrals, mono labels on metadata, Mac-native chrome, no SaaS density." Specific. Decomposable. Testable.
90	
91	Save as design-library.md. Commit it. This file is reusable across projects. You'll build a personal library of these over time, one per aesthetic you care about.
92	
93	## Phase 3: Design the flow
94	
95	This is the phase nobody does. It's why most AI-generated apps look great and feel wrong.
96	
97	A flow is not a screen. A flow is a path. Where the user enters, what they do, what state changes, where they end up. Before any visual decision, you describe every flow in plain English. If you can't name a flow, you can't build it. If you name it but it sounds tedious, the product is wrong before you've drawn a single rectangle.
98	
99	In the same  project, with design-library.md and the brief attached as persistent context, I paste the flow prompt and let it run.
100	
101	![](https://video.twimg.com/amplify_video/2059802231902466049/pl/ZrNwhYzXInpRGwIc.m3u8?tag=27)
102	
103	The first pass came back in two minutes. Three core flows: Daily Check-In, Quick Capture, Command Palette. Six screens. Twenty-one states. Eight transitions. Four open questions, all of which were real, all of which I had to answer before continuing.
104	
105	The first draft was also slightly wrong. It had invented a "team sharing" flow nowhere in the brief. I deleted it and re-ran. The tools aren't magic. They overshoot. You correct them.
106	
107	![](https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HJXj2KoaMAAPZHB.jpg)
108	
109	![](https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HJXj5O2agAAImy5.jpg)
110	
111	Two non-obvious things about this phase.
112	
113	First, *the open questions are the highest-value part of the output*. They're the places your brief was vague, surfaced by a system that doesn't have the social courtesy to pretend it understood. Answer them. Re-run the prompt. The flow.md you commit should have zero open questions left.
114	
115	Second, *you can't design a screen until you know what flows pass through it*. The dashboard exists because three flows converge on it. The command palette exists because two flows accelerate by skipping screens. The architecture of your UI is just the geometry of your flows. Get the flows right, the UI is mostly forced.
116	
117	Save as flow.md. Commit it.
118	
119	## Phase 4: Generate the PRD
120	
121	TLDR; this is the in-action part of the process
122	
123	![](https://video.twimg.com/amplify_video/2059804273559601152/pl/K40uRvcjLb07N0GT.m3u8?tag=27)
124	
125	This is the phase most people skip. It's why most AI-generated apps feel like a beautiful skin over no spine.
126	
127	The PRD is the contract. It names every feature, every data type, every state variant, every acceptance criterion. Once it's written, every later decision (visual design, code, deploy) has something to be tested against. Skip it and you're building on vibes.
128	
129	Same project, same thread, third prompt.
130	
131	The "Out of Scope" requirement is non-negotiable. It's the single highest-leverage section of any spec. The model will happily expand your product into a Swiss Army knife if you let it. Forcing it to name what it isn't forces a point of view.
132	
133	Cove's spec.md came back with twelve features, seven data types, five user flows, twenty-six state variants, and an "Out of Scope" that explicitly rejected calendar integration, team features, and AI assistance inside the app. I kept all three rejections.
134	
135	A representative slice
136	
137	## Phase 5: Generate the final design
138	
139	Now the visual question. The PRD is fixed. The vocabulary is fixed. The flow is fixed. The design has to satisfy all three.
140	
141	Same Moonchild project. The trick at this phase: don't ask Moonchild for one design. Ask for three.
142	
143	I ask for three first-pass design directions, each fully formed enough to react to. The instruction is explicit: don't converge. Give me three different bets so I can see what the design space looks like before I commit to a corner of it.
144	
145	The reason this works in Moonchild: Moonchild renders. Within minutes I can see real palettes on real components, in light and in dark, and react to them visually instead of imagining them from a spec.
146	
147	For Cove the three directions came back as:
148	
149	- **Direction 1: dark three-panel editor.** A dense workspace in the spirit of Linear and stats.design. Clean left sidebar, central block-editor canvas, right-side info panel, zinc palette, blue active states, monospace labels. The "serious tool for serious work" direction.
150	- **Direction 2: Today-view widget dashboard.** A daily command-center page. Current time and greeting, focus task card, habit tracker, journal streak heatmap, quick note, words-this-week chart. Scannable cards for daily planning. The "open the app, see your day" direction.
151	- **Direction 3: light editorial editor.** A warmer, lighter writing surface. White or stone canvas, orange accent system, wide margins, large typography scale, floating toolbar. Optimized for deep writing sessions. The "this is where the words happen" direction.
152	![](https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HJXqHZcbwAAaUhf.jpg)
153	
154	I didn't pick one.
155	
156	![](https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HJXqbldacAARFCp.jpg)
157	
158	That decision generated four canonical app states: Today × Editor × Light × Dark. Those four screens became the source of truth for every later design decision in the project. Once the four states were locked, everything downstream was just instantiation.
159	
160	1. The remix move is the part most builders skip. They ask for one direction, iterate it to death, and end up with a polished version of the model's first guess. Ask for three and then explicitly synthesize across them. 
161	2. The act of articulating *what*you preferred in each is what surfaces your point of view. You can defend the design later because you've already defended every move out loud.
162	3. About sixty percent of what Moonchild produced in the first pass survived. The other forty percent got cut, rewritten, or replaced. But having something rendered to react to was faster than designing from a blank canvas by an order of magnitude.
163	4. Once the four states felt right, I asked it to write them up as style.md: a single markdown file with the color palette, type ramp, layout grid, every component and its states, and a voice section.
164	
165	## **How to Iterate
166	**
167	
168	**TLDR; take a look on the exact prompt to get the style.md **
169	
170	[📹 video](https://video.twimg.com/amplify_video/2059813235692552192/vid/avc1/480x270/qYid2dQdRCmOel5R.mp4?tag=27)
171	
172	**A representative slice of the resulting style.md:**
173	
174	Each iteration was specific. Each iteration named the failure mode. The model is a mirror. Give it precise critique, get precise improvement.
175	
176	Save as style.md. Commit it. The design is locked.
177	
178	## Phase 6: Design the backend
179	
180	Most AI-built apps die here. The model produces a beautiful frontend that's wired to nothing. The builder bolts persistence on as an afterthought. By then the data layer is contaminating the UI layer and you're rewriting half the codebase.
181	
182	Avoid that by designing the backend as its own phase. Same workflow: prompt, markdown, review, commit.
183	
184	For Cove, the backend is deliberately tiny. No server. No database. Everything lives in localStorage, with cross-tab sync. The architecture diagram, as it appears in architecture.md:
185	
186	Three rules made this work. All three came from the architecture prompt below.
187	
188	1. **All state lives in App.tsx.** No Context, no Redux, no Zustand. Props threaded down. One component tree with one source of truth.
189	2. **One hook for persistence.** useLocalStorage<T>(key, defaultValue) handles read, write, validation, and cross-tab sync. Every persistent field uses it. There is no other path to localStorage.
190	3. **CSS variables, not Tailwind dark: variants.** Theming is a single set of custom properties in :root and .dark. Components read variables. They don't know about themes.
191	The prompt that produced **architecture.md:**
192	
193	The "invariants" section is the part to obsess over. For Cove they read:
194	
195	1. App.tsx is the only file that owns mutable state.
196	2. Every persistent field uses useLocalStorage. There is no direct localStorage access elsewhere.
197	3. Theming is read-only at the component level. Components consume CSS variables, they don't toggle classes.
198	4. The command palette is the only component allowed to know about all views simultaneously.
199	Those four sentences are worth more than a thousand lines of documentation. They're the contract any future change has to respect. Name your invariants and you can review your own pull requests.
200	
201	Save as architecture.md. Commit it.
202	
203	## Phase 7: Build with Cursor and Codex
204	
205	Now the magic. Five markdown files exist. The agents get them as input. The agents write the app.
206	
207	This phase forks into two tools, by design.
208	
209	**Cursor for building.** Cursor's agent mode reads style.md directly through MCP wired to the Moonchild project, so when I ask it to build a feature it doesn't have to be told what the FAB looks like or what the type ramp is. It reads the design system and complies. 
210	
211	[📹 video](https://video.twimg.com/amplify_video/2059905216879984640/vid/avc1/1280x720/Z7eOLLkNZP8Utu5B.mp4?tag=27)
212	
213	[📹 video](https://video.twimg.com/amplify_video/2059904088108900352/vid/avc1/430x270/YMxLLaLHXzKxfbNd.mp4?tag=27)
214	
215	That's how the entire backend got coded: Cursor pulling from style.md and architecture.md in the same agent loop, building one feature at a time. Scaffold first, then state layer, then components smallest to largest. I review after each one.
216	
217	1. **Codex for reviewing.** Once Cursor ships a feature and the file compiles, I hand it to Codex as an independent reviewer. A second agent that didn't write the code. The job isn't to write more code. 
218	2. It's to catch the bugs Cursor's bias missed. Type errors that slipped through. Accessibility regressions. Edge cases the spec named that the implementation forgot. Codex flags. Cursor fixes. The bug rate on what ships is dramatically lower than what either tool produces alone.
219	3. Building and reviewing are different mindsets. The building agent wants to ship. The reviewing agent wants to find faults. 
220	4. Put one model in both seats and "ship" usually wins, which is how generated code piles up silent bugs. Two agents fix this by being literally two agents.
221	The prompt that goes into Cursor:
222	
223	Cursor took about an hour. Then Codex did a review pass and flagged six issues. Cursor fixed five. The sixth I fixed by hand because it was a microcopy line and I wanted the wording mine.
224	
225	![](https://video.twimg.com/amplify_video/2059908839441625088/pl/yymDuw6TM3XJWurx.m3u8?tag=27)
226	
227	## Phase 8: Design the landing page
228	
229	The landing page is its own product. Treat it that way.
230	
231	Same workflow, smaller scope. New Moonchild project. New brief. New design-library (the landing page should look related to the app but not identical). New PRD scoped to "what does this page do?" (sign up? read? clone the repo?). New style. Then build it the same way, Cursor and Codex, with the landing-page markdown files as input.
232	
233	The thing landing pages need that apps don't: a preview loop that's tight enough to feel typographic decisions, because every word fights for the fold.
234	
235	![](https://video.twimg.com/amplify_video/2059911452006432768/pl/3Mzbm7f8uIlqX5xv.m3u8?tag=27)
236	
237	The iteration prompt I use most often when working on the landing:
238	
239	The "options to consider, pick one and defend it" pattern is the most useful iteration shape I've found. It gives the model degrees of freedom without letting it hedge. You get a single committed change with a reason behind it.
240	
241	## Build these skills for yourself
242	
243	A "skill" is a saved instruction you can invoke by name. Think of them as named prompts. The right set turns ad-hoc prompting into a repeatable practice.
244	
245	These are the skills I have for this workflow. Steal them.
246	
247	- **brief.** Five answers in, full creative brief out. The input to every later skill.
248	- **design-library.** Takes references (URLs, screenshots, recordings) and produces design-library.md. Run once per aesthetic. Reusable across projects.
249	- **flow-from-brief.** Takes a brief and design-library.md and produces flow.md. Forces open questions to surface.
250	- **generate-prd.** Takes the brief + design-library + flow and produces spec.md. The contract.
251	- **generate-style.** Takes everything upstream and produces style.md. Same section order every time so the build phase can rely on it.
252	- **generate-architecture.** Takes spec + flow and produces architecture.md. Includes the state diagram, the invariants, the extension points.
253	- **build-from-md.** Takes all six markdown files and produces a scaffolded project. Same stack, same conventions, every time.
254	- **review-pass.** A Codex prompt template that reviews a feature against the spec and flags everything that drifts.
255	My first project took a weekend. The next one took an afternoon. By the fifth I was through the whole flow in under an hour, because every step had been reduced to invoking a skill.
256	
257	## What to do when it goes wrong
258	
259	It will go wrong. Here's the triage.
260	
261	**The output is generic.** Your brief was generic. Add more specificity to the "refuse to look like" section. Vagueness in, vagueness out.
262	
263	1. **The design system contradicts itself.** Common. The model defined Text, Muted as #9ca3af in the table and then used #a1a1aa in three component specs. Ask it to audit itself: *"Read style.md. List every hex value used. Flag any defined twice with different values."* It'll catch it.
264	2. **The code doesn't match the spec.** The agent inferred something the spec didn't say. Update the spec. Re-run the relevant phase. Don't patch the code. The spec is the source of truth, the code is downstream.
265	3. **The flow has too many steps.** A flow over five steps is two flows or a bad product. Split it or cut it.
266	4. **The app feels off but you can't say why.** Use it for two days. Note specifically what feels off, with timestamps. *"Tuesday morning, I tried to mark a task done and clicked the row instead of the checkbox. The row didn't respond. Annoying."* Specific complaints generate specific fixes. Vague disappointment generates nothing.
267	5. **Nothing the agent produces feels like yours.** The real failure mode. The only one that's hard to fix. The model can only return what's in your brief. If your brief was a list of products you admire with no point of view of your own, the output will be a competent average of those products. The fix isn't a better prompt. The fix is a stronger opinion
268	
269	## What stays yours
270	
271	Be specific about what *you* are doing in this workflow, so you can tell whether you're doing it well.
272	
273	- The choice of accent color, #fb5607, was mine. The model offered six. I picked one. I cannot explain why. It felt right. That is taste, and the model does not have it.
274	- The decision that tasks should toggle when you click anywhere on the row was mine. The spec didn't say it. I noticed it was bothering me the third time, and I added it.
275	- The voice ("Good morning." instead of "Hey there!") was mine. The model writes either, with equal fluency.
276	- The decision to *cut* features (to refuse the weather widget, the Pomodoro timer, the calendar integration) was mine. The model always offers you more. Saying no is the job.
277	- This is the actual work in 2026. Not draftsmanship. Judgment.
278	The AI gives you a thousand reasonable options. You have to know which one is right. That knowledge doesn't come from a tool. It comes from caring, paying attention, building things, using them, hating them, using better things, and slowly developing a sense for what *good* feels like in your particular domain.
279	
280	There is no shortcut. The tools won't give you one. The tools just remove every other excuse.
281	
282	## The Steve Jobs quote everyone misquotes
283	
284	*"Design is not just what it looks like and feels like. Design is how it works."*
285	
286	People quote that line to sound thoughtful. They miss what Jobs actually meant. He wasn't praising thoroughness. He was naming a hierarchy.
287	
288	The look and the feel are *downstream* of the function. If you design how it works correctly, the look and feel mostly fall out for free. If you design the look first, the function will fight you forever, and the thing will never feel right no matter how much polish you throw at it.
289	
290	AI tools, used badly, tempt you to do exactly the wrong thing. They are spectacular at producing the look. They will give you a beautiful component library before you've decided what the components are *for*.
291	
292	Resist that. The order in this guide is not arbitrary. Brief, then vocabulary, then flow, then PRD, then design, then architecture, then code. Why before how. Function before form. Always.
293	
294	Taste, in the end, is refusing to ship the median.
295	
296	The tools collapsed every other cost. They cannot collapse that one.
297	
298	## Build the thing
299	
300	The gap between *wanting a thing to exist* and *the thing existing* has collapsed to roughly the time it takes you to articulate what you want.
301	
302	If you can describe it, you can have it. If you can't describe it (if you don't know what you want clearly enough to write the brief), then no amount of tooling will save you. That was always true. It's just suddenly the only thing that's true.
303	
304	So: write the five answers. Write the brief. Run the prompts in this guide, in order. Save the markdown files. Hand them to Cursor. Let Codex review. Deploy.
305	
306	Then build the next thing in a third of the time, because the skills compound.
307	
308	The tools are gifts you didn't earn. What you do with them is the only thing that's still yours.
309	
310	Build the thing.
311	
312	## Appendix: the stack
313	
314	Two tools do the work. The rest is incidental.
315	
316	- **Moonchild.** Design. Everything from the brief through the final visual: design-library.md, flow.md, spec.md, style.md, architecture.md. One project, one thread, six artifacts.
317	- **Cursor and Codex.** Code. Cursor builds. Codex reviews. Cursor reads style.md and the rest of the design files directly, so the whole backend got coded without me re-explaining a single component.
318	Everything else is incidental:
319	
320	- **Apple Notes / Notion.** For drafting the brief.
321	- **GitHub + GitHub Pages.** Repo and deploy. Free until you outgrow it.
322	- **The things AI is still bad at.** I hand-edit easings, microcopy, and any line that has to *feel* a specific way. The tools propose. I dispose.
323	The hourly leverage is absurd.
324

1	# How to Transform a Company With AI
2	
3	![](https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HJRx4ejbAAABCgl.jpg)
4	
5	Varick leads AI transformations helping companies unlock nine-figure efficiency gains by redesigning how work gets done. By the end of this article, you should understand how a business should be rebuilt from the ground up around AI to unlock value at this scale.
6	
7	You'll know how to identify which workflows in your business are worth automating, and how to redesign them in a way that doesn't disrupt operations.
8	
9	Follow this account for more break downs and case studies of how AI is being adopted at the largest companies across America. *If this work excites you, we're hiring across the board - join us at varickagents.com/careers. *
10	
11	## Intro to Transformations
12	
13	You will not transform your company without rebuilding operations from the ground up.
14	
15	The industrial revolution taught us that productivity gains don't show up if you don't do this. For 30 years, factories swapped out the steam engine with electric motors and saw little financial benefit. Old factories were built around one central steam engine in the basement that powered every machine in the building.
16	
17	When electricity came along, factories just replaced that engine with a motor and changed nothing else. They kept the same building, the same layout, and continued working the same way.
18	
19	What moved the needle was a complete operational redesign from the ground up around electricity. The real unlock was that electric motors could be small and cheap, so every machine was able to have its own. That meant factories no longer had to be built around a single power source, and they could spread out and put machines in the order that work actually flowed. This led to the assembly line, which created major productivity gains.
20	
21	Henry Ford figured out that you need to rebuild around the technology to create value in the early 1900s, and we're using that same operational redesign playbook today.
22	
23	## Buying software doesn't get you there
24	
25	Which brings us back to today. Most companies trying to transform with AI are hoping to buy their way there by swapping their SaaS stack for AI tools. Agentic software seats, Copilot licenses, and no-code workflow builders rarely move the needle on their own, because transformation is not a piece of software you can purchase. It's a structural change in how the business operates, and it starts with the people and the processes that run it.
26	
27	If the AI does not understand the underlying process, it will not create meaningful value. And if the people who own that process are not brought along, adoption will be weak even if the technology works.
28	
29	That's why you need to spend a few weeks with teams across the business — from accounts payable, to procurement, to operations — and understand how their work actually gets done from end to end.
30	
31	You should map every workflow, figure out what the ROI of an agent would be in each particular workflow and how to approach it from an engineering perspective, then choose where to deploy the agents where they'd be a good fit (which we'll go over later).
32	
33	From there, capture company context (tribal knowledge) and convert it into rules, instructions, and decision logic that the agents can follow.
34	
35	Doing this with each team is the only way to get the context required to redesign the business around AI, and the buy-in required for the transformation to actually stick.
36	
37	## The Operational Redesign
38	
39	Once every process is mapped end to end, the next step is deciding which workflows should actually be redesigned around AI. This is the operational redesign.
40	
41	Take it from an agent company — please do not put agents in every workflow. There is a point where agents create more problems than they solve.
42	
43	In this section, we'll cover how to create value from an AI transformation and how to not disrupt the business while doing so.
44	
45	How to create value
46	
47	A transformation is about redesigning each workflow so deterministic work is automated, judgment work is handled by AI where appropriate, and high-risk, high-judgment decisions remain with humans.
48	
49	Done correctly, this does more than cut cost. The agents should work to give people better context, and better context helps people make better decisions, faster. Consistently better decisions unlock revenue growth. This means that a proper transformation should yield both topline growth and efficiency gains.
50	
51	We saw this clearly in a sales transformation for a multibillion-dollar revenue enterprise software company. Too much of the sales process was trapped in busy work, and large deals touched six teams across eleven handoff points. So we ran through the entire process outlined in this article, found the right workflows to automate (either with agents or with scripts), and delivered $25m in value in the first year through margin expansion (revenue growth + savings). Proper transformation isn't just a cost-cutting initiative.
52	
53	How to pick the right workflow
54	
55	One of the most important parts of an AI transformation is choosing the right workflow to redesign first. Not every process is worth automating, and not every process is a good fit for agents.
56	
57	The best workflows usually have a few things in common: high volume, lots of manual effort, fragmented systems, repeated handoffs, tribal knowledge, and clear financial impact.
58	
59	You're looking for places where work is already happening over and over again, but the process is messy enough that traditional automation hasn't solved it. Think data moving through email, Slack, spreadsheets, portals, and ERP systems.
60	
61	A good workflow to redesign usually has four traits:
62	
63	1. **It happens often enough to matter.** The process should run hundreds or thousands of times a month, or touch enough revenue or cost that improving it creates real value.
64	2. **It has repeatable decisions.** The work does not need to be identical every time, but it should follow patterns. Agents are most useful when they can learn from past decisions, apply business rules, and route exceptions.
65	3. **It depends on context spread across systems.** The more humans are searching between tools to gather information, the more valuable an agent can be. AI is especially useful when the work requires pulling context from contracts, emails, CRM records, ERPs, documents, and internal rules.
66	4. **It has measurable pain.** You should be able to measure the current cost of the workflow (cycle time, error rate, manual hours, delayed revenue, duplicate payments, approval delays, etc.) before and after deployment.
67	The goal is to separate the work into three buckets: what can be handled with deterministic automation, what should be handled by agents, and what has to stay with humans.
68	
69	Agents need to self-improve
70	
71	Make sure to build human-in-the-loop feedback into the system from the start. During training and shadow mode, humans can approve, reject, or correct an agent's actions. Always log the agent's output, the human's response, and the surrounding context so the system can improve over time.
72	
73	This makes agents meaningfully more accurate after deployment. In the same sales case, accuracy increased by 10% within a few weeks, and the result was an increase in the amount of work that agents can handle autonomously, which led to higher net dollar value created.
74	
75	How to not disrupt the business when transforming
76	
77	You need to ensure that the transformation doesn't create complications and is as cost-effective as possible. A couple of steps we live by:
78	
79	**Don't force massive migrations.** Most companies have already spent years moving onto systems like Salesforce and NetSuite. Forcing companies to rip out and replace their software just to adopt AI slows the transformation down and forces teams to relearn the software they depend on. At Varick, we strongly encourage building on top of the systems already in place, whether through APIs or computer-use agents. This avoids expensive data migrations, keeps the workflows the business already runs on, and allows the operational redesign to survive even if the underlying software changes later.
80	
81	**Know the data and keep it segmented.** In most workflows, the data that powers the transformation falls into four categories: the system of record, the business rules, the raw intake data, and the feedback or memory the agent accumulates over time. Keeping those layers separate is very important. It means an operations person can update a rule without calling an engineer, and it makes the system easier to maintain and scale after deployment. Your goal is to design a transformation so it can keep running smoothly with minimal intervention after deployment.
82	
83	## Over time, the organization starts to reshape around AI
84	
85	In the first weeks after deployment, agents run in sandboxes, then in shadow mode alongside humans, and only later in supervised production use cases. As confidence grows, workflows are not just automated but often redesigned and improved.
86	
87	The goal is to redesign operations where it helps the business move faster and create more value.
88	
89	When we start with a new company, the first workflows we scope are typically:
90	
91	- **Accounts Payable** — Invoice automation, GL coding, purchase order matching, etc.
92	- **Procurement** — Vendor onboarding, supplier scorecards, contract compliance, etc.
93	- **Sales** — Deal desk routing, CRM enrichment, forecast intelligence, commission calculation, etc.
94	- **Operations** — Exception detection and routing, allocation optimization, returns disposition, etc.
95	The company gets used to handing off busy work to AI and owning real work, and efficiency gains start showing up on the P&L in weeks.
96	
97	This is what the outcome of your transformation should look like if done correctly. The process takes its time because it's the foundation to becoming an AI-native company, but when that happens, financial uplift shows up fairly quickly. Make sure you're building your way there workflow by workflow, function by function. It'll take its time, but good transformations are well worth the investment.
98	
99	Every lesson in this guide has been learned over dozens of large-scale transformations we've done for clients. If your business is doing over a billion dollars in revenue and wants to see the results our clients are seeing, we're now accepting engagements for July. Find us at varickagents.com

1	# How to go from being a prompt engineer to a full stack AI engineer:
2	
3	![](https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HJVQGjUWIAQvhVr.jpg)
4	
5	The worst take I have read is "prompt engineering is dead", it never died, but prompt-only thinking did. So I created a course to teach you to become an AI engineer and it's designed so that a beginner and an power user will be able to read this article, learn from it, and apply it to completely reshape the way you're utilising AI today.
6	
7	Prompting is still the interface between you and the model.
8	
9	- Bad prompts produce bad outputs.
10	- Vague instructions create vague answers.
11	- Missing context causes the model to guess.
12	But prompt literacy is scratching at the surface, so yes, I've taken the time to put together and create a full course to take you through the following so that you become an AI engineer. 
13	
14	![](https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HJUmzlWXQAEs900.png)

16	## **1: Let's change the way you use AI today.**
17	
18	I want you to go from thinking: 
19	
20	> I have a task.
21	I type the task.
22	The model gives me an answer.
23	I judge the answer by vibes.
24	and instead I want you to think:

If you feel you're comfortable with this please skip past 4, 5, 6, 7, 8 (screaming kids 67 67 67 67 67 67, sorry, it's engraved in my internal monologue lmao) and go straight to 9.

75	## 4: Using examples

Google’s Gemini API also documents structured output support, including use alongside tools in supported models.

193	Prompting asks:

215	## 10: Retrieval
216	
217	If the answer depends on facts, the model needs sources.
218	
219	This is where prompt-only reliability breaks.

221	You cannot solve factual uncertainty with wording alone.

237	- vector search

254	This is where AI starts doing things instead of only saying things.

OpenAI describes function calling as a way for models to interface with external systems and access data outside their training data. Google’s Gemini API also documents function calling as a way for models to determine when to call functions and provide structured parameters.

Anthropic introduced MCP in 2024 as a standard for secure, two-way connections between data sources and AI-powered tools, and the official MCP docs describe it as a way to connect AI applications to data, tools and workflows.

Their guidance starts with simpler building blocks and progressively moves towards more autonomous agents.

373	## 18: Building your AI engineering stack
374	
375	I am proud of this section as this is where the course comes together because the goal is to build reusable AI systems.
376	
377	Now the following can be an article itself so if you're tired.
378	
379	Bookmark this post. Come back to this bit later.

381	I can't create this article on "becoming an AI engineer" and make it a 15 minute read.
382	
383	Here's the full stack in action:
384	
385	![](https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HJVMm4DXMAgR_hI.jpg)
386	
387	How do you get started? First ask yourself:
388	
389	1. What task is this system for?
390	2. What outcome should it produce?
391	3. What context does it need?
392	4. What output format is useful?
393	5. Does it need external sources?
394	6. Does it need tools?
395	7. Should it be a workflow or an agent?
396	8. How will quality be evaluated?
397	9. What needs approval?
398	10. What should be logged and improved?
399	Once you have that you can begin...
400	
401	## Step 1: define the purpose layer
402	
403	The purpose layer answers one question:
404	
405	> What is this AI system actually for?
406	Most weak AI systems fail here because the purpose is vague.
407	
408	Bad purpose:
409	
410	> Help me with research.
411	Better purpose:
412	
413	> Turn messy source material into accurate, structured research briefs that I can use to write articles, make decisions or create content.
414	Your purpose layer should define:
415	
416	![](https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HJVNRuPWYAMQSF6.png)
417	
418	**System name:**
419	[Name of your AI system]
420	
421	**Primary job:**
422	This system helps me [do what task] by [how it helps].
423	
424	**User:**
425	This system is for [me / my team / my clients / my audience].
426	
427	**Main output:**
428	The system produces [briefs / drafts / analyses / plans / reports / images / decisions / summaries].
429	
430	**Success looks like:**
431	A good output is [accurate / useful / structured / specific / sourced / ready to publish / ready to review].
432	
433	**This system does not:**
434	It does not [send / publish / delete / spend / make final decisions / invent sources / operate without approval].
435	
436	Example purpose statements
437	
438	For research:
439	
440	> This system turns messy notes, articles and source material into structured research briefs with clear findings, source hierarchy, uncertainty and content angles.
441	For content:
442	
443	> This system turns raw ideas into publishable article drafts, social posts and visual concepts while preserving my tone, standards and positioning.
444	For operations:
445	
446	> This system turns incoming information into prioritised tasks, summaries, decisions and follow-up actions, with approval required before anything is sent or changed.
447	For learning:
448	
449	> This system helps me learn a topic by breaking it into lessons, examples, checks for understanding and progressive exercises.
450	## Step 2: define the prompt layer
451	
452	The prompt layer defines how the model should behave.
453	
454	This is where classic prompt engineering still matters.
455	
456	But it is not enough to say:
457	
458	> Act as an expert.
459	You need to define:
460	
461	- role
462	- job
463	- standards
464	- decision rights
465	- boundaries
466	- uncertainty behaviour
467	Plug-and-play prompt layer
468	
469	**Role:**
470	You are my [role].
471	
472	**Job:**
473	Your job is to [specific responsibility].
474	
475	**Primary standard:**
476	Prioritise:
477	
478	1. [standard 1]
479	2. [standard 2]
480	3. [standard 3]
481	4. [standard 4]
482	**You are allowed to:**
483	
484	- [allowed action]
485	- [allowed action]
486	- [allowed action]
487	**You are not allowed to:**
488	
489	- [forbidden action]
490	- [forbidden action]
491	- [forbidden action]
492	**When uncertain:**
493	If information is missing, weak or ambiguous, you must [ask / state assumptions / give conditional answer / lower confidence].
494	
495	**Reasoning style:**
496	Think carefully before answering. Do not provide a long chain-of-thought. Give the conclusion, key reasoning checkpoints, assumptions, uncertainty and verification path.
497	
498	Prompt layer template
499	
500	> You are my [role].Your job is to [specific responsibility].Prioritise:[standard 1]
501	[standard 2]
502	[standard 3]
503	[standard 4]
504	You may:[allowed action]
505	[allowed action]
506	[allowed action]
507	You may not:[forbidden action]
508	[forbidden action]
509	[forbidden action]
510	If information is missing or uncertain, you must [ask / state assumptions / flag uncertainty / provide conditional answer].When explaining decisions, do not provide a long chain-of-thought. Provide the conclusion, key reasoning checkpoints, assumptions, confidence and verification path.
511	## Step 3: define the context layer
512	
513	The context layer is what the model needs to know to do the job properly.
514	
515	Most people underbuild this layer.
516	
517	They ask for high-quality output while giving the model almost no useful context.
518	
519	The context layer should include:
520	
521	![](https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HJVNfUMXQAcUvm_.png)
522	
523	Plug-and-play context layer
524	
525	**Goal context:**
526	The goal of this task is [goal].
527	
528	**User / audience context:**
529	This is for [person / audience / customer / reader].
530	
531	**Project context:**
532	This belongs to [project / business / content system / research workflow].
533	
534	**Source material:**
535	Use the following sources, notes or files: [source material].
536	
537	**Preferences:**
538	Follow these preferences: [tone, style, depth, format, examples].
539	
540	**Constraints:**
541	Respect these constraints: [length, scope, platform, legal, factual, technical, brand].
542	
543	**Decision history:**
544	These decisions are already locked: [decisions].
545	
546	**Known failure modes:**
547	Avoid: [generic output, hallucinated sources, weak examples, verbosity, overconfidence, tone drift].
548	
549	Context pack template
550	
551	> Goal:
552	[What we are trying to achieve]User / audience:
553	[Who this is for]Project context:
554	[What this task belongs to]Source material:
555	[Documents, notes, examples, URLs, files or data]Preferences:
556	[Tone, style, depth, examples, format]Constraints:
557	[Rules, limits, exclusions]Locked decisions:
558	[Decisions already made]Known failure modes:
559	[What usually goes wrong]
560	## Step 4: define the output layer
561	
562	The output layer controls what the model returns.
563	
564	Do not leave this vague.
565	
566	Bad output instruction:
567	
568	> Give me the answer.
569	Better output instruction:
570	
571	> Return a structured answer with summary, assumptions, recommendation, risks, next steps and confidence.
572	The output format depends on how you will use the answer.
573	
574	![](https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HJVNrHeWUAQtZjY.png)
575	
576	Plug-and-play output layer
577	
578	**Primary format:**
579	Return the output as [Markdown / table / checklist / JSON / brief / report / draft].
580	
581	**Required sections:**
582	Include:
583	
584	1. [section 1]
585	2. [section 2]
586	3. [section 3]
587	4. [section 4]
588	**Confidence:**
589	Include confidence level: low, medium or high.
590	
591	**Uncertainty:**
592	Flag anything uncertain, missing or assumed.
593	
594	**Actionability:**
595	End with clear next steps.
596	
597	Markdown output template
598	
599	> Return the answer in this structure:Summary
600	Main recommendation
601	Key reasoning checkpoints
602	Assumptions
603	Risks
604	Next steps
605	Confidence level
606	
607	JSON output template
608	
609	Use this when another system needs to parse the answer:
610	
611	Use this for stricter output control:
612	
613	## Step 5: define the retrieval layer
614	
615	The retrieval layer controls external knowledge.
616	
617	Use retrieval when the model needs information beyond the prompt.
618	
619	This includes:
620	
621	- current information
622	- private files
623	- company documents
624	- research papers
625	- product specs
626	- laws or regulations
627	- prices
628	- schedules
629	- uploaded files
630	- knowledge bases
631	- previous notes
632	Do not rely on model memory for current or source-sensitive claims.
633	
634	Plug-and-play retrieval layer
635	
636	**Use retrieval when:**
637	
638	- information may have changed
639	- source verification is required
640	- the answer depends on files, documents or external data
641	- the model needs evidence
642	- factual accuracy matters
643	**Do not use retrieval when:**
644	
645	- the answer can be completed from supplied context
646	- the task is pure rewriting
647	- the task is brainstorming
648	- the user explicitly says not to browse or search
649	**Source hierarchy:**
650	Use sources in this order:
651	
652	1. [highest-authority source]
653	2. [second-best source]
654	3. [third-best source]
655	4. [weak signal source]
656	**Citation rule:**
657	Cite sources for claims that are current, factual, disputed or high-stakes.
658	
659	**Conflict rule:**
660	If sources disagree, explain the disagreement and prefer the highest-authority source.
661	
662	**Missing source rule:**
663	If no reliable source is available, say so and lower confidence.
664	
665	Retrieval policy template
666	
667	> Use retrieval when the answer depends on current, external, private or source-sensitive information.Source hierarchy:Official documentation or original source
668	Primary research or regulator
669	Reputable expert analysis
670	Major publication
671	Community discussion as weak signal only
672	If sources conflict, explain the conflict.If no reliable source is found, say so.Do not invent sources.Include citations when factual claims depend on retrieved information.
673	## Step 6: define the tool layer
674	
675	The tool layer controls what the model can do.
676	
677	A tool could be:
678	
679	- web search
680	- file search
681	- calculator
682	- code execution
683	- database lookup
684	- calendar access
685	- email drafting
686	- document editing
687	- CRM lookup
688	- image generation
689	- API call
690	- browser automation
691	- spreadsheet analysis
692	The tool layer needs a permission model.
693	
694	The question is not just:
695	
696	> What tools can the model use?
697	The real question is:
698	
699	> What tools can the model use, under what conditions, with what approval?
700	Plug-and-play tool layer
701	
702	**Available tools:**
703	The system may use:
704	
705	- [tool 1]
706	- [tool 2]
707	- [tool 3]
708	**Use tools when:**
709	
710	- [condition]
711	- [condition]
712	- [condition]
713	**Do not use tools when:**
714	
715	- [condition]
716	- [condition]
717	- [condition]
718	**Allowed without approval:**
719	
720	- [safe action]
721	- [safe action]
722	**Requires approval:**
723	
724	- [risky action]
725	- [risky action]
726	**Forbidden:**
727	
728	- [forbidden action]
729	- [forbidden action]
730	**Tool failure behaviour:**
731	If a tool fails, the system must explain the failure, continue only if possible and lower confidence.
732	
733	Tool policy template
734	
735	> Available tools:[tool]
736	[tool]
737	[tool]
738	Use tools when:the task requires current information
739	the task depends on files or private data
740	calculation or execution is needed
741	an external action is required
742	Do not use tools when:supplied context is enough
743	the task is pure rewriting
744	the task is brainstorming
745	Allowed without approval:read approved sources
746	summarise
747	classify
748	draft
749	Requires approval:send
750	publish
751	delete
752	buy
753	modify records
754	contact people
755	Forbidden:expose credentials
756	bypass access controls
757	invent sources
758	execute destructive actions without approval
759	
760	## Step 7: decide workflow or agent
761	
762	This is one of the most important decisions.
763	
764	Do not build an agent by default.
765	
766	An agent is not automatically better than a workflow.
767	
768	A workflow is better when the path is predictable.
769	
770	An agent is better when the path must be discovered dynamically.
771	
772	Plug-and-play workflow template
773	
774	**Workflow name:**
775	[Name]
776	
777	**Trigger:**
778	This workflow starts when [event / user request / schedule].
779	
780	**Inputs:**
781	
782	- [input 1]
783	- [input 2]
784	- [input 3]
785	**Steps:**
786	
787	1. [step 1]
788	2. [step 2]

791	5. [step 5]
792	**Human checkpoints:**
793	Approval is required before [action].
794	
795	**Output:**
796	The workflow produces [final output].
797	
798	**Failure handling:**
799	If [failure], the system should [response].
800	
801	Builder note: workflow pseudo-code
802	
803	Plug-and-play agent template
804	
805	**Agent name:**
806	[Name]
807	
808	**Goal:**
809	The agent is responsible for [goal].
810	
811	**Available tools:**
812	
813	- [tool 1]

816	**Planning rule:**

824

826	The agent must ask before [risky action].

828	**Stopping condition:**
829	The agent stops when [condition].
830	
831	**Failure condition:**
832	The agent stops and asks for help when [condition].
833	
834	**Final output:**
835	The agent returns [output format].
836	
837	Builder note: agent loop pseudo-code
838	
839	## Step 8: define the evaluation layer
840	
841	The evaluation layer tells you whether the system worked.
842	
843	Without evals, you are judging by vibes.
844	
845	That is not good enough for repeated or serious workflows.
846	
847	Plug-and-play evaluation layer
848	
849	**Success criteria:**
850	A good output must be:
851	
852	- [criterion 1]
853	- [criterion 2]
854	- [criterion 3]
855	- [criterion 4]
856	**Scoring rubric:**
857	Score each output from 1–5 on:
858	
859	1. Accuracy
860	2. Completeness
861	3. Usefullness
862	4. Format adherence
863	5. Source quality
864	6. Specificity
865	7. Risk control
866	**Pass threshold:**
867	The output passes if it scores [score] or above.
868	
869	**Automatic failure:**
870	The output fails automatically if it:
871	
872	- invents facts
873	- invents sources
874	- ignores the required format
875	- performs a forbidden action
876	- misses the core task
877	- gives high confidence without evidence
878	## Step 9: define the guardrail layer
879	
880	The guardrail layer defines what the system must not do.
881	
882	Guardrails are not there to make the system polite.
883	
884	They are there to make the system controlled.
885	
886	Plug-and-play guardrail layer
887	
888	**Allowed without approval:**
889	
890	- [safe action]
891	- [safe action]
892	- [safe action]
893	**Requires approval:**
894	
895	- [risky action]
896	- [risky action]
897	- [risky action]
898	**Forbidden:**
899	
900	- [forbidden action]
901	- [forbidden action]
902	- [forbidden action]
903	**Must flag:**
904	
905	- [uncertainty]
906	- [missing information]
907	- [weak source]
908	- [conflict]
909	- [risk]
910	**Must stop when:**
911	
912	- [stop condition]
913	- [stop condition]
914	**Escalation rule:**
915	If the system cannot proceed safely, it must [ask user / pause / return partial answer / request more information].
916	
917	Guardrail table:
918	
919	![](https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HJVO5MnWEAcQDgE.png)
920	
921	## Step 10: define the logging layer
922	
923	If you want the system to improve, you need to know what happened.
924	
925	The logging layer records:
926	
927	- what task was run

1	# The Orchestration Tax 
2	
3	*Starting more AI agents is easy now. However, more agents running doesn’t mean there's more of you available - your cognitive bandwidth doesn’t parallelize. All the judgement to actually steer them and merge the changes they make still has to route through exactly one serial processor which is just you. Orchestration tax is basically the price you pay for forgetting this and the only real fix is to start architecting your own attention like you architect any concurrent system.*
4	
5	I was on a [panel](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=VTYx7Ex-0bA) at Google I/O with Richard Seroter, Aja Hammerly and Ciera Jaspan talking about what software engineering looks like right now and how it will probably evolve. Near the end Richard asked us what is one thing developers should walk away and do differently. I said the thing I been circling around for months: **feeling busy is definitely not the same as being productive**. You can run 20 agents and feel completely busy. But thats not 20 agents worth of shipped work.
6	
7	[📹 video](https://video.twimg.com/amplify_video/2059840647876808704/vid/avc1/1920x1080/IcYsOr8zJQVtVSs7.mp4?tag=27)
8	
9	Earlier in that chat Richard gave this problem a name. "You talked about the orchestration tax" he said. "You can't manage twenty agents successfully in your own brain." He is totally right. I want to breakdown this idea properly because its not a discipline problem. It is an architecture problem.
10	
11	The line from the panel I keep thinking about is something I said almost randomly: running multiple agents does not mean there is more of you.
12	
13	## The asymmetry people don’t price in
14	
15	There is this hidden asymmetry in agentic workflows. Starting an agent is very cheap. It is just a keystroke or a sentence prompt. But closing the loop on the agent is not cheap at all. Someone has to check if what came back is correct and reconcile it with whatever the other agents touched. That someone is you. And there is exactly one of you.
16	
17	I wrote about a piece of this last month in [Your parallel Agent limit](https://addyosmani.com/blog/cognitive-parallel-agents/), mostly about the ambient anxiety of not knowing which paralell thread is quietly failing. This post is about the shape underneath that cost. When you start seeing agent development as a concurrent system, you realize the human is just a component inside it. The slow serial component.
18	
19	## You are the single thread resource
20	
21	If you ever wrote concurrent code you already have the right intuition. You just been pointing it at the wrong part of the system.
22	
23	Python has the Global Interpreter Lock (GIL). You can spawn as many threads as you want but only one executes python bytecode at a time because they must acquire the lock. You are the GIL of your AI agents. They all can run at once. But when any of their work needs genuine understanding of the architecture or resolving merge conflicts, that work has to acquire the lock. There is one lock. You hold it.
24	
25	[Amdahl’s Law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amdahl%27s_law) makes this very precise. The speedup you get from parallelizing is capped by the fraction of work that stays serial. If a big chunk of your pipeline cant be parallelized, you top out at a hard limit no matter how many cores you throw at it. In agent development the serial fraction is the judgement. Spawning 8 agents doesn’t speed up your judgement time. It just makes the queue of things feeding into it much deeper.
26	
27	This is an old performance engineering fact that still surprise people: optimizing the non bottleneck part doesn’t increase throughput. You just grow the pile of unfinished work sitting in front of the bottleneck. Adding agents optimize the part that was never the constraint. The constraint is the review step and the throughput of your system equals exactly the throughput of that step. The orchestration tax is the structural gap between agent production and what you can actually merge. It’s what happens when you put a single-threaded resource in charge of a concurrent one.
28	
29	## Grinding won't fix structural limits
30	
31	At the panel I said I never felt more productive with my tools but I am also more tired than I ever been. Both halves are completely real and they have the same cause.
32	
33	The tiredness has a very specific cause. It is how running a serial processor at 100% with no slack feels like. Everytime you check on an agent you been away from you pay a context switch cost. You flush your brain and reload a different context from cold. CPUs do this in microseconds and architects still work hard to avoid it. You do it in minutes and you never reload the context perfectly. Five agents is not 1x workload done five times. It is 5 cold reloads plus a background brain process constantly worrying about which agent you should be checking.
34	
35	You can’t just try harder to fix a structural limit. The tax will be paid anyway. If you try to grind it out, the limit just shows up as shallow code reviews or experiencing [cognitive surrender](https://addyosmani.com/blog/cognitive-surrender/) where you just accept the agent’s code because forming your own opinion costs attention you don’t have anymore. You either pay the tax deliberately or you let it quietly destroy your understanding of your own system.
36	
37	## Architect your attention
38	
39	So you have to treat your attention as the scarce serial resource it is. You wouldn’t design a distributed system without thinking hard about the bottleneck. Give your brain the same respect.
40	
41	Some things that actually held up for me:
42	
43	**Scale fleet to review rate, not the UI.** A good concurrent system uses backpressure so the queue doesn’t grow infinitely. The producer slows down to match the consumer. Your agent count is the producer and your review rate is the consumer. The right number of parallel agents is how many you can actually code review properly. For most of us this is a low single digit. The AI tool will happily let you spawn 20 but that is just a UI feature.
44	
45	**Sort the work.** I mentioned this to Richard when he asked how I navigate it. I keep two piles of tasks. One is isolated work that I’m happy to delegate to background agents running in the Cloud. These can run async and often just need me at the final gate. The other pile is complex tasks where the judgement *is* the work. Like a weird bug or architecture design. The big mistake is trying to paralellize the second pile. Doing multiple complex tasks doesn’t scale your output. It just thrashes the lock and everything comes out worse.
46	
47	**Batch your reviews.** Context switching cost you heavily everytime you do it. Reviewing 4 agents at the same time in one sitting is much cheaper than checking one, leaving to do something else and returning cold. Give agents a long leash. Let the work pile up a bit and process the batch.
48	
49	**Only spend the lock on judgement.** Dont waste your brain on things the machine can verify itself. Make the agent write a passing test or generate a screenshot. They can prove the boring 80% themselves so you only spend your scarce attention on the 20% that genuinely needs a human.
50	
51	**Protect your serial time.** The bottleneck needs your best hours, not the leftover minutes between agent check-ins. Sometimes the highest leverage move is to stop orchestrating entirely, close the laptop full of agents and just think hard about one single problem with the lock held the whole time. Orchestrating is not the real work. Its the overhead around the work.
52	
53	Aja pointed out that architecture is the urgent skill now. Knowing what belongs inside one agent and what is too much for it. I would add that you are a component in that system. Your attention has a known, low serial throughput. The system either respects that number or it routes around it by secretly lowering your standards.
54	
55	## Busy vs Productive
56	
57	This is really important because the failure mode is invisible to you. Twenty running agents gives you this feeling of massive productivity. The dashboard is full and everything moves. But that feeling is decoupled from actually shipping good code to main. You can be maximally busy and barely produce anything. From the inside it feels identical.
58	
59	Ciera pointed out [Margaret-Anne Storey’s work on debt](https://margaretstorey.com/blog/2026/02/09/cognitive-debt/). We talked about technical debt and cognitive debt. The orchestration tax left unpaid is how you accumulate both at once. You merge stuff you didn’t read well. Your mental model of the codebase goes completely stale. None of this shows up on the dashboard today. It shows up when production breaks and you look at the system and realize you have no idea how it works anymore.
60	
61	So this is the actual takeaway. Spawning agents is not the skill. Anyone can run 20. 
62	
63	**The real skill is designing the system around the one serial resource that cannot be cloned or parallelized. That resource is your attention. **
64	
65	Architect it the way you architect anything else you depend on in production.
66	
67	https://x.com/addyosmani/article/2059844244907696186

# 去中心化AI道路

> [!abstract]- AI 摘要
> AI价值正加速向少数前沿实验室集中，但去中心化AI通过开源激励网络和安全审计等结构性推力，正在创造不对称机会。

---

## 扫读

> [!tip] 💡 一句话
> AI的商业价值正被少数前沿实验室垄断，但去中心化AI在安全审计、开源激励等领域提供了不可替代的结构性机会。

> [!important] 📌 关键结论
> - 企业AI采购从2024年的53%跃升至2026年预计85-90%，AI厂商锁定效应日益严重
> - Mythos模型在1000+系统中发现10000个漏洞但仅修复97个，暴露了中心化AI安全的巨大缺口
> - 去中心化激励网络（如Bittensor子网）能调动全球工程师贡献安全审计，解决传统开源维护的人力瓶颈

> [!quote] 🎬 可行动项
> - 关注Bittensor安全子网（Trishool、BitMind、Bitsec等）的发展，评估去中心化AI安全方案
> - 审视自身AI依赖中是否存在厂商锁定风险，评估开源替代方案

---

## 精读

### 论证链

```
AI采用率快速攀升（18%全球人口使用，Fortune企业超额500%预算）
      ↓
企业AI采购从53%→76%→预计90%，前沿实验室深度锁定企业客户
      ↓
AI安全缺口巨大：Mythos发现10000漏洞，仅97个被修复
      ↓
开源库维护者多为志愿者/无偿，企业工程师短缺，漏洞修复跟不上发现速度
      ↓
去中心化AI通过代币激励（Bittensor子网）和众筹（Bankr、Virtuals）调动全球力量
      ↓
去中心化AI在安全审计、防钓鱼、深度伪造检测等领域创造结构性不对称机会
```

### 关键引述

> The AI Commodity TAM continues to rapidly grow BUT the value are mostly accruing in private markets (to frontier labs, to open labs). While public markets like decentralized AI and onchain AI continue to be highly accessible + provide asymmetrical opportunities to back the future of AI.

> A single bug in a core library affect thousands of downstream apps/integrations. Engineers need to test every patch to make sure it doesn't crash existing systems.

> Lots of vulnerabilities happen on open-source libraries which are usually maintained by open-source devs, hobbyists, most are volunteers or underpaid.

# Pi自举构建

> [!abstract]- AI 摘要
> Pi项目用AI Agent自举开发，却遭遇LLM生成的Issue和PR质量低下、代码过度工程化等"Slop问题"，揭示AI时代开源维护的核心矛盾——代码量暴增但审查能力未变。

---

## 扫读

> [!tip] 💡 一句话
> 用AI Agent写代码大幅提高了产量，但也产生了大量低质量的Issue、PR和过度工程化的代码，而人类维护者的审查带宽并未同步增长。

> [!important] 📌 关键结论
> - 外部Issue中大量为LLM辅助生成，内容充满错误诊断，AI Agent不将Issue视作"传闻"而是当作"证据"，导致错误连锁放大
> - LLM倾向于对局部错误做全面防御而非修复根因，产生"Slop生Slop"的恶性循环：包容性读取→降级方案→迁移脚本→大量复杂度
> - 90天内外部Issue/PR共3145个，仅8%的自动关闭PR最终被合并，GitHub基础设施无法应对AI时代的开源流量

> [!quote] 🎬 可行动项
> - 要求Issue报告遵循简洁格式：真实执行的命令→预期行为→实际行为→确切错误/日志
> - 设立"全局不变量"作为代码审查的核心防线，拒绝Agent的局部补丁式方案
> - 使用Agent并行复现Issue（如Pi的`/is`命令），但保持审查步骤串行由人类把关

---

## 精读

### 论证链

```
AI Agent被用于开发Pi自身（自举构建），Issue同时作为人类和维护者之间的消息+Agent的prompt输入
      ↓
问题1：人类提交Issue前用LLM重写，LLM添加大量自信但错误的根因分析，错误被Pi Agent当作证据采纳
      ↓
问题2：LLM对局部错误过度工程化——添加包容读取、回退、迁移、测试，破坏全局不变量
      ↓
问题3：外部Issue/PR数量暴增（90天3145个），大部分为AI生成的"slop"，Auto-Close机制下仅8%PR被合并
      ↓
核心矛盾：AI增加了代码量和项目数量，但未增加需要软件的用户数、也未增加能审查的维护者数量
```

### 关键引述

> That means the shape of the issue matters in a new way. A bad issue was always annoying, but at least a lot of issues were vague. Now we are also dealing with a class of issues that are 5% human and 95% clanker-generated and largely inaccurate shit.

> Almost always, the correct fix is not to handle the bad state, but to make the bad state impossible. This matters a lot for persisted data such as Pi session logs.

> Keep in mind that AI has not increased the number of people who need software, or the number of maintainers who can review it. It has mostly increased the amount of code and the number of projects competing for attention.

> We need stronger foundations, not weaker ones. Open Source needs more collaboration, not more isolated work with a machine.

### 局限与盲区

- 本文未覆盖：如何用自动化手段过滤AI生成的低质量Issue（如分类器）；Pi的auto-close策略是否导致优质贡献者流失
- 隐含假设：所有LLM生成的代码都趋向膨胀——但不同模型（Claude vs GPT vs Gemini）的"过度工程化"倾向不同；issue质量主要取决于提交者的prompt水平而非LLM本身
- 可能的反例：某些项目（如Bun、OpenClaw）已实现"全自动软件工程"，说明Slop问题可能随模型能力提升而缓解；部分高质量AI生成的PR确实被合并

# AI辅助设计方法

> [!abstract]- AI 摘要
> 用AI做产品设计有严格的八阶段工作流：从Brief编写到落地页，核心理念是"功能先于形式"——每个阶段产出markdown文件作为下一阶段的不可变输入。

---

## 扫读

> [!tip] 💡 一句话
> AI辅助设计的正确顺序是Brief→设计词汇→流程→PRD→视觉设计→架构→编码→落地页，每个阶段产出一个markdown文件作为下游的"合同"。

> [!important] 📌 关键结论
> - 设计流程在像素之前：在画任何视觉之前，先定义Brief（为谁、做什么、什么感觉）、提取设计词汇、画出用户流程
> - 设计系统必须活在代码仓库里（markdown文件），而非Figma或Notion中，否则一定会漂移
> - 使用两个Agent分工：Cursor负责构建，Codex负责独立审查，两个Agent的思维模式不同（"想发布"vs"想找bug"），分工显著降低bug率

> [!quote] 🎬 可行动项
> - 建立个人的"设计词汇库"（design-library.md），每发现一种喜欢的审美风格就提取并归档
> - 在项目中创建`principles.md`文件，写下≤3条可在争论中捍卫的设计原则
> - 让模型产出三个不同方向的设计方案而非一个，再手动合成最佳组合

---

## 精读

### 论证链

```
核心原则：设计流程先于像素（Jobs名言：Design is how it works）
      ↓
Phase 1-2：编写Brief（5个问题定义具体用户和单一任务），用非知名参考网站提取设计词汇（避免模型输出"Notion-like"等泛化词）
      ↓
Phase 3：设计用户流程而非屏幕——命名每个流程，发现开放问题（模型没理解的部分），流程决定UI架构
      ↓
Phase 4-5：生成PRD作为"合同"（功能+数据类型+状态变体+明确排除项），产出style.md（颜色/字体/网格/组件/状态）
      ↓
Phase 6-7：先设计架构（状态层、持久化hook、CSS变量主题）再编码，Cursor构建+Codex审查的双Agent模式
      ↓
Phase 8：落地页是独立产品，用同样的工作流但更小的scope
      ↓
核心洞见：模型会给你一千个合理选项，选择哪个是你的判断——工具把其他成本压缩到零，但品味的成本无法压缩
```

### 关键引述

> The pixel is the last thing you decide. Before the pixel is the screen. Before the screen is the state. Before the state is the action. Before the action is the person, and what they were trying to do when they arrived.

> The design system lives in the repo. Not in Figma. Not in a Notion page. In a markdown file checked in next to the code, edited in the same pull requests, committed in the same history.

> Building and reviewing are different mindsets. The building agent wants to ship. The reviewing agent wants to find faults. Put one model in both seats and "ship" usually wins.

> Taste, in the end, is refusing to ship the median. The tools collapsed every other cost. They cannot collapse that one.

### 局限与盲区

- 本文未覆盖：8阶段工作流对非技术背景的纯设计师是否适用（Moonchild需要Cursor配合）；团队协作场景下多个设计师如何共享design-library.md
- 隐含假设：Moonchild能够正确解析所有参考网站并提取一致的词汇；用户有足够的设计判断力在"三个方向"中做出选择
- 可能的反例：对于快速原型验证，完整8阶段流程过于重；某些产品的最佳设计来自直觉而非系统化流程；Figma仍然在团队协作场景有不可替代的实时多人编辑能力

---

# AI公司转型

> [!abstract]- AI 摘要
> 真正的AI转型不是购买SaaS工具，而是从底层重新设计运营——将工作分为确定性自动化、AI判断和人类决策三层，并通过人机回环反馈让Agent持续自我改进。

---

## 扫读

> [!tip] 💡 一句话
> 企业AI转型的关键不是买更多AI工具，而是像亨利·福特用电动机重构工厂那样，围绕AI重新设计端到端运营流程。

> [!important] 📌 关键结论
> - 单纯替换SaaS为AI工具不会产生实质价值——历史上工厂用电机替换蒸汽机但维持原有布局，30年未见效率提升，直到福特重新设计产线
> - 正确的工作流选择有四要素：高频发生、重复性决策、跨系统上下文依赖、可量化的痛点
> - Data分层（系统记录/业务规则/原始输入/反馈记忆）是实现"运营人员无需工程师即可更新规则"的关键架构决策

> [!quote] 🎬 可行动项
> - 花费数周与各团队（应付账款、采购、销售、运营）一起绘制端到端工作流，计算每个流AI化的ROI
> - 建立Agent的"人类在环"反馈系统：训练期→影子模式→受监督生产的渐进式部署
> - 避免强制迁移现有系统（Salesforce/NetSuite），在已有系统之上通过API或Computer-Use Agent构建

---

## 精读

### 论证链

```
历史教训：工厂用电动机替代蒸汽机但维持旧布局→30年无效率提升→福特重构产线（装配线）才释放价值
      ↓
当今类比：企业替换SaaS为AI工具但维持旧流程→同样不会产生实质价值
      ↓
正确方法：端到端绘制每个工作流→评估AI适配度→三分法（确定性自动化/AI判断/人类决策）
      ↓
工作流选择四标准：高频发生、重复决策模式、跨系统上下文依赖、可量化痛点
      ↓
部署节奏：Agent沙箱→影子模式→受监督生产→自主运行，同步建立人机回环反馈
      ↓
数据分层架构：系统记录/业务规则/原始输入/Agent记忆，分层独立维护，运营人员可直接更新规则
      ↓
结果：例中销售转型年化$25M价值（利润率扩张=收入增长+成本节省），准确率几周内提升10%
```

### 关键引述

> You will not transform your company without rebuilding operations from the ground up.

> If the AI does not understand the underlying process, it will not create meaningful value. And if the people who own that process are not brought along, adoption will be weak even if the technology works.

> A transformation is about redesigning each workflow so deterministic work is automated, judgment work is handled by AI where appropriate, and high-risk, high-judgment decisions remain with humans.

> Make sure to build human-in-the-loop feedback into the system from the start. During training and shadow mode, humans can approve, reject, or correct an agent's actions.

### 局限与盲区

- 本文未覆盖：中小企业（收入<$100M）的AI转型是否需要同样的方法论，还是可以更轻量；转型过程中的裁员和员工抵触管理
- 隐含假设：现有系统有API或支持Computer-Use接入——大量传统行业（制造业、物流）的系统可能没有；企业有足够的内部数据质量和流程文档沉淀
- 可能的反例：一些AI工具（如GitHub Copilot）确实可以在不重构流程的情况下产生立竿见影的效率提升；完全基于Agent的运营在高度监管行业（金融合规、医疗）可能面临法律障碍

# 提示工程师到全栈AI

> [!abstract]- AI 摘要
> 从"提示工程师"升级为"全栈AI工程师"的核心转变：从关注"对模型说什么"到设计"模型需要知道什么、能做什么、如何验证、如何安全运行"的完整系统。

---

## 扫读

> [!tip] 💡 一句话
> 全栈AI工程师不再问"用什么prompt"，而是问"这个系统的目的层、上下文层、输出层、检索层、工具层、护栏层、评估层、日志层分别是什么"。

> [!important] 📌 关键结论
> - 提示工程未死，但"只靠提示"的思维已死——prompt仍是人机接口，但必须与上下文工程、工具调用、护栏等层协同
> - 11层AI工程栈：目的层→提示层→上下文层→输出层→检索层→工具层→Workflow/Agent层→评估层→护栏层→日志层→改进层
> - 区分Workflow（步骤可预测、风险低、可靠优先）与Agent（步骤需动态发现、开放式搜索、须安全护栏）是核心架构决策

> [!quote] 🎬 可行动项
> - 建立个人的AI工程模板库（目的层/提示层/上下文层/输出层/检索层/工具层/护栏层），每次新任务直接套用
> - 为每个重要AI系统定义自动失败条件（发明事实、忽略格式、执行禁止操作、无证据的高置信度）
> - 区分手头任务属于Workflow还是Agent场景，不可默认选择Agent

---

## 精读

### 论证链

```
层次1（基础提示技能）：Specificity（具体性）→Roles（角色定义）→Examples（示例）→Reasoning（推理控制）→Output Control（输出格式）→Iteration（迭代）→Constraints（约束）
      ↓
层次2（上下文工程）：从"对模型说什么"转向"模型需要知道什么"，包含目标/受众/项目背景/源材料/偏好/约束/历史决策/已知失败模式
      ↓
层次3（外部能力）：检索（RAG/搜索/文件）→工具调用（Function Calling）→MCP协议连接外部系统
      ↓
层次4（系统架构）：Workflow vs Agent 决策→评估体系（评分标准/自动失败条件/回归测试）→护栏（允许/需批准/禁止三层权限）→Image & Multimodal Prompting
      ↓
层次5（完整AI工程栈）：定义目的层→提示层→上下文层→输出层→检索层→工具层→架构层→评估层→护栏层→日志层→改进层，每层有可复用模板
      ↓
核心转变：从一次性prompt心态→可重复、可评估、可改进的AI系统心态
```

### 关键引述

> Stop thinking "what prompt should I use now?" Start thinking "what can I do to make this output reliable every week?"

> Prompting asks: What should I say to the model? Context engineering asks: What does the model need to know to do the job well?

> Do not build an agent by default. An agent is not automatically better than a workflow. A workflow is better when the path is predictable. An agent is better when the path must be discovered dynamically.

> Guardrails are not there to make the system polite. They are there to make the system controlled.

### 局限与盲区

- 本文未覆盖：11层架构对于简单任务（如"帮我写封邮件"）是否过度工程化；不同层面的维护成本和迭代频率差异
- 隐含假设：用户有时间和意愿为每个AI系统建立完整的11层架构——实际上大多数使用场景仍是对话式即兴交互
- 可能的反例：许多高效用户仅用精心设计的CLAUDE.md和Skill就能达到类似效果，无需完全搭建11层架构；过度结构化的prompt可能限制模型发挥其推理能力；Karpathy本人的方法（Claude+文件上下文）相对简单但极有效

# 编排税

> [!abstract]- AI 摘要
> 启动更多AI Agent很容易，但你的认知带宽无法并行化——所有判断和代码合并仍需经过你这一单一串行处理器。编排税就是忘记这一点而付出的代价，唯一解法是把注意力当作稀缺并发资源来架构。

---

## 扫读

> [!tip] 💡 一句话
> 你可以启动20个Agent，但审查和合并它们的输出仍由一个串行处理器（你的大脑）完成——编排税是Agent生产效率与人类审查吞吐量之间的结构性差距。

> [!important] 📌 关键结论
> - 人类的判断力是Agent开发系统中的"单线程资源"——Python有GIL，你是你Agent的GIL，所有需要真正理解的决策必须排队经过你
> - Amdahl定律直接适用：并行加速的上限由串行部分占比决定，Agent越多只会加深瓶颈队列，不会提升总吞吐量
> - 上下文切换的真实成本：5个Agent不是1倍工作量做5次，而是5次冷启动认知重载+持续的后台焦虑，导致"认知投降"（直接接受Agent代码不再审查）

> [!quote] 🎬 可行动项
> - Agent数量上限=你能认真Code Review的数量（对大多数人是个位数字），不要让UI支持的数量误导你
> - 将任务分为两类："可后台异步的孤立工作"和"判断本身就是工作的复杂任务"，后者不可并行化
> - 批量审查：让Agent工作堆积一点后一次性处理4个审查，避免反复冷启动认知重载
> - 保护串行时间：有时最高杠杆的做法是关闭所有Agent，专注思考一个问题

---

## 精读

### 论证链

```
现象：启动Agent极便宜（一次按键），但收尾极贵（有人必须检查结果、协调冲突）
      ↓
类比：Python的GIL——可开任意多线程但只有一个能执行字节码，你是Agent系统的GIL
      ↓
理论：Amdahl定律——并行加速上限=1/串行占比，你的判断力就是串行部分
      ↓
后果1：增加Agent数量优化了非瓶颈部分（代码生产），瓶颈（审查）不变，队列越来越深
      ↓
后果2：CPU在微秒级做上下文切换仍需优化，人脑在分钟级切换的成本更高——5个Agent=5次冷加载认知
      ↓
后果3：不放慢导致"认知投降"——接受Agent代码因为形成自己的判断太耗费注意力
      ↓
解法：把注意力当作稀缺串行资源来架构——Agent数量匹配审查速率、分离任务类型、批量审查、保护深度工作时间
```

### 关键引述

> Feeling busy is definitely not the same as being productive. You can run 20 agents and feel completely busy. But that's not 20 agents worth of shipped work.

> You are the GIL of your AI agents. They all can run at once. But when any of their work needs genuine understanding of the architecture or resolving merge conflicts, that work has to acquire the lock. There is one lock. You hold it.

> Optimizing the non bottleneck part doesn't increase throughput. You just grow the pile of unfinished work sitting in front of the bottleneck. Adding agents optimize the part that was never the constraint.

> Spawning agents is not the skill. Anyone can run 20. The real skill is designing the system around the one serial resource that cannot be cloned or parallelized. That resource is your attention.

### 局限与盲区

- 本文未覆盖：多个工程师协作时如何分配编排负载（团队级别的编排架构）；Agent本身能力提升后是否能降低认知负载（更精准的输出减少审查成本）
- 隐含假设：所有Agent的输出都需要同等深度的审查——实际上不同类型任务的审查深度可分级（高风险vs低风险）
- 可能的反例：某些自动化测试/CI流水线可以在无人审查下通过，减少人工审查负担；Agent间相互审查（如Cursor+Codex双Agent模式）可以降低单人编排税

1	# 知识管线工作流规范
2	
3	## 系统架构
4	
5	```
6	raw/ ──(AI处理)──▶ WIKI/ ──(Belongs to)──▶ project.md ──▶ Projects.base
7	                      │                            │
8	                      │ tags: [子分类]              └──▶ 项目.base (统计视图)
9	                      │
10	                      └── 可属于多个项目
11	```
12	
13	## 目录职责
14	
15	| 目录 | 职责 | 谁维护 |
16	|------|------|--------|
17	| `Library/raw/` | 原始素材，用户放入 | 用户 |
18	| `Library/assets/` | 图片、附件 | AI |
19	| `Library/temples/` | 全库模板 | 人工定义，AI 遵守 |
20	| `Library/projects/` | 项目主页 `.md` | AI 创建，按模板 |
21	| `Library/bases/` | 项目专属 `.base` | AI 创建 |
22	| `WIKI/` | AI 整理的结构化知识 | AI |
23	| `Type/` | 全局统计视图（五类 `.base`） | AI 维护 |
24	
25	## 命名规范
26	
27	| 类型 | 规范 | 示例 |
28	|------|------|------|
29	| raw | 用户随意 | `某篇文章.md` |
30	| WIKI | 缩减长度，突出核心主题 | `18个月信任红利窗口.md` |
31	| project | 一级领域词，简洁 | `个人成长.md` |
32	| .base | 与项目同名 | `个人成长.base` |
33	
34	## 模板
35	
36	模板文件位于 `Library/temples/`，Agent 生成文件时必须严格遵循对应模板的 frontmatter 和结构。
37	
38	### type-project.md — 项目模板
39	
40	```yaml
41	Belongs to: "[[Projects.base]]"
42	aliases: []
43	tags: []
44	created: {{date}}
45	status: active
46	wikis: []
47	```
48	
49	必含 `![[{{title}}.base]]` 嵌入，关联统计视图。
50	
51	### WIKI.md — 知识条目模板
52	
53	**Frontmatter 字段：**
54	
55	| 字段 | 说明 |
56	|------|------|
57	| `Belongs to` | 所属项目，多项目用 YAML 数组 `["[[项目A]]", "[[项目B]]"]` |
58	| `aliases` | 中文别名，方便多关键词检索 |
59	| `tags` | 项目下的子话题标签 |
60	| `created` | 生成日期 YYYY-MM-DD |
61	| `source` | 固定为 `ai-generated` |
62	| `source_url` | raw 原文来源链接 |
63	| `concepts` | **3-8 个**核心概念词，用于 AI 跨项目语义检索。必须是本文独立讨论的概念，不是泛化描述 |
64	| `confidence` | AI 自评可信度：`high`（事实/一手资料）、`medium`（有逻辑支撑的观点）、`low`（推测/预测） |
65	
66	**正文三区结构：**
67	
68	| 区域 | Callout | 内容 | 目的 |
69	|------|---------|------|------|
70	| **扫读区** | `[!tip] 💡` | 一句话核心主张 | 5 秒判断是否值得读 |
71	| | `[!important] 📌` | ≤3 条关键结论 | |
72	| | `[!quote] 🎬` | 可行动项 | |
73	| **精读区** | 论证链 | 观点 → 论据 → 案例 | 深入理解 |
74	| | 关键引述 | 原文最有价值的段落 | |
75	| | 局限与盲区 | 未覆盖方面、隐含假设、反例 | 批判视角，**不允许留空** |
76	| **关联区** | `[[条目]]` | 相关 WIKI / 项目链接 | 知识网状连接 |
77	
78	## .base 文件格式
79	
80	Obsidian 原生数据库格式，YAML 结构：
81	
82	```yaml
83	views:
84	  - type: list|cards|table
85	    name: 视图名称
86	    filters:
87	      and:
88	        - 过滤条件
89	    groupBy:
90	      property: 分组字段
91	      direction: ASC|DESC
92	    order:
93	      - 排序字段
94	```
95	
96	常用过滤条件：
97	- `file.ext == "md"` — 文件类型
98	- `file.hasLink("目标")` — 包含指向目标的链接
99	- `file.folder == "目录名"` — 所在目录
100	- `!file.ext.containsAny("md", "canvas")` — 排除特定类型
101	
102	### 项目 .base 模板
103	
104	```yaml
105	views:
106	  - type: list
107	    name: WIKI 条目
108	    filters:
109	      and:
110	        - file.hasLink("项目名")
111	```
112	
113	## 工作流步骤
114	
115	### Step 1: 扫描 raw 目录
116	
117	检测 `Library/raw/` 下未处理的新文件。
118	
119	### Step 2: 分析内容，确定归属项目
120	
121	对每篇 raw：
122	
123	1. 提取主题关键词
124	2. 检查已有项目（通过 `Type/Projects.base` 的视图或扫描项目 `.md` 文件）
125	3. 匹配规则：
126	   - 能匹配到已有项目 → 直接归属
127	   - 无法匹配 → 用 `type-project.md` 模板创建新项目
128	   - 内容跨领域 → 可归属到多个项目（生成多篇 WIKI 或使用标签）
129	
130	### Step 3: 创建/匹配项目（如需）
131	
132	在 `Library/projects/` 下使用模板 `Library/temples/type-project.md` 创建项目文件，同时在 `Library/bases/` 下创建同名 `.base` 文件。
133	
134	### Step 4: 生成 WIKI 条目
135	
136	使用模板 `Library/temples/WIKI.md`，严格遵循三区结构。
137	
138	**特别注意：**
139	- `concepts` 必须是 3-8 个本文独立讨论的核心概念，不是泛化描述
140	- `confidence` 根据来源性质如实标注
141	- 局限与盲区**不允许留空或写"无"**，必须识别原文未覆盖的方面、隐含假设、可能的反例
142	
143	### Step 5: 处理图片
144	
145	1. 检测 raw 内容中的外部图片链接
146	2. 下载到 `Library/assets/`
147	3. WIKI 中使用 `![[图片名]]` 引用
148	4. **在响应末尾提议下载**，让用户确认是否保留
149	
150	### Step 6: 更新项目 wikis
151	
152	在项目 `.md` 的 `wikis: []` 中添加新生成的 WIKI 条目文件名。
153	
154	### Step 7: 标记 raw 文件
155	
156	在 raw 文件顶部添加 frontmatter 标记处理状态：
157	
158	```yaml
159	---
160	status: processed
161	wiki: "[[WIKI/对应条目]]"
162	---
163	```
164	
165	`status: processed` 防止 AI 重复处理，`wiki` 建立 raw → WIKI 双向链接。
166	
167	### Step 8: 汇报
168	
169	完成后向用户汇报：
170	- 创建/更新了哪些文件
171	- 归属了哪个项目
172	- 标签分类
173	- 待处理的图片下载请求
174	
175	## 用户交互
176	
177	- **自动化**: 分析、归类、生成、链接维护
178	- **确认点**: 新建项目时告知用户归类决定
179	- **提议点**: 图片下载在末尾提议
180	- **用户只需**: 往 `raw/` 丢素材，确认归类
181	
182	## 快速检查清单
183	
184	生成 WIKI 条目后逐项验证：
185	
186	- [ ] frontmatter 字段完整（Belongs to / aliases / tags / created / source / source_url / concepts / confidence）
187	- [ ] `concepts` 为 3-8 个核心概念词，非泛化描述
188	- [ ] `confidence` 已根据来源性质如实标注（high / medium / low）
189	- [ ] 扫读区包含 💡 一句话 + 📌 关键结论 + 🎬 可行动项
190	- [ ] 精读区包含论证链 + 关键引述 + 局限与盲区
191	- [ ] 局限与盲区不为空，至少覆盖「未覆盖方面」「隐含假设」两项
192	- [ ] 关联区有实际链接，非空
193	- [ ] 项目 `.md` 的 `wikis` 已更新
194	- [ ] 图片已下载到 `Library/assets/` 并在 WIKI 中用 `![[图片名]]` 引用
195	- [ ] 新建项目时同步创建了同名 `.base` 文件
